Pepsin's proenzyme, pepsinogen, is released by the chief cells in the stomach wall, and upon mixing with the hydrochloric acid of the gastric juice, pepsinogen activates to become pepsin.

nodes.name: Peptidase family A1
nodes.description: Aspartic proteases are a catalytic type of protease enzymes that use an activated water molecule bound to one or more aspartate residues for catalysis of their peptide substrates. In general, they have two highly conserved aspartates in the active site and are optimally active at acidic pH. Nearly all known aspartyl proteases are inhibited by pepstatin.Aspartic endopeptidases EC 3.4.23. of vertebrate, fungal and retroviral origin have been characterised. More recently, aspartic endopeptidases associated with the processing of bacterial type 4 prepilin and archaean preflagellin have been described.Eukaryotic aspartic proteases include pepsins, cathepsins, and renins. They have a two-domain structure, arising from ancestral duplication. Retroviral and retrotransposon proteases (retroviral aspartyl proteases) are much smaller and appear to  be homologous to a single domain of the eukaryotic aspartyl proteases. Each domain contributes a catalytic Asp residue, with an extended active site cleft localized between the two lobes of the molecule. One lobe has probably evolved from the other through a gene duplication event in the distant past. In modern-day enzymes, although the three-dimensional structures are very similar, the amino acid sequences are more divergent, except for the catalytic site motif, which is very conserved. The presence and position of disulfide bridges are other conserved features of aspartic peptidases.

nodes.name: NRZ tethering complex
nodes.description: The yeast Dsl1 complex, which comprises Dsl1, Tip20, and Sec39/Dsl3, has been shown to participate, as a vesicle-tethering complex, in retrograde trafficking from the Golgi apparatus to the endoplasmic reticulum. Its metazoan counterpart NRZ complex, which comprises NAG, RINT1, and ZW10, is also involved in Golgi-to-ER retrograde transport, but each component of the complex has diverse cellular functions including endosome-to-Golgi transport, cytokinesis, cell cycle checkpoint, autophagy, and mRNA decay.

nodes.name: RZZ complex
nodes.description: The spindle assembly checkpoint (SAC) ensures proper chromosome segregation by delaying anaphase onset in response to unattached kinetochores. Checkpoint signalling requires the kinetochore localization of the Mad1-Mad2 complex that in more complex eukaryotes depends on the Rod-Zwilch-ZW10 (RZZ) complex.

nodes.name: H1 histones
nodes.description: Histone H1 is one of the five main histone protein families which are components of chromatin in eukaryotic cells. Though highly conserved, it is nevertheless the most variable histone in sequence across species.

nodes.name: H2A histones
nodes.description: Histone H2A is one of the five main histone proteins involved in the structure of chromatin in eukaryotic cells.

nodes.name: H2B histones
nodes.description: Histone H2B is one of the 4 main histone proteins involved in the structure of chromatin in eukaryotic cells. Featuring a main globular domain and long N-terminal and C-terminal tails, H2B is involved with the structure of the nucleosomes.

nodes.name: H3 histones
nodes.description: Histone H3 is one of the five main histone proteins involved in the structure of chromatin in eukaryotic cells. Featuring a main globular domain and a long N-terminal tail, H3 is involved with the structure of the nucleosomes of the 'beads on a string' structure. Histone proteins are highly post-translationally modified however Histone H3 is the most extensively modified of the five histones. The term 'Histone H3' alone is purposely ambiguous in that it does not distinguish between sequence variants or modification state. Histone H3 is an important protein in the emerging field of epigenetics, where its sequence variants and variable modification states are thought to play a role in the dynamic and long term regulation of genes.

nodes.name: H4 histones
nodes.description: Histone H4 is one of the five main histone proteins involved in the structure of chromatin in eukaryotic cells. Featuring a main globular domain and a long N-terminal tail, H4 is involved with the structure of the nucleosome of the 'beads on a string' organization. Histone proteins are highly post-translationally modified. Covalently bonded modifications include acetylation and methylation of the N-terminal tails. These modifications may alter expression of genes located on DNA associated with its parent histone octamer. Histone H4 is an important protein in the structure and function of chromatin, where its sequence variants and variable modification states are thought to play a role in the dynamic and long term regulation of genes.

nodes.name: CCM adhesion complex
nodes.description: The three CCM proteins can exist in a trimeric complex, and each of these essential multi-domain adaptor proteins also interacts with a range of signaling, cytoskeletal and adaptor proteins, presumably accounting for their roles in a range of basic cellular processes including cell adhesion, migration, polarity and apoptosis.

nodes.name: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins
nodes.description: Heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoproteins (hnRNPs) are complexes of RNA and protein present in the cell nucleus during gene transcription and subsequent post-transcriptional modification of the newly synthesized RNA (pre-mRNA). The presence of the proteins bound to a pre-mRNA molecule serves as a signal that the pre-mRNA is not yet fully processed and therefore not ready for export to the cytoplasm. Since most mature RNA is exported from the nucleus relatively quickly, most RNA-binding protein in the nucleus exist as heterogeneous ribonucleoprotein particles. After splicing has occurred, the proteins remain bound to spliced introns and target them for degradation.  hnRNPs are also integral to the 40s subunit of the ribosome and therefore important for the translation of mRNA in the cytoplasm. However, hnRNPs also have their own nuclear localization sequences (NLS) and are therefore found mainly in the nucleus. Though it is known that a few hnRNPs shuttle between the cytoplasm and nucleus, immunofluorescence microscopy with hnRNP-specific antibodies shows nucleoplasmic localization of these proteins with little staining in the nucleolus or cytoplasm. This is likely because of its major role in binding to newly transcribed RNAs. High-resolution immunoelectron microscopy has shown that hnRNPs localize predominantly to the border regions of chromatin, where it has access to these nascent RNAs.The proteins involved in the hnRNP complexes are collectively known as heterogeneous ribonucleoproteins. They include protein K and polypyrimidine tract-binding protein (PTB), which is regulated by phosphorylation catalyzed by protein kinase A and is responsible for suppressing RNA splicing at a particular exon by blocking access of the spliceosome to the polypyrimidine tract. hnRNPs are also responsible for strengthening and inhibiting splice sites by making such sites more or less accessible to the spliceosome. Cooperative interactions between attached hnRNPs may encourage certain splicing combinations while inhibiting others.

nodes.name: Rho guanine nucleotide exchange factors
nodes.description: Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) are proteins or protein domains that activate monomeric GTPases by stimulating the release of guanosine diphosphate (GDP) to allow binding of guanosine triphosphate (GTP). A variety of unrelated structural domains have been shown to exhibit guanine nucleotide exchange activity. Some GEFs can activate multiple GTPases while others are specific to a single GTPase.

nodes.name: HECT domain E3 ubiquitin protein ligases
SUN family
nodes.description: SUN proteins are type-II transmembrane proteins with nuclear-oriented N-termini and lumenal C-termini. Named for SUN domain family members (Sad1p, Unc-84) they all share a conserved SUN domain at the C-terminus of the lumenal domain. This lumenal region of SUN proteins also includes an extended coiled-coil domain. The nucleoplasmic domain of SUN proteins is structurally less characterized, but at least in some mammalian family members, has been shown to be capable of nuclear localization independent of the rest of the protein.

nodes.name: IFT-A complex
nodes.description: Intraflagellar transport (IFT)-A and -B complexes mediate retrograde and anterograde ciliary protein trafficking, respectively. The IFT-A complex is divided into a core subcomplex, composed of IFT122/IFT140/IFT144, which is associated with TULP3, and a peripheral subcomplex, composed of IFT43/IFT121/IFT139, where IFT139 is most distally located.

nodes.name: IFT-B complex
nodes.description: IFT52 is a key component of the IFT-B complex and ensures the interaction of the two subcomplexes, IFT-B1 and IFT-B2.

nodes.name: IFT-B1 complex
nodes.description: The IFT-B1 complex consists of 9-10 stably associated core subunits.

nodes.name: IFT-B2 complex
nodes.description: Thought to be peripheral components of the IFT-B complex, IFT172, 80, 57, 54, and 20 form a stable sub-complex (IFT-B2). IFT-B2 interacts with tubulin/microtubules and connects them to the core IFT-B1 complex through interaction with IFT88/52.

nodes.name: BMP antagonists, cystine knot containing
nodes.description: BMP signal transduction is closely regulated by a set of structurally diverse, extracellularly secreted protein antagonists that bind BMPs with high and specific affinity and disrupt ternary receptor complex formation. Human BMP antagonists do not share significant sequence similarity overall; however, identity increases towards the C terminus, also termed the cystine knot domain [or von Willebrand type C (VWC) domain]. The cystine knot is a defining feature of most BMP antagonists and comprises six cysteine residues: two pairs of disulphide bonds that form a ring and a third cysteine pair that bonds through the ring completing the knot.

nodes.name: Long independently transcribed non-coding RNAs
nodes.description: The HGNC defines long independently transcribed non-coding (LINC) RNAs as long non-coding RNA genes that do not overlap on either strand, or share a bidirectional promoter with, a protein coding gene and do not host either snoRNA or microRNA genes at the time of naming. These lincRNA genes are assigned the root symbol LINC# followed by a unique 5-digit number e.g. LINC00115.

nodes.name: Antisense RNAs
nodes.description: The HGNC defines antisense RNAs as long non-coding RNA genes that are on the opposite strand of the genomic span of a protein coding gene, including the intronic and UTR regions of the opposite protein coding gene. Please note this nomenclature is not intended to suggest that there is a shared function between the protein coding gene and antisense RNA. Antisense lncRNA genes are assigned the format [protein coding gene symbol]-AS + sequential number e.g. ABCA9-AS1 for 'ABCA9 antisense RNA 1'.

nodes.name: Overlapping transcripts
nodes.description: The HGNC defines overlapping transcripts as long non-coding RNA genes that overlap a protein coding gene on the same strand. These lncRNA genes are assigned the format [protein coding gene symbol]-OT + sequential number e.g. ACER2-OT1 for 'ACER2 3' UTR overlapping transcript'.

nodes.name: Intronic transcripts
nodes.description: The HGNC defines intronic transcripts as long non-coding RNA genes that are located within an intron on the SAME strand as a protein coding gene. These lncRNA genes are assigned the format [protein coding gene symbol]-IT + sequential number e.g. AKT2-IT1 for 'AKT2 intronic transcript 1'.

nodes.name: Divergent transcripts
nodes.description: The HGNC defines divergent transcripts as long non-coding RNA genes that are within 300-500 nucleotides of a protein coding gene on the opposite strand. These lncRNA genes are named with the format [protein coding gene symbol]-DT e.g. DHX33-DT for 'DHX33 divergent transcript'.

nodes.name: Long non-coding RNAs with non-systematic symbols
Long non-coding RNAs with FAM root symbol
nodes.description: Homologous long non-coding RNA genes may be named together using the root symbol FAM# for 'family with sequence similarity'. Note that this root symbol is also used for protein coding families - this gene groups shows only the non-coding genes named with the FAM# root.

nodes.name: minichromosome maintenance 2-7 complex
nodes.description: The eukaryotic minichromosome maintenance 2-7 complex is the core of the inactive MCM replication licensing complex and the catalytic core of the Cdc45-MCM-GINS replicative helicase.

nodes.name: CMG helicase complex
nodes.description: The CMG (Cdc45-MCM-GINS) complex is the eukaryotic replicative helicase, the enzyme that unwinds double-stranded DNA at replication forks.

nodes.name: Linker of nucleoskeleton and cytoskeleton complex subunits
nodes.description: The LINC complex (Linker of Nucleoskeleton and Cytoskeleton) is a protein complex associated with both inner and outer membranes of the nucleus. It is composed of SUN-domain proteins and KASH-domain proteins. The SUN-domain proteins are associated with both nuclear lamins and chromatin and cross the inner nuclear membrane. They interact with the KASH domain proteins in the perinuclear (lumen) space between the two membranes. The KASH domain proteins cross the outer nuclear membrane and interact with actin filaments, microtubule filaments (through dynein and kinesin motors), intermediate filaments (through spectrin), centrosomes and cytoplasmic organelles. The number of SUN-domain and KASH-domain proteins increased in evolution.

nodes.name: KASH domain containing
nodes.description: KASH domains are conserved C-terminal protein regions less than ~30 amino acids. KASH is an acronym for Klarsicht, ANC-1, Syne Homology. KASH domains always follow a transmembrane domain. Most proteins containing KASH domains are thought to be involved in the positioning of the nucleus in the cell. KASH domains interact with proteins containing SUN domains in the space between the outer and inner nuclear membranes to bridge the nuclear envelope, and may transfer force from the nucleoskeleton to the cytoplasmic cytoskeleton and enable mechanosensory roles in cells. KASH proteins are thought to largely localize to the outer nuclear membrane, although there are reports of inner nuclear membrane localization of some KASH protein isoforms.

nodes.name: FHF complex
nodes.description: The FHF complex may function to promote vesicle trafficking and/or fusion via the homotypic vesicular protein sorting complex (the HOPS complex)

nodes.name: Outer dynein arm docking complex subunits
nodes.description: The outer dynein arm-docking complex (ODA-DC), which was first identified in the green alga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii, is a protein complex that mediates the binding of axonemal dynein and doublet microtubules.

nodes.name: IQ motif containing GTPase activating protein family
Dynein 1 complex subunits
nodes.description: Cytoplasmic dynein-1 is a major microtubule-based motor critical for cell division. Dynein is essential for the formation and positioning of the mitotic spindle as well as the transport of various cargos in the cell.

nodes.name: Dynein 2 complex subunits
nodes.description: The motor protein that powers the movement of the particles from the tip of the flagellum to the base (retrograde IFT) is called cytoplasmic dynein 1b in Chlamydomonas and cytoplasmic dynein 2 in vertebrates.

nodes.name: Dyneins, axonemal outer arm complex subunits
Dyneins, axonemal inner arm I1/f complex subunits
Dishevelled binding antagonist of beta catenin family
Piwi like RNA-mediated gene silencing family
U11 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein
nodes.description: A ribonucleoprotein complex that contains small nuclear RNA U11, a heptameric ring of Sm proteins, as well as several proteins that are unique to the U11 snRNP, most of which remain associated with the U11 snRNA both while the U11 snRNP is free or assembled into a series of spliceosomal complexes.

nodes.name: Axonemal radial spoke subunits
nodes.description: The radial spoke is a multi-unit protein structure found in the axonemes of eukaryotic cilia and flagella. Although experiments have determined the importance of the radial spoke in the proper function of these organelles, its structure and mode of action remain poorly understood.

nodes.name: Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase subunits
nodes.description: Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase (MCCC) is a heteromultimeric complex that is composed of two subunits which are encoded by distinct genes.

nodes.name: ATPase F1/V1 alpha/A and beta/B subunit family
nodes.description: The ATP synthase F1 domain and V-ATPase V1 domain alpha/A and beta/B subunits are encoded by homologous genes, shown together here.

nodes.name: TLDc domain containing
nodes.description: The TLDc domain is a highly conserved protein motif present in several mammal proteins that share a protective function against oxidative stress.

nodes.name: SWI/SNF related BAF chromatin remodeling complexes
2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase family
nodes.description: In molecular biology, 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase (2-5A synthetase) is an enzyme (EC 2.7.7.84) that reacts to interferon signal. It is an antiviral enzyme that counteracts viral attack by degrading RNAs, both viral and host. The enzyme uses ATP in 2'-specific nucleotidyl transfer reactions to synthesize 2'-5'-oligoadenylates, which activate latent ribonuclease (RNASEL), resulting in degradation of viral RNA and inhibition of virus replication.The C-terminal half of 2'-5'-oligoadenylate synthetase, also referred to as domain 2 of the enzyme, is largely alpha-helical and homologous to a tandem ubiquitin repeat. It carries the region of enzymatic activity between at the extreme C-terminal end.

nodes.name: Class I HDAC complexes
nodes.description: HDAC1, 2 and 3 form the catalytic subunit of multiprotein complexes to mediate gene transcription although HDAC8 is fully active in isolation. HDAC1 and HDAC2 form the catalytic core of multiple corepressor complexes, including NuRD (nucleosome remodeling and deacetylase), Sin3 (switch intensive 3) CoREST (corepressor of RE1-silencing transcription) and MiDAC (mitotic deacetylase), while HDAC3 forms the key component of the SMRT/NCoR (silencing mediator of retinoic acid and thyroid hormone receptors/nuclear receptor corepressor) complex. As part of these complexes, the HDACs become maximally activated and are targeted to specific regions of chromatin.

nodes.name: MiDAC complex subunits
nodes.description: MiDAC is one of seven distinct, large multi-protein complexes that recruit class I histone deacetylases to the genome to regulate gene expression.

nodes.name: Metallopeptidases
nodes.description: A metalloproteinase, or metalloprotease, is any protease enzyme whose catalytic mechanism involves a metal. An example of this would be ADAM12 which plays a significant role in the fusion of muscle cells during embryo development, in a process known as myogenesis.  Most metalloproteases require zinc, but some use cobalt. The metal ion is coordinated to the protein via three ligands. The ligands coordinating the metal ion can vary with histidine, glutamate, aspartate, lysine, and arginine. The fourth coordination position is taken up by a labile water molecule.  Treatment with chelating agents such as EDTA leads to complete inactivation. EDTA is a metal chelator that removes zinc, which is essential for activity. They are also inhibited by the chelator orthophenanthroline.

nodes.name: Glyoxalase domain containing
nodes.description: VOC members are metalloenzymes highly divergent in sequence and biological functions, but universally share the use of the βαβββ structural motif (also known as the glyoxylase fold) to build a divalent metal-containing active site. VOC enzymes catalyze a range of chemical reactions including isomerization, epimerization, oxidative C-C bond cleavage and nucleophilic substitution

nodes.name: Aminoacyl tRNA synthetase complex interacting multifunctional proteins
Eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2 alpha kinases
Zinc fingers PCLO-type
nodes.description: Piccolo zinc fingers were found to interact with the dual prenylated rab3A and VAMP2/Synaptobrevin II receptor PRA1. There are eight conserved cysteines in Piccolo-type zinc fingers, suggesting that they coordinate two zinc ligands.

nodes.name: MD-2 related lipid recognition domain containing
Protein kinase AMP-activated catalytic subunit alpha family
nodes.description: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a heterotrimeric alpha/beta/gamma subunit complex that functions as a central regulator of energy homeostasis. Alternative isoforms of the catalytic alpha subunit are encoded by PRKAA1 and PRKAA2. The alpha subunits contain a canonical Ser/Thr kinase domain, an autoinhibitory domain (AID), an adenine nucleotide sensor segment termed an alpha-linker, and a beta subunit-interacting C-terminal domain (alpha-CTD), the latter of which contains the ST loop, which harbors proposed phosphorylation sites.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers TRAF-type
nodes.description: This gene group contains genes that encode proteins with a TRAF-type zinc finger domain. Some of the proteins that have this domain are mammalian signal transducers associated with the cytoplasmic domain of the 75kDa tumour necrosis factor receptor. A heterocomplex, homodimer or heterodimer of TRAF1 and TRAF2, binds to the N-terminal of the inhibitor of apoptosis proteins 1 and 2 (IAPS) and recruits them to the tumour necrosis factor receptor 2.

nodes.name: Bridge-like lipid transfer protein family
nodes.description: Bridge-like lipid transporter proteins are key regulators of intraorganellar lipid trafficking. The BLTP proteins form physical bridges that span the gap between a donor and a receiver organelle and are are formed by multiple repeats of one motif: a repeating beta groove (RBG), which forms an extremely long semi-open tube with a hydrophobic interior.

nodes.name: Protein kinase A subunits
nodes.description: In cell biology, protein kinase A (PKA) is a family of enzymes whose activity is dependent on cellular levels of cyclic AMP (cAMP). PKA is also known as cAMP-dependent protein kinase (EC 2.7.11.11). PKA has several functions in the cell, including regulation of glycogen, sugar, and lipid metabolism. It should not be confused with 5'-AMP-activated protein kinase (AMP-activated protein kinase).

nodes.name: Lysophospholipid acyltransferases
nodes.description: Phospholipids can be produced by several metabolic routes, and a key reaction that utilizes lysophospholipids and acyl-CoAs as substrates to produce phospholipids is catalyzed by a class of enzymes called lysophospholipid acyltransferases (LPLATs). Based on their primary structures, these LPLATs are divided into two families, the 1-acylglycerol-3-phosphate O-acyltransferase (AGPAT) and the membrane bound O-acyltransferase (MBOAT) families. These two families also contain non-LPLAT members.

nodes.name: thymocyte selection associated high mobility group box family
SLC51 subunits
nodes.description: The heteromeric organic solute transporter SLC51 (also known as Ost alpha-Ost beta) is the key basolateral plasma membrane bile acid and steroid conjugate carrier in many human tissues, including the small intestine, liver, and other steroidogenic organs. SLC51A (OST-alpha) is a 7-TM domain  subunit, presumed to be the main catalytic subunit of the transporter. SLC51B (Ost-beta) is predicted to contain a single transmembrane (TM) domain, and to be oriented in the plasma membrane with its N terminus in the extracellular space and its C terminus in the cytosol. SLC51B is required for both proper trafficking of SLC51A and formation of the functional transport unit.

nodes.name: Solute carrier family 54, mitochondrial pyruvate carriers
Solute carrier family 55, LETM mitochondrial cation/proton exchangers
Solute carrier family 57, NIPA-like magnesium transporters
Solute carrier family 63, sphingosine phosphate transporters
Solute carrier organic anion transporter family
Lysosomal protein transmembrane family
nodes.description: The Lysosomal protein transmembrane (LAPTM) family represents an important group of multi-pass transmembrane proteins localized to lysosomal or late endosomal membranes. Among them, LAPTM4B and LAPTM5 are the most extensively studied. LAPTM4B contains canonical lysosomal targeting signals and localizes predominantly to late endosomes/lysosomes. Functionally, it regulates lysosomal stability, promotes autophagosome maturation, and enhances cellular adaptation to metabolic stress. In contrast, LAPTM5 is predominantly expressed in hematopoietic and immune cells. It plays a key role in regulating immune and inflammatory responses.

nodes.name: SID1 transmembrane family
nodes.description: SIDT1 and SIDT2 are homologs of the C. elegans systemic RNA interference defective 1 (SID-1) gene. SIDT1 and SIDT2 have a common domain architecture of SID-1 family proteins comprising the extracellular/luminal two beta-sandwich domains (ECD1 and ECD2) and a unique transmembrane domain (TMD) with eleven transmembrane helices. They have been implicated in cholesterol and dsRNA transport.

nodes.name: Gfo/Idh/MocA-like oxidoreductase domain containing
nodes.description: The Gfo/Idh/MocA protein family members have very low sequence identity but the 3D structures of the proteins are very similar, consisting of two main domains: an N-terminal dinucleotide-binding domain containing a typical Rossmann fold3 and a C-terminal α/β-domain participating in substrate binding and oligomerisation. [Note the BLVRA gene included here encodes a protein with the N-terminal, but not C-terminal domain].  Did not group this under oxidoreductases because GFOD1 seems to be a pseudoenzyme that does not bind NAD/NADP. [st20260902].

nodes.name: FERRY complex subunits
nodes.description: The FERRY complex is proposed to function as a Rab5 effector to shuttle mRNA to the cell periphery for local translation.

nodes.name: Fibril associated collagens with interrupted triple helices
Membrane associated collagens with interrupted triple helices
Flavoproteins
nodes.description: Flavoproteins are proteins that contain a nucleic acid derivative of riboflavin. These proteins are involved in a wide array of biological processes, including removal of radicals contributing to oxidative stress, photosynthesis, and DNA repair. The flavoproteins are some of the most-studied families of enzymes.  Flavoproteins have either FMN (flavin mononucleotide) or FAD (flavin adenine dinucleotide) as a prosthetic group or as a cofactor. The flavin is generally tightly bound (as in adrenodoxin reductase, wherein the FAD is buried deeply). About 5-10% of flavoproteins have a covalently linked FAD. Based on the available structural data, FAD-binding sites can be divided into more than 200 different types.90 flavoproteins are encoded in the human genome; about 84% require FAD and around 16% require FMN, whereas 5 proteins require both. Flavoproteins are mainly located in the mitochondria. Of all flavoproteins, 90% perform redox reactions and the other 10% are transferases, lyases, isomerases, ligases.

nodes.name: Kirre like nephrin family adhesion molecules
Small MAF bZIP transcription factor family
Large MAF bZIP transcription factor family
Molybdenum cofactor synthesis proteins
nodes.description: The biosynthesis of Molybdenum cofactor (Moco) is one of the most ancient biological processes found in life. The complex chemical transformations required for this process are strictly conserved throughout all domains of life, comprising three major chemical rearrangements. Each synthesis step is hereby defined by the relatively stable and isolatable reaction product, cyclic pyranopterin monophosphate (cPMP), molybdopterin (MPT) and finally Moco/Wco. Individual reaction steps are catalyzed by single multi-domain or multiple proteins that are highly conserved in their structure and function.   In humans, cPMP is produced via the actions of the mitochondrial proteins MOCS1A and MOCS1B (encoded by MOCS1). Subsequently, cPMP is converted to MPT by a heterotetramer (encoded by MOCS2) consisting of two small MOCS2A subunits and two large MOCS2B subunits in the cytosol. The so-called MPT-synthase complex is regenerated after the reaction, which is facilitated by the MOCS3 protein. Finally, MPT is adenylylated by the G-domain of gephyrin (GPHN) and the Mo is inserted by the E-domain of gephyrin. Mature Moco is either directly incorporated into sulfite oxidase (SUOX) and mitochondrial amidoxime reducing components (MTARC1 and MTARC2) – or Moco is sulfurated by the Moco sulfurase (MOCOS). The latter serves as cofactor for enzymes of the Xanthine dehydrogenase/aldehyde oxidase family (XDH and AOX1).

nodes.name: Basic leucine zipper ATF-like transcription factor family
nodes.description: Basic leucine zipper transcription factor ATF-like (BATF), BATF2 and BATF3 are basic leucine zipper (bZIP) proteins that form heterodimers with JUN proteins.

nodes.name: Canonical Notch ligands
nodes.description: The canonical Notch ligands are members of the Delta/Serrate/Lag-1 (DSL) family of proteins. When they bind to Notch receptors this induces a conformational change (regulated intramembrane proteolysis) in the receptor, freeing its Notch intracellular domain (NICD). The NICD can then translocate to the nucleus and promote gene transcription.

nodes.name: DREAM complex subunits
nodes.description: The dimerization partner, RB-like, E2F and multi-vulval class B (DREAM) complex is a protein complex responsible for the regulation of cell cycle-dependent gene expression. The complex is evolutionarily conserved, although some of its components vary from species to species. In humans, the key proteins in the complex are RBL1 (p107) and RBL2 (p130), both of which are homologs of RB (p105) and bind repressive E2F transcription factors E2F4 and E2F5; DP1, DP2 and DP3, dimerization partners of E2F; and MuvB, which is a complex of LIN9/37/52/54 and RBBP4.

nodes.name: MuvB complex subunits
nodes.description: MuvB complexes are key to regulating the cell-division cycle. The MuvB complex can form part of the transcriptional repressor complex DREAM, or part of the activator complexes MMB and FOXM1-MuvB.  When cells are not actively dividing, the DREAM complex represses G1/S and G2/M genes. The expression of mitotic genes in the G2/M stage of the cell cycle can be regulated by MuvB activator complexes which include either the oncogenic transcription factor B-MYB or FOXM1.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers A20-type
nodes.description: This gene group represents genes encoding proteins with the zinc finger domain found in TNFAIP3, also known as A20. TNFAIP3 is an inhibitor of cell death that inhibits NF-kappaB activation via the tumour necrosis factor receptor associated factor pathway. The zinc finger domains appear to mediate self-association in TNFAIP3. These fingers also mediate IL-1-induced NF-kappa B activation.

nodes.name: RNA binding fox-1 homologs
nodes.description: The RNA-binding Fox-1 homolog (RBFOX) proteins represent an ancient family of splicing factors, conserved through evolution. All members share an RNA recognition motif (RRM), and a particular affinity for the GCAUG signature in target RNA molecules.

nodes.name: ELAV like RNA binding protein family
Proteins encoded by multiple genes
nodes.description: This group lists protein coding genes that encode a protein that is identical to that encoded by another gene or genes. The list was constructed from a set of UniProt accessions that are associated with multiple genes. The list is limited to genes on the current reference assembly and excludes proteins encoded by read-through transcripts. Genes that encode the same protein share root symbols. Note the H3C root is associated with two different proteins - one encoded by a cluster of genes on 6p22.1 and the other by a cluster of three genes on 1q21.2 (H3C13-15).

nodes.name: LAR protein receptor tyrosine phosphatase family
Integrase like retrotransposon derived
nodes.description: All genes in this group contain domains that are homologous to retroviral integrase proteins.

nodes.name: SH3 and cysteine rich domain family
SplA/ryanodine receptor domain and SOCS box containing family
Complexins
nodes.description: Complexin (also known as synaphin) refers to a one of a small set of eukaryotic cytoplasmic neuronal proteins which binds to the SNARE protein complex (SNAREpin) with a high affinity. These are called synaphin 1 and 2. In the presence of Ca2+, the transport vesicle protein synaptotagmin displaces complexin, allowing the SNARE protein complex to bind the transport vesicle to the presynaptic membrane.  Complexin acts as both an inhibitor and a facilitator of synaptic vesicle fusion and neurotransmitter release. In one conformation, it clamps SNAREpin complexes, preventing vesicle fusion, while in a different conformation it releases the SNAREpins, allowing synaptotagmin to trigger fusion.   Whereas complexin is not necessary for synaptic vesicle exocytosis, it does increase neurotransmitter release by 60–70% as demonstrated by complexin gene knockout in mice. A number of human neurological diseases have been linked to a deficiency of complexin.  Synaphin can promote exocytosis by promoting interaction between the complementary syntaxin and synaptobrevin transmembrane regions that reside in opposing membranes prior to fusion.

nodes.name: Reticulons
nodes.description: Reticulons (RTNs in vertebrates and reticulon-like proteins or RNTls in other eukaryotes) are a group of evolutionary conservative proteins residing predominantly in endoplasmic reticulum, primarily playing a role in promoting membrane curvature. In addition, reticulons may play a role in nuclear pore complex formation, vesicle formation, and other processes yet to be defined. They have also been linked to oligodendrocyte roles in inhibition of neurite outgrowth. Some studies link RTNs with Alzheimer's disease and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.All eukaryotes studied so far carry RTN genes in their genomes. The reticulons are absent only in archaea and bacteria. Mammals have four reticulon genes, RTN1, RTN2, RTN3, RTN4. Plants possess a greater number of reticulon isoforms, with 21 having been identified in the commonly used model organism Arabidopsis thaliana.The genes possess a number of exons and introns and are accordingly spliced into many isoforms. C-terminal region of RTNs contains a highly conservative reticulon homology domain (RHD) while other parts of the protein may vary even within a single organism.A peculiar feature of RTN4's isoform RTN4A (Nogo-A) is its ability to inhibit axonal growth. This reticulon subform is curiously absent in fish, a taxon known for the heightened ability of its CNS to regenerate after injury.  Transmembrane 33 (TMEM33) exogenously suppresses reticulon 4C function and therefore may play a role in dictating membrane curvature through inhibition of reticulon function.

nodes.name: Leucine rich repeats and calponin homology domain containing
Angiopoietins
nodes.description: Angiopoietin is part of a family of vascular growth factors that play a role in embryonic and postnatal angiogenesis. Angiopoietin signaling most directly corresponds with angiogenesis, the process by which new arteries and veins form from preexisting blood vessels. Angiogenesis proceeds through sprouting, endothelial cell migration, proliferation, and vessel destabilization and stabilization. They are responsible for assembling and disassembling the endothelial lining of blood vessels. Angiopoietin cytokines are involved with controlling microvascular permeability, vasodilation, and vasoconstriction by signaling smooth muscle cells surrounding vessels. Angiopoietin-1 is critical for vessel maturation, adhesion, migration, and survival. Angiopoietin-2, on the other hand, promotes cell death and disrupts vascularization. Yet, when it is in conjunction with vascular endothelial growth factors, or VEGF, it can promote neo-vascularization.

nodes.name: CERF complex
nodes.description: The CERF complex has intrinsic nucleosome-dependent ATPase activity and remodels chromatin in an ATP-dependent fashion.

nodes.name: ISWI complexes
nodes.description: ISWI complexes contain the product of either SMARCA1 or SMARCA5, co-orthologs of the S. cerevisiae genes ISWI1 and ISWI2, with one or more regulatory subunit(s).

nodes.name: ACF complex
nodes.description: An ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complex, that regulates the even spacing of nucleosomes along the chromatin thus promoting chromatin assembly and the repression of transcription. The BAZ1A subunit can enhance and direct the process provided by the ATPase subunit, SMARCA5, probably through targeting pericentromeric heterochromatin in late S phase. Moves end-positioned nucleosomes to a predominantly central position. The ATPase activity of the complex is regulated by the length of flanking DNA. Also involved in facilitating the DNA replication process.

nodes.name: WICH complex
nodes.description: Chromatin remodeling complex required for maintaining chromatin structure by regulating the spacing of nuclesomes during replication. It is recruited to the replication foci through a direct interaction between the BAZ1B subunit and the DNA clamp PCNA. It opens up chromatin after nucleosome assembly upstream of the replication fork and prevents aberrant heterochromatin formation shortly after DNA replication. The BAZ1B subunit phosphorylates H2A.X Tyr-142 regulating the H2A.X DNA damage response. Particularly important during embryonic and neonatal development, especially for craniofacial features.

nodes.name: NoRC complex
nodes.description: NoRC remodels nucleosomes at the rDNA promoter and recruits histone deacetylases, histone methyltransferase and DNA methyltransferases leading to heterochromatin formation and transcriptional silencing. The interaction of NoRC with the short RNA transcripts is mediated by the TAM domain of BAZ2A and it is required for NoRC binding to chromatin and heterochromatin formation.

nodes.name: RSF complex
nodes.description: A nucleosome remodeling complex that participates in chromatin assembly and facilitates DNA transcription. The RSF1 subunit functions as the histone chaperone through an association with the H3/H4 tetramer and is independent of the histone tails. The histone octamer (composed of H2A, H2B, H3 & H4) is required for the RSF complex to bind DNA. The SMARCA5 subunit provides the energy for the nucleosome spacing activity and is dependent on the histone tails.

nodes.name: ATP-dependent chromatin remodeling complexes
nodes.description: ATP dependent remodeling complexes mobilize nucleosomes along DNA, promote the exchange of histones, or completely displace nucleosomes from DNA. These remodeling complexes are often categorized based on the domain organization of their catalytic subunit.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers U11-48K-like CHHC-type
nodes.description: The CHHC U11-48K-type zinc finger contains four invariant Cys and His residues with a consensus sequence of C-x(5,7)-H-x(7,9)-H-x(3,4)-C. It stochiometrically binds zinc ions in a one-to-one ratio. The structure of the CHHC U11-48K-type zinc finger consists of a β hairpin followed by a helix. the zinc ion is coordinated by Cys and His residues from the β hairpin and by His and Cys residues from the helix, respectively. The helical region has an α-helical conformation that is interrupted in the middle by a single pi-helical turn (PMID:19217400).

nodes.name: Zinc fingers UBZ1 CCHH-type
nodes.description: The ubiquitin-binding zinc finger (UBZ) is a type of zinc-coordinating β-β-α fold domain found mainly in proteins involved in DNA repair and transcriptional regulation. UBZ domains coordinate a zinc ion with cysteine or histidine residues; depending on their amino acid sequence, UBZ domains are classified into several families (PMID: 19213613), PMID: 27062441). Type 1 UBZs are CCHH-type zinc fingers found in tandem UBZ domains of TAX1-binding protein 1 (TAX1BP1).

nodes.name: Zinc fingers UBZ4 CCHC-type
nodes.description: The ubiquitin-binding zinc finger (UBZ) is a type of zinc-coordinating β-β-α fold domain found mainly in proteins involved in DNA repair and transcriptional regulation. Type 4 UBZs are CCHC-type zinc fingers found in Y-family translesion polymerase kappa, Werner helicase-interacting protein 1 (WRNIP1), and Rad18.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers ZNF750 C2HC-type
nodes.description: ZNF750 is a transcription factor that controls epithelial homeostasis by inhibiting progenitor genes while inducing differentiation genes (PMID: 25228645). Proteins containing this domain also include proline-rich protein 35. Its function is not clear.

nodes.name: Arginine methyltransferases
nodes.description: This group is currently identical to the 7BS protein arginine methyltransferases

nodes.name: Nuclear RNase P complex subunits
nodes.description: Ribonuclease P (RNase P) is an important ribonucleoprotein (RNP), responsible for the maturation of the 5' end of precursor tRNAs (pre-tRNAs).

nodes.name: RNase MRP complex subunits
nodes.description: Human RNase MRP is a ribonucleoprotein (RNP) enzyme that processes precursor rRNA (pre-rRNA) at ITS1 site 2 and may have additional activities.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers C2HC NEMO-type
nodes.description: The CCHC [NEMO]-type zinc finger consists of a short antiparallel beta-sheet, where beta1 and beta2 strands are connected by a type IV beta-turn, and an alpha-helix. This BetaBetaAlpha fold is stabilized by tetrahedral coordination to a zinc ion.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers UBZ3 CCHH-type
nodes.description: The UBZ domain adopts a classical C2H2 zinc-finger structure characterized by a β-β-α fold; there are 4 different types of UBZ zinc finger with this group representing the CCHH-type zinc finger found in polymerase eta.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers UBZ2 CCHC-type
nodes.description: The UBZ domain adopts a classical C2H2 zinc-finger structure characterized by a β-β-α fold; there are 4 different types of UBZ zinc finger with this group representing the CCHC-type zinc finger found in FAAP20.

nodes.name: Bromodomain and WD repeat domain containing
Zinc fingers ZC2HC1-type
nodes.description: This zinc finger domain [is] found in a group of proteins mainly from animals, including members of the ZC2HC1 family and bryophyte SOSEKI proteins that locally interpret global polarity cues and can influence cell division orientation to coordinate cell polarisation relative to body axes.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers MYST C2HC-type
nodes.description: This C2HC zinc finger domain is found in the MYST family of histone acetyltransferases.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers Nanos C2HC-type
nodes.description: The structure of the nanos-type zinc finger is composed of two independent zinc-finger (ZF) lobes, the N-terminal ZF1 and the C-terminal ZF2, which are connected by a linker helix. These lobes create a large cleft. Zinc ions in ZF1 and ZF2 are bound to the CCHC motif by tetrahedral coordination.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers FOG C2HC-type
nodes.description: Transcriptional cofactors of the Friend of GATA (FOG) family are diverse in sequence but their individual Znf regions share considerable homology. They contain either eight or nine Znfs that are related to the classical CCHH Znfs (which have a conserved C-X(2,5)-C-X(12)-H-X(2,5)-H sequence). Several of the fingers in each FOG protein, however, have an altered consensus sequence in which the final zinc binding histidine is replaced with a cysteine. It is only these variant CCHC ZbFs that mediate interactions with GATA N-terminal zinc fingers (NFs).  The FOG-type CCHC zinc finger comprises a short β hairpin followed by an α helix. It resembles classical CCHH fingers in structure.

nodes.name: Aurora kinase family
nodes.description: The aurora kinases (AURKs) comprise an evolutionarily conserved family of serine/threonine kinases involved in mitosis and meiosis.

nodes.name: Polo like kinase family
nodes.description: The Polo like kinases are a family of serine/threonine kinases characterized by the presence of an N-terminal protein kinase domain and a C-terminal polo-box domain (PBD) involved in substrate binding and regulation of kinase activity. The truncated protein kinase domain in PLK5 is predicted to be catalytically inactive but the protein retains important functions in neuron biology.

nodes.name: PIM kinase family
nodes.description: The Pim kinases are a family of constitutively active serine/threonine kinases, widely associated with cell survival, proliferation, and migration.

nodes.name: FET protein family
nodes.description: Members of the FET protein family, consisting of FUS, EWSR1, and TAF15, bind to RNA and contribute to the control of transcription, RNA processing, and the cytoplasmic fates of messenger RNAs in metazoa. FET proteins can also bind DNA, which may be important in transcription and DNA damage responses. FET proteins are of medical interest because chromosomal rearrangements of their genes promote various sarcomas and because point mutations in FUS or TAF15 can cause neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and frontotemporal lobar dementia.

nodes.name: Tribbles pseudokinase family
nodes.description: The Tribbles (TRIB) family of serine/threonine pseudokinases function as important signalling mediators and scaffold subunits via the binding and modulation of several signalling molecules, including kinases, phosphatases, transcription factors and components of the ubiquitin–proteasome system.

nodes.name: Unitary pseudogenes
nodes.description: This group represents genes that are named as unitary pseudogenes. Unitary pseudogenes are a type of pseudogene that arises from the loss of function, rather than duplication or retrotransposition. These pseudogenes lack a functioning parent gene in the genome but have functional orthologs.

nodes.name: PEAK pseudokinase family
nodes.description: The PEAK family of pseudokinase scaffolds are important regulators and integrators of cellular signaling and also play oncogenic roles in a variety of human cancers.

nodes.name: NIMA related kinase family
nodes.description: The NIMA family of serine/threonine kinases is a diverse group of protein kinases implicated in a wide variety of cellular processes, including cilia regulation, microtubule dynamics, mitotic processes, cell growth, and DNA damage response.

nodes.name: Glycogen synthase kinase 3 family
nodes.description: The Glycogen synthase kinase 3 family are constitutively active multi-functional serine/threonine kinases that are involved in diverse physiological pathways ranging from metabolism, cell cycle, gene expression, development and oncogenesis to neuroprotection.

nodes.name: Hexokinase family
nodes.description: Hexokinases phosphorylate a variety of hexose sugars, although their preferred substrate is glucose. GCK has a single hexokinase domain while the other family members have two hexokinase domains but only HK2 has been shown to have two active sites.

nodes.name: Carbohydrate kinases
nodes.description: Carbohydrate kinases catalyze the transfer of a phosphate group, usually from ATP, to a carbohydrate substrate molecule.

nodes.name: Caspase-2 PIDDosome complex
nodes.description: Caspase-2-driven apoptosis is elicited in blood cells failing cytokinesis and extra centrosomes are necessary to trigger this cell death. Activation of caspase-2 depends on the PIDDosome multi-protein complex, and priming of PIDD1 at extra centrosomes is necessary for pathway activation

nodes.name: Kinases
nodes.description: Kinases catalyze the transfer of a phosphate group, usually from ATP, to a substrate molecule. Kinases can be divided into groups based on their substrate.

nodes.name: Protein kinase families
nodes.description: Most protein kinases belong to a single superfamily containing a eukaryotic protein kinase (ePK) catalytic domain. Kinases are classified into a hierarchy of groups, families, and subfamilies primarily by sequence comparison of their catalytic domains. A smaller number of atypical protein kinase (aPK) families contain proteins reported to have biochemical kinase activity, but which lack sequence similarity to the ePK domain, and their close homologs.

nodes.name: Serine/threonine protein kinase families
nodes.description: Serine/threonine kinases catalyze the phosphorylation of serine and/or threonine residues in proteins.

nodes.name: Cholinesterase family
nodes.description: Cholinesterases may be classified as acetylcholinesterase (EC 3.1.1.7) and butyrylcholinesterase (EC 3.1.1.8) on the basis of differential specificity for acetylcholine and butyrylcholine hydrolysis. Several inhibitors have also been shown to be selective for one of the two enzymes. AChEs are primarily associated with nerve and muscle, typically with localization at synaptic contacts, while BChE is synthesized in the liver with substantial amounts appearing in serum.

nodes.name: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase subunits
nodes.description: Propionyl-CoA carboxylase (PCC) is the enzyme which catalyzes the carboxylation of propionyl-CoA to methylmalonyl-CoA and is encoded by the genes PCCA and PCCB to form a hetero-dodecamer. Within the holoenzyme, PCCA catalyzes the ATP-dependent carboxylation of the biotin carried by the biotin carboxyl carrier (BCC) domain, while PCCB then transfers the carboxyl group from carboxylated biotin to propionyl-CoA. Dysfunction of PCC leads to the inherited metabolic disorder propionic acidemia.

nodes.name: Acetyl-CoA carboxylase family
nodes.description: Acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylases (commonly called ACCs) have crucial roles in fatty acid metabolism in most living organisms. Acetyl-coenzyme A carboxylase is a biotin-dependent enzyme and catalyzes the carboxylation of acetyl-CoA to produce malonyl-CoA through its two catalytic activities, biotin carboxylase (BC) and carboxyltransferase (CT). It is a multi-subunit enzyme in most prokaryotes, whereas it is a large, multi-domain enzyme in most eukaryotes.

nodes.name: Telomerase holoenzyme subunits
nodes.description: A reverse transcriptase complex that is essential for maintenance of telomeres. Catalytic subunit TERT and RNA template TERC are essential for telomerase activity, adding telomeric repeats (TTAGGG) at chromosome ends to compensate for the telomere loss that is caused by incomplete genome end replication Elongates the single-stranded G-rich 3' protruding ends of chromosomal DNA using TERC RNA as a template. WRAP53 (also known as TCAB1) binds to the CAB box in TERC and facilitates localization of the telomerase complex to Cajal bodies. In S-phase, telomerase holoenzyme complex is targeted from Cajal bodies to telomeres by binding of TERT to the shelterin subunit, ACD.

nodes.name: RIG-I RNA sensor family
nodes.description: The RIGI family of RNA sensors are pattern recognition receptors that recognize pathogen RNA and trigger an innate immune response.

nodes.name: Pattern recognition receptors
nodes.description: Pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) are responsible for sensing the presence of microorganisms by recognizing structures conserved among microbial species, which are called pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). PRRs are also responsible for recognizing endogenous molecules released from damaged cells, termed damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). The intracellular signaling cascades triggered by these PRRs lead to transcriptional expression of inflammatory mediators that coordinate the elimination of pathogens and infected cells.

nodes.name: Prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase family
nodes.description: Prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthases catalyze the committed step in prostaglandin synthesis and act both as a cyclooxygenases and peroxidases.

nodes.name: Peroxidases
nodes.description: This group contains genes that encode peroxidase activities. Peroxidases are oxidoreductases that catalyze the reduction of hydrogen peroxide or organic hydroperoxides.

nodes.name: CDC7 kinase family
nodes.description: CDC7 encodes a conserved serine/threonine kinase that serves as a critical regulator of origin firing during DNA replication.

nodes.name: Pyruvate carboxylase family
nodes.description: Pyruvate carboxylase (PC) is a nuclear encoded mitochondrial enzyme that catalyzes the conversion of pyruvate to oxaloacetate. PC is a biotinylated homotetramer that contains three major regions encompassing the biotin-carboxylase, transcarboxylation, and biotin-binding domains.

nodes.name: Biotin-dependent carboxylases
nodes.description: Biotin-dependent carboxylases have two distinct enzymatic activities and catalyze their reactions in two steps. First, a biotin carboxylase (BC) component catalyzes the MgATP-dependent carboxylation of the N1′ atom of the biotin cofactor, using bicarbonate as the CO2 donor. Biotin is covalently linked through an amide bond to a lysine side chain in the biotin carboxyl carrier protein (BCCP) component. In the second step of the reaction, a carboxyltransferase (CT) component catalyzes the CO2 transfer from carboxybiotin to the acceptor of the carboxyl group. Depending on the organism and the enzyme, the components can be separate subunits or part of a multi-domain protein.

nodes.name: Homeodomain interacting protein kinase family
nodes.description: The homeodomain interacting protein kinases are a family of nuclear dual-specificity serine/threonine and tyrosine kinases that belong to the CMGC superfamily of protein kinases. HIPKs act as transcriptional regulators and corepressors for homeodomain transcription factors and regulate a diverse range of cellular functions, including cytokinesis and apoptosis, ultimately playing roles in adipogenesis, tumor suppression, angiogenesis, and inflammation. Based on similarity of the kinase domain sequence, HIPK kinases are most closely related to DYRK kinases. Three of four HIPK protein kinases in humans, HIPK1, HIPK2, HIPK3, and HIPK4, share a common domain architecture. HIPK1–3 consist of a highly conserved N-terminal kinase domain and several C-terminal regulatory domains including the homeoprotein-interacting domain (HID). HIPK4 stands out as a unique family member because it consists of only a kinase domain.

nodes.name: Doublecortin like kinase family
nodes.description: The doublecortin-like kinases (DCLKs) are members of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMK) clade of serine/threonine kinases. DCLK proteins contain N-terminal doublecortin-like (DCX) domains, microtubule-binding elements that play a role in microtubule dynamics, neurogenesis, and neuronal migration.

nodes.name: Protein kinase D family
nodes.description: Protein kinase D is encoded by a family of three closely related genes (PRKD1-3). PRKDs are members of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMK) clade of serine/threonine kinases.

nodes.name: Protein serine kinase H family
nodes.description: The protein serine kinase H family are members of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMK) clade of serine/threonine kinases. PSKH1 is an active kinase with a crucial role in kidney development. PSKH2 is closely related to PSKH1 but has an Asn rather than Asp residue at the active site and is likely to be a pseudokinase.

nodes.name: Testis specific serine kinase family
nodes.description: The testis specific serine kinase family are members of the calcium/calmodulin-dependent kinase (CAMK) clade of serine/threonine kinases.

nodes.name: CatSpermasome complex
nodes.description: Sperm-specific cation channel, CatSper mediated Ca2+ signalling initiates the tyrosine phosphorylation cascade thereby controlling sperm motility. Also plays a central role in sperm chemotaxis, and mediates the Ca2+ influx induced by the steroid sex hormone progesterone in human sperm. Defective CatSper function affects migration, possibly preventing sperm reaching the site of fertilization, thereby displaying an infertility phenotype in mice and humans. Deletions of CatSper2 and CatSper epsilon variants c.2394_2399del are associated with CatSper-related male infertility. Complex contains the largest number of subunits of any known ion channel with CatSper1-4 conforming to the canonical domain-swapped voltage-gated ion channel fold in a counterclockwise direction, while the auxiliary subunits CatSper-beta, gamma, delta and epsilon exist in a pavilion-like structure that stabilizes the entire complex through interactions with CatSper4, 1, 3 and 2 respectively.

nodes.name: Checkpoint kinase 1 family
nodes.description: Checkpoint kinase 1 (CHEK1) is a serine/threonine kinase required for checkpoint-mediated cell cycle arrest and activation of DNA repair in response to the presence of DNA damage or unreplicated DNA. CHEK1 belongs to the PRKAA related kinase group; it has no paralogs and is placed in its own subfamily.

nodes.name: 3M complex subunits
nodes.description: The 3M complex maintains microtubule and genome integrity. OBSL1 and CCDC8 form a complex with CUL7 and regulate the level and centrosomal localization of CUL7, respectively.

nodes.name: Inosine monophosphate dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: Inosine-5′-monophosphate dehydrogenase (IMPDH) is an essential enzyme in purine biosynthesis where it catalyzes the first committed step in GTP synthesis. In humans, there are two isoforms of IMPDH that share 84% sequence identity: IMPDH2 is up-regulated in proliferating cells while IMPDH1 plays a housekeeping role and is expressed in most tissues. Missense mutations in both genes lead to disease in humans. Mutations in IMPDH1 result in autosomal dominant blindness in the form of retinitis pigmentosa (RP) or Leber congenital amaurosis (LCA). Mutations in IMPDH2 are associated with severe juvenile neuropathies.

nodes.name: Guanosine monophosphate reductase family
nodes.description: Guanosine monophosphate reductase catalyzes the irreversible NADPH-dependent deamination of GMP to IMP. The two human genes encoding guanosine monophosphate reductase share 79% amino acid sequence identity.

nodes.name: IMPDH/GMPR family
nodes.description: IMP dehydrogenase (IMPDH) and GMP reductase (GMPR) belong to the same family of (beta/alpha)8 TIM-barrel enzymes. They bind the same ligands with similar affinities and share a common set of catalytic residues. Both enzymes catalyze a hydride transfer reaction involving a nicotinamide cofactor hydride, and both reactions proceed via the same covalent intermediate. In the case of IMPDH, this intermediate reacts with water while in GMPR it reacts with ammonia. In both cases, the two chemical transformations are separated by a conformational change. In IMPDH, the conformational change involves a mobile protein flap while in GMPR the cofactor moves.

nodes.name: Dihydrofolate reductase family
nodes.description: Dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR) activity is an important enzymatic function that resides within the one carbon metabolism (OCM) pathway. Its central role in cellular metabolism in support of cell division and proliferation has made DHFR an attractive and successful drug target. Methotrexate is a direct inhibitor of DHFR. There are two human genes capable of encoding dihydrofolate reductase: intron-containing DHFR and a retrogene, DHFR2, which shares 92% amino acid sequence identity with DHFR. Although DHFR2 is transcribed, targeted proteomics analysis found only a low abundance of translated protein in human embryonic heart and no evidence of DHFR2 protein in adult cells. DHFR2 functionality may lie at the RNA level.

nodes.name: Aromatic amino acid hydroxylase family
nodes.description: The members of the family of aromatic amino acid hydroxylases, phenylalanine hydroxylase, tyrosine hydroxylase, and tryptophan hydroxylase, are defined both by their amino acid substrates and by the use of a tetrahydropterin to provide the electrons for the monooxygenation reaction these enzymes catalyze.

nodes.name: Vitamin K epoxide reductase complex subunit 1 family
nodes.description: Vitamin K epoxide reductase is a crucial enzyme in blood coagulation and the target of the most commonly used oral anticoagulant warfarin. There are two isoforms of this enzyme encoded by VKORC1 and VKORC1L1. The proteins share ~50% amino acid sequence identity and catalyze both vitamin K epoxide reductase and vitamin K quinone reductase enzymatic activities.

nodes.name: NALCN channel complex subunits
nodes.description: NALCN regulates the resting membrane potential by mediating the Na+ leak current in neurons, and it functions as a channelosome in complex with NALF1, UNC79, and UNC80. Dysfunction of the NALCN channelosome causes a broad range of neurological and developmental diseases called NALCN channelopathies in humans.

nodes.name: Retrotransposon Gag derived ARC
nodes.description: Evolutionary analysis indicates that ARC is derived from a vertebrate lineage of Ty3/gypsy retrotransposons, which are also ancestors to retroviruses. These findings suggest that Gag retroelements have been repurposed during evolution to mediate intercellular communication in the nervous system.

nodes.name: Retrotransposon derived ASPRV1
nodes.description: ASPRV1 is one of the human genes that have been domesticated from retrotransposons during vertebrate evolution. The protein expressed from this gene was defined as a retrovirus Gag-like protein as — besides its enzymatic domain — it contains a domain that is homologous to that of the Gag structural domain of the canonical retroviral polyprotein. The evolutionary origin was demonstrated by the homology between its Gag-like and protease domains and those of the retrovirus/retrotransposon proteins.

nodes.name: Helix-turn-helix motif Psq family
nodes.description: Helix-turn-helix motif of pipsqueak (HTH-Psq) proteins are a family of transcription factors derived from a pogo-type transposase, known as the pipsqueak transposase.

nodes.name: LINE1 element derived gene
nodes.description: Mammalian genomes comprise many active and fossilized retroelements. The obligate requirement for retroelement integration affords host genomes an opportunity to 'domesticate' retroelement genes for their own purpose, leading to important innovations in genome defense and placentation. While many such exaptations involve retroviruses, the L1TD1 gene is the only known domesticated gene whose protein-coding sequence is almost entirely derived from a LINE-1 (L1) retroelement.

nodes.name: FLYWCH family
nodes.description: FLYWCH is a distinct DNA-binding family known to have originated from the Mutator transposase.

nodes.name: Ribonucleotide reductase subunits
nodes.description: The importance of ribonucleotide reductase (RNR) lies in its unique ability to catalyze the rate-limiting step of the reduction of ribonucleotides (NDPs) to the corresponding deoxyribonucleotides (dNDPs), the precursors of DNA. Mammalian RNRs consist of two homodimeric subunits, which associate to form the holoenzyme. The large RRM1 dimer contains the catalytic site, whereas the smaller dimer (RRM2 or RRM2B) contains an oxygen-requiring di-iron tyrosyl-radical site, which is essential for catalysis.

nodes.name: PiggyBac transposable element derived family
nodes.description: Most mammalian genomes contain decayed piggyBac transposons. They ceased their activity due to several mutations or rearrangements. The human genome contains at least five domesticated piggyBac genes, designated from PGBD1 to PGBD5. On the one hand, PGBD1 and PGBD2 were probably present in the common ancestor of mammals, while PGBD3 and PGBD4 are restricted to primates. On the other hand, PGBD5, the only sequences interrupted by multiple introns, are not only orthologous in mammals and fish but also in lamprey and lancelet suggesting an ancient domestication event about 525 Ma before cephalocordates and vertebrates split from urochordates.

nodes.name: Harbinger transposase derived genes
nodes.description: The human genome encodes two proteins with homology to proteins encoded by Harbinger elements: HARBI1, a domesticated transposase-derived protein, and NAIF1, which contains a trihelix motif similar to that described in the Harbinger Myb-like protein. Physical interaction, subcellular localization, and DNA-binding activities of HARBI1 and NAIF1 suggest strong functional homologies between the Harbinger3_DR system and their related, host-encoded counterparts.

nodes.name: Mariner transposase derived genes
nodes.description: Genes in this family contain a tranposase domain derived from domestication of a mariner transposable element.

nodes.name: RAG transposon derived genes
nodes.description: The RAG1 and RAG2 genes have been derived from a RAG transposon related to Transib DNA transposons approx. 500–600 million years ago .

nodes.name: Synuclein family
nodes.description: Synucleins are small, highly conserved proteins that are intrinsically disordered or unstructured and prone to aggregation. Synucleins are abundant proteins that are mainly found in neural tissue. Although synucleins have been well-studied in the context of neurodegeneration and cancer, a clear biological function for synuclein proteins remains poorly understood.

nodes.name: Glutathione peroxidase family
nodes.description: Glutathione peroxidases are enzymes that catalyse the reduction of H2O2 or organic hydroperoxides to water or the corresponding alcohols, typically in a glutathione-dependent manner. Five family members (GPX1-4, GPX6) are selenoproteins with a selenocysteine residue at the active site while the other three (GPX5, 7-8) have a cysteine residue at the active site.

nodes.name: Heme peroxidase family
nodes.description: Heme-containing peroxidases have a highly conserved structure and evolved to catalyze the oxidation of various substrates in the presence of H2O2 to serve diverse functions. MPO, EPX, and LPO have antimicrobial activities and serve in the first line of host defense, whereas TPO has an essential role in the biosynthesis of thyroid hormones. PDXN is involved in protein cross-linking in the extracellular matrix (ECM). PXDNL shares a high level of identity with PXDN but has lost its enzymatic activity.

nodes.name: ZIC family zinc fingers
nodes.description: The ZIC family comprises five members (ZIC1-5), homologous with the odd-paired (OPA) gene in Drosophila melanogaster. These transcription factors contain five Cys2His zinc finger domains, constituting one of the most abundant transcription factor families in human cells. ZIC proteins significantly contribute to transcriptional regulation and chromatin remodeling.

nodes.name: Gamete adhesion and fusion factors
nodes.description: During fertilization, the sperm approaches the egg and overcomes the egg coat before reaching the egg plasma membrane, the oolemma. Successful fertilization culminates in close apposition of the two plasma membranes during sperm–egg binding and eventual membrane fusion. This process is regulated and driven by surface proteins on both plasma membranes, and in analogy to the neuronal synapse, it was coined the fertilization synapse [PMID:26970099].

nodes.name: KRAB domain containing
nodes.description: The Krueppel-associated box (KRAB) is a domain of around 75 amino acids that is found in the N-terminal part of about one third of eukaryotic Krueppel-type C2H2 zinc finger proteins (ZFPs). It is enriched in charged amino acids and can be divided into subregions A and B, which are predicted to fold into two amphipathic α-helices. The KRAB A and B boxes can be separated by variable spacer segments and many KRAB proteins contain only the A box

nodes.name: Fibrinogen chains
nodes.description: Fibrinogen is a hexameric coagulation factor containing 2 polypeptide chains encoded by each of the 3 fibrinogen genes (FGA, FGB, and FGG). These genes are clustered within a 65-kilobase region on human chromosome 4. During coagulation, fibrinogen is converted to fibrin via thrombin-mediated proteolytic cleavage.

nodes.name: CILK1, MAK, MOK protein kinase family
nodes.description: The CILK1, MAK and MOK protein kinases are subfamily of CMGC kinases that share very similar N-terminal catalytic domains but differ markedly in the structural organization and features in their C-terminal non-catalytic domains.

nodes.name: SRSF protein kinase family
nodes.description: SRSF protein kinases (SPRKs) constitute a subfamily of CMGC serine-threonine kinases that specifically phosphorylate serine residues within regions that are rich in serine-arginine dipeptide motifs, also called SR domains. The serine-arginine splicing factors (SRSFs) are the primary substrates for the SRPKs.

nodes.name: Ubiquitins
nodes.description: Ubiquitin is produced by four distinct genes: two of these, UBA52 and RPS27A, encode a single copy fused to ribosomal subunits, whereas the other two, UBB and UBC, are polyubiquitin genes encoding three and nine head-to-tail repeats of ubiquitin, respectively. Free ubiquitin is cleaved from these gene products by peptidases that belong to the deubiquitylating family of enzymes (DUBs). Ubiquitylation principally occurs at lysine residues of substrate proteins, creating an isopeptide bond. Ubiquitination was initially recognised as a signal for proteasome-mediated degradation but is now known to be fundamental to the control of many cellular processes.

nodes.name: Serum/glucocorticoid regulated kinase family
nodes.description: The serum and glucocorticoid kinase (SGK) family of serine/threonine kinases consists of three isoforms, SGK1, SGK2 and SGK3. This family of kinases is highly homologous to the AKT kinase family, sharing similar upstream activators and downstream targets. SGKs have been implicated in the regulation of cell growth, proliferation, survival and migration: cellular processes that are dysregulated in cancer.

nodes.name: Microtubule associated serine/threonine kinase family
nodes.description: The MAST kinases are highly conserved across nearly all eukaryotic groups, from single-celled protists to complex plants and animals. MAST1-4 are atypical in the AGC family. These large kinases possess multiple functional domains outside the AGC kinase core including the N-terminal domain of unknown function (DUF1908) and C-terminal PDZ domain. MASTL is shorter than the others as it only contains the kinase domain.

nodes.name: G protein-coupled receptor kinase family
nodes.description: The G protein–coupled receptor kinases (GRKs) are a family of serine/threonine protein kinases that phosphorylate agonist-bound, or activated, G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs) as their primary substrates.

nodes.name: STK38/LATS kinase family
nodes.description: The STK38/LATS family of kinases is a subclass of the AGC group of serine/threonine protein kinases. Members of the STK38/LATS family are vital components of conserved pathways controlling essential cellular processes, such as proliferation (cell cycle progression) and cell death. Notably, all STK38/LATS kinases share two unique characteristics, a conserved N-terminal regulatory domain (NTR) in proximity to the catalytic domain and an insertion between subdomains VII and VIII of the catalytic domain.

nodes.name: DMPK kinase family
nodes.description: The DMPK kinases are members of the AGC kinase family with a conserved domain architecture of N-terminal kinase domains followed by a predicted coiled-coil domain and C-terminal regulatory domains that mediate a variety of protein-protein and protein-membrane interactions. While many AGC kinases are regulated by phosphorylation of motifs in their activation loop or C-terminal tail, the DMPK kinases are not. Instead, their N-terminal capped-helix bundle (CHB) domain cooperates with the C-terminal tail to maintain the kinase domain in a homodimeric, active conformation with an ordered activation loop. Protein kinases of the DMPK family are critical regulators of actomyosin contractility in cells.

nodes.name: CDC42 binding protein kinase family
nodes.description: The CDC42 binding protein kinase family are serine/threonine kinases within AGC kinases that share a kinase domain closely related to DMPK. CDC42BP kinases are downstream effectors of CDC42 that play key roles in actin-myosin regulation and activities including cell adhesion, motility and invasion.

nodes.name: Rho associated coiled-coil containing protein kinase family
nodes.description: Rho associated coiled-coil kinases (ROCKs) are effectors of Rho family of small GTPases. ROCKs have multiple functions that include regulation of cellular contraction and polarity, adhesion, motility, proliferation, apoptosis, differentiation, maturation and remodeling of the extracellular matrix (ECM). ROCKs have an N-terminal kinase domain, a coiled-coiled region, Rho-binding domain, a pleckstrin homology domain and a cysteine-rich domain at the C-terminal.

nodes.name: Large tumor suppressor kinase family
nodes.description: LATS1 and LATS2 are serine/threonine kinases of the AGC subfamily, most closely related to the serine/threonine kinase 38 family (also known as nuclear Dbf2-related kinases or NDRs). The LATS family have emerged as central regulators of cell fate, by modulating the functions of numerous oncogenic or tumor suppressive effectors, including the canonical Hippo effectors YAP1/WWTR1 (YAP/TAZ), the Aurora mitotic kinase family, estrogen signaling and the tumor suppressive transcription factor p53.

nodes.name: Serine/threonine kinase 38 family
nodes.description: STK38 and STK38L (also know as NDR1 and NDR2) are highly related AGC family serine/threonine kinases that are evolutionarily conserved from yeast to mammals. In various organisms they have been implicated in cellular proliferation, transcriptional asymmetry, DNA damage response, innate immunity, ciliogenesis, mitochondrial health and neuronal development.

nodes.name: Protein kinase N family
nodes.description: The protein kinase N (PKN) family of serine/threonine protein kinases belongs to the AGC subfamily of protein kinases and is closely related to the protein kinase C (PKC) family. The PKN catalytic domains share approximately 50% sequence identity with the PKC family members. However, the N-terminal regulatory regions are radically different between the PKN and PKC kinases. All PKN family members exhibit three unique polybasic coiled-coil homology region 1 (HR1)-domains (also called antiparallel coiled-coil (ACC)-domains), which confer binding and regulation by the Rho family of small GTPases as well as a lipid regulated autoinhibitory C2-like domain.

nodes.name: Small ubiquitin like modifier family
nodes.description: The small ubiquitin like modifiers (SUMOs) comprise a family of post-translational protein modifiers that are ~11 kDa in size and structurally resemble ubiquitin. However, they share only ~20% amino acid sequence identity with ubiquitin and carry out distinct cellular functions. SUMO1, SUMO2 and SUMO3 are ubiquitously expressed and are the best studied paralogs, whereas SUMO4 and SUMO5 show low, tissue-specific expression and their functions remain enigmatic. Mature forms of SUMO2 and SUMO3 share ~97% sequence identity and are commonly referred to as SUMO2/3, but they share only ~47% sequence identity to SUMO1. SUMO4 is most similar to SUMO2/3 but contains a unique proline residue (P90) at the C-terminus that prevents efficient maturation. Nonetheless, genetic studies have linked SUMO4 to both type 1 and 2 diabetes, suggesting a possible role for non-conjugated SUMO4. The most recent addition to the family, SUMO1P1 (aka SUMO5), may be a pseudogene of SUMO1 but has nevertheless been shown to regulate dynamics of PML nuclear bodies when expressed exogenously in cells.

nodes.name: L-lactate dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: L-lactate dehydrogenase (LDH, EC1.1.1.27) is a key enzyme that catalyzes the interconversion of L-lactate and pyruvate with nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) as a coenzyme. This enzyme exists in a tetrameric form by combination of M (muscle, LDHA) and H (heart, LDHB) subunits in various proportions in different somatic tissues. There are five major tetrameric LDH complexes consisting of LDHA and/or LDHB subunits. Expression of LDHC, LDHAL6A and the intronless gene LDHAL6B is restricted to testes where they may play a role in spermatogenesis.

nodes.name: Lipid kinases
nodes.description: Lipid kinases catalyze the phosphorylation of lipids.

nodes.name: Sphingosine kinase family
nodes.description: Sphingosine kinases catalyzes the formation of sphingosine-1 phosphate (S1P). S1P plays an important role in regulation of a variety of biological processes through intracellular and extracellular actions.

nodes.name: HOOK family
nodes.description: There are three Hook proteins expressed in mammalian cells, characterized by three conserved regions: a globular N-terminal Hook domain, a central coiled-coil domain that drives dimerization and forms a 31-nm helix that aligns along the Arp1 filament, and a divergent, predicted unstructured C-terminal domain thought to mediate cargo binding.

nodes.name: HOOK related protein family
nodes.description: Hook-related proteins (HkRP) like Girdin (CCDC88A), DAPLE (CCDC88C), and Gipie (CCDC88B) are actin-binding proteins, implicated in actin organization and in cell motility.

nodes.name: Endocannabinoid hydrolases
nodes.description: The endocannabinoid system (ECS) defines two types of endogenous agonist: esters and amides of fatty acids. The esters and amides are synthesised by two independent enzyme systems; separate hydrolases also terminate their action. The functions of these endocannabinoids are primarily mediated through two G protein-coupled receptors (encoded by CNR1 and CNR2).

nodes.name: 2-arachidonoylglycerol hydrolases
nodes.description: The endocannabinoid 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG) is a lipid mediator involved in various physiological processes. In response to neural activity, 2-AG is synthesized post-synaptically, then activates pre-synaptic type 1 cannabinoid recep  tors, resulting in transient and long-lasting reduction of neurotransmitter release. The signalling competence of 2-AG is tightly regulated by the balanced action between 'on demand' biosynthesis and degradation. The major enzymatic route for 2-AG inactivation in brain is via hydrolysis; three serine hydrolases (MGLL, BHD6 AND ABHD12) account for approx. 99% of brain 2-AG hydrolase activity.

nodes.name: N-arachidonoylethanolamine hydrolases
nodes.description: N-arachidonoylethanolamine (AEA), also known as anandamide, is an endogenous cannabinoid that is a partial agonist of both cannabinoid receptors (CNR1 and CNR2). Termination of AEA signalling is mediated by hydrolytic enzymes. Fatty acid amide hydrolase (FAAH) appears to be a primary regulator of AEA (and other N-acylethanolamine) levels inside the cell. N-Acylethanolamine acid amidase (NAAA) is a lysosomal enzyme, particularly associated with macrophages, which is also able to hydrolyse N-acylethanolamines, including AEA. FAAH2, in contrast to FAAH and NAAA, is not found in murids, but is found in human, and is also able to hydrolyse AEA and other N-acylamides, with a physical association with intracellular lipid droplets. The differential tissue and subcellular locations of these enzymes is presumed to regulate AEA (and other N-acylamides) in a differential manner.
