nodes.name: Xanthine dehydrogenase/aldehyde oxidase family
nodes.description: AOX1 and XDH are classified as molybdo-flavoenzymes, since they require FAD besides Moco to oxidize their substrates. The primary structure of AOX1 and XDH is very similar and the catalytically active form of both types of enzymes is a homodimer consisting of two 150 kDa subunits. The monomeric subunit of both AOX1 and XDH is divided into three distinct regions: an amino-terminal 25-kDa domain containing two non-identical 2Fe/2S redox centers, a central 40-kDa domain where the FAD-binding site is located and a carboxy-terminal 85-kDa domain consisting of the Moco-binding site mapping close to the substrate pocket. XDH and AOX1 differ in their substrate specificity. XDH acts preferentially on the two purines, hypoxanthine and xanthine, oxidizing them to xanthine and uric acid, respectively. XDH is a key enzyme in the catabolism of purines. In contrast, the physiological role of human AOX1 is still a matter of debate but the substrate specificity is much broader and AOX1 is known to play an important role in the metabolism of drugs and other xenobiotics.

nodes.name: Tyrosinase family
nodes.description: The three protein-coding members of the tyrosinase family play a crucial role in determining melanin production and coloration of animal pigment cells. These proteins are anchored to the melanosomal membrane through a C-terminal fragment. They share approximately 40% amino acid identity and the same structural features, including a signal peptide, a Cys-rich domain, two metal binding sites and a transmembrane domain. Tyrosinase (TYR) catalyzes the first two steps of the Raper–Mason pathway, the hydroxylation of l-tyrosine to l-DOPA and the subsequent oxidation of l-DOPA to l-dopaquinone. The first activity is called tyrosine hydroxylase, and the second one o-diphenol oxidase, catechol oxidase or DOPA oxidase. Dopachrome tautomerase (DCT, previously TYRP2) catalyzes the conversion of dopachrome to 5,6-dihydroxyindole-2-carboxylic acid (DHICA). TYRP1 is abundant in melanocytes and mutations can result in oculocutaneous albinism type 3 (OCA3) but the precise role of TYRP1 in human melanogenesis remains unclear.

nodes.name: MCU complex subunits
nodes.description: The mitochondrial calcium uniporter channel exists as a channel composed of a total of 4 MCU subunits and up to 4 SMDT1 subunits. In some cases, the dominant-negative MCU paralog, MCUB, replaces MCU subunits within the complex. The channel is gated by dimers of MICU1/2 or, in some tissues, dimers of MICU1/3. The accessory subunit MCUR1 also binds to and regulates the channel. Two uniporter channels can dimerize, and the function of these dimers is regulated by interactions between the MICU2 subunit associated with each channel.

nodes.name: Serine/threonine kinase 32 family
nodes.description: STK32A, STK32B and STK32C are closely related serine/threonine kinases that form a subfamily within the AGC family kinases.

nodes.name: Protein kinase A family
nodes.description: Protein kinase A (PKA) is composed of two regulatory (R) subunits forming a dimer, and two catalytic (C) subunits bound to the R subunits. Five different established or putative C subunit encoding genes have been identified in the human genome; PRKACA, PRKACB, PRKX, PRKY, and PRKACG. The PKA C subunit encoded by PRKACA was the first PK for which the 3D structure was solved and it has been extensively studied. Several structure-function-relationships encoded by PRKACA have proved to be conserved features of protein kinases (PKs) in general. The conserved catalytic core consists of an N-terminal lobe, called the small lobe or N-lobe, comprising mainly β-strands and a single α-helix. Located C-terminally is the large lobe or C-lobe, consisting mostly of α-helices. Between the small and large lobes is the active site cleft which binds an ATP molecule and two divalent cations. These cations are essential in the process of transferring the γ-phosphate of ATP to Ser or Thr residues on PKA substrates. The N- and C-terminal parts of PKs outside of the conserved catalytic core are termed the N- and C-tail, respectively. In the AGC subfamily of PKs, which includes PKA, the C-tail shares conserved features important for AGC kinase functioning, including a docking site for the AGC kinase activator PDK1. In contrast, the N-tail is highly variable even among the different PKA C subunits.

nodes.name: Protein kinase G family
nodes.description: The protein kinase G family comprises two closely related genes (PRKG1 and PRKG2) that encode cGMP-dependent serine/threonine kinases (often referred to as cGKs). These enzymes have a rod-like structure and are activated at submicromolar to micromolar concentrations of cGMP. They are composed of three functional domains: an N-terminal (A) domain, a regulatory (R) domain, and a catalytic (C) domain. The regulatory domain contains two tandem cGMP-binding sites that interact allosterically and bind cGMP with high and low affinity. Occupation of both binding sites induces a large change in secondary structure to yield a more elongated molecule. The catalytic domain contains the MgATP- and peptide-binding pockets. Binding of cGMP to both sites in the R domain releases the inhibition of the catalytic center by the N-terminal autoinhibitory/pseudosubstrate site and allows the phosphorylation of serine/threonine residues in target proteins and in the N-terminal autophosphorylation site. In addition to controlling activation and inhibition of the catalytic center, the N terminus has two other functions: dimerization, cGKs are homodimers that are held together by a leucine zipper present in the N terminus, and targeting, the enzymes are targeted to different subcellular localizations by their N termini.

nodes.name: HUSH complex
nodes.description: Mediates epigenetic repression, responsible for position-effect variegation of integrated transgenes in human cells. Recruited to genomic loci rich in H3K9me3, where subsequent recruitment of the histone methyltransferase SETDB1 (Q15047) is required for further H3K9me3 deposition to maintain transcriptional silencing. Acts with MORC2 (Q9Y6X9) to repress LINE-1 class I transposable elements.

nodes.name: Membrane Attack complex
nodes.description: The complement membrane attack complex (MAC) is classically known as a cytolytic effector of innate and adaptive immunity that forms pores in the plasma membrane of pathogens or targeted cells, leading to osmolysis.

nodes.name: SAND domain containing
nodes.description: The SAND domain is a conserved sequence motif found in a number of nuclear proteins, including the Sp100 family and NUDR (HGNC note - 'NUDR' is an alias and this gene has the approved symbol DEAF1). These are thought to play important roles in chromatin-dependent transcriptional regulation and are linked to many diseases. We have determined the three-dimensional (3D) structure of the SAND domain from Sp100b. The structure represents a novel alpha/beta fold, in which a conserved KDWK sequence motif is found within an alpha-helical, positively charged surface patch.

nodes.name: Glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase family
nodes.description: Glutamate-oxalacetate transaminase (GOT) is a pyridoxal phosphate-dependent enzyme that exists in cytoplasmic and mitochondrial forms, GOT1 and GOT2, respectively. The two enzymes belong to the class-I pyridoxal-phosphate-dependent aminotransferase family, and are homodimeric, showing close homology. GOT1 is an important regulator of glutamate levels, as it is involved in the biosynthesis of L-glutamate from L-aspartate or L-cysteine. In addition, the aspartate aminotransferase activity is involved in hepatic glucose synthesis during development and in adipocyte glyceroneogenesis. GOT2 catalyzes the irreversible transamination of the L-tryptophan metabolite L-kynurenine to form kynurenic acid and the reversible transamination of L-aspartate + 2-oxoglutarate = oxaloacetate + L-glutamate. GOT2 plays a key role in amino acid metabolism and the metabolite exchange between mitochondria and cytosol. It also facilitates cellular uptake of long-chain free fatty acids.

nodes.name: Transaminases
nodes.description: Transaminases (or Aminotransferases) (Enzyme Commission [EC] 2.6.1.-) are pyridoxal 5′-phosphate–dependent enzymes that catalyze the transamination reactions between amino acid donor and keto acid acceptor substrates.

nodes.name: Branched chain amino acid transaminase family
nodes.description: Branched chain aminotransferases (BCATs) (EC 2.6.2.42) catalyze transamination of the branched chain amino acids (BCATs) leucine, isoleucine, and valine. Structurally, the BCATs belong to the fold type IV class of pyridoxal phosphate (PLP) enzymes. Vertebrate BCATs are homodimers. In eukaryotes there are two isozymes, one is cytosolic (BCAT1) and the other is mitochondrial (BCAT2). In mammals, BCAT1 is largely restricted to the central nervous system and BCAT2 is in most tissues.

nodes.name: Glutamine--fructose-6-phosphate transaminase family
nodes.description: The key enzyme in the de novo production of UDP-GlcNAc through the hexosamine biosynthesis pathway is glutamine--fructose-6-phosphate amidotransferase (GFPT). GFPT is present in all cellular organisms, including prokaryotes and eukaryotes, underscoring the importance of this enzyme and the HBP for normal cell function. The two mammalian paralogs, GFPT1 and GFPT2, share 75–80% amino acid sequence identity. GFPT1 is found more ubiquitously, whereas GFPT2 seems to have higher expression in tissues of the central nervous system. GFPT comprises an N-terminal 27 kDa glutaminase domain that catalyzes the hydrolysis of glutamine to glutamate and ammonia. The C-terminus harbors the 40 kDa isomerase domains that use ammonia to convert fructose-6-P (a glycolytic intermediate) to glucosamine-6-phosphate (GlcN-6-P). This reaction is the rate-limiting step of the de novo synthesis of hexosamines.

nodes.name: Glutamic--pyruvic transaminase family
nodes.description: Glutamic--pyruvic transaminase (also known as alanine aminotransferase) catalyzes the reversible transamination between alanine and 2-oxoglutarate to generate pyruvate and glutamate, playing a key role in the intermediary metabolism of glucose and amino acids. There are two isoforms in human encoded by GPT and GPT2 that show differential expression and subcellular localisation.

nodes.name: Dual-specificity tyrosine-regulated kinase family
nodes.description: Dual-specificity tyrosine-regulated kinases (DYRKs) comprise a family of protein kinases within the CMGC group of the eukaryotic kinome. DYRK proteins are defined as dual-specificity protein kinases because they have phosphorylation activity on tyrosine, serine, and threonine residues, although the tyrosine phosphorylation activity is restricted to auto-phosphorylation.

nodes.name: Pre-mRNA processing factor kinase PRP4K family
nodes.description: PRP4K is the sole member of a CMGC kinase subfamily.

nodes.name: Protein kinase C family
nodes.description: The protein kinase C family of serine/threonine protein kinases belong to the AGC subfamily of protein kinases. PRKCs (often called PKCs) can be subdivided into three groups based on structure: the group of the conventional PRKC enzymes containing PRKCA, PRKCB and PRKCG isoforms; novel PRKCs consisting of PRKCD, PRKCE, PRKCH and PRKCQ; and the group of atypical PRKCs consisting of PRKCZ and PRKCI isoforms.

nodes.name: 3-phosphoinositide dependent protein kinase 1 family
nodes.description: PDPK1 is the sole member of this AGC kinase subfamily.

nodes.name: MAPEG superfamily
nodes.description: The MAPEG superfamily (Membrane Associated Proteins in Eicosanoid and Glutathione metabolism)is defined according to enzymatic activities, sequence motifs, and structural properties. Certain MAPEG members are recognized for their critical roles in eicosanoid biosynthesis others have functions in host protection against oxidative stress and detoxification of exogenous lipophilic xenobiotics. Typically, members of this family use reduced glutathione to catalyze the transformation of lipophilic substrates arriving from the lipid bilayer into conjugated products with amphipathic properties. In addition, most of these enzymes display a peroxidase activity toward lipid hydroperoxides. MAPEG family members share certain structural and functional properties. They all seem to form a homotrimer with the three active sites located at the interfaces between two adjacent monomers, their catalytic activity is enabled by the formation and stabilization of glutathione thiolate anion by a conserved arginine residue and they are all situated at the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) and nuclear membrane.

nodes.name: Epsin family
nodes.description: Epsins are a family of endocytic adaptor proteins composed of 3 paralogs: EPN1, EPN2 and EPN3. Epsins are known to be involved in the first steps of endocytosis in particular there is evidence that they have a specific role in cargo selection and coat assembly. From a structural perspective, epsins share a similar protein structure. They possess an epsin N-terminal homology (ENTH) domain necessary to bind PtdIns(4,5)P2 at the PM, two or three ubiquitin interacting motifs (UIMs) known to bind to ubiquitinated cargoes, and the aspartate-proline-tryptophan (DPW) and asparagine-proline-phenylalanine (NPF) motifs that interact with the clathrin machinery. Since the protein structure of the three isoforms is similar, redundant functions have been observed in endocytosis, regulation of the actin cytoskeleton during clathrin-mediated endocytosis, and development.

nodes.name: Ethanolamine kinase family
nodes.description: The ethanolamine kinases, and closely related choline kinases, catalyze the first step of the Kennedy pathway, which is the ATP-dependent phosphorylation of ethanolamine or choline, forming PE or PC, respectively, and the byproduct ADP. Mammalian cells carry two ethanolamine-specific kinases: ETNK1 and ETNK2 that have negligible choline kinase activity.

nodes.name: Choline kinase family
nodes.description: Choline kinases catalyse the conversion of choline to phosphocholine, which is further converted to cytidine diphosphate-coline (CDP-choline) in the biosynthesis of phosphatidylcholine (PC). PC is a major constituent of the phospholipid bilayer which constitutes the eukaryotic cell membrane, and regulates cell signal transduction. Functional choline kinase exists as a dimer, and can form homodimers or heterodimers with differential dynamics dependent on the tissue type. CHKA homodimers display higher enzymatic activity than CHKB homodimers and CHKA/B heterodimers with tissues differing in their relative expression of the varying isoforms.

nodes.name: Creatine kinase family
nodes.description: The enzyme creatine kinase catalyses the reversible transfer of a phosphoryl group from ATP to creatine. There are four distinct creatine kinase isoforms — two cytosolic isoforms (CKM and CKB) and two mitochondrial isoforms (CKMT1 and CKMT2) — all of which are encoded by different genes. The tandemly duplicated genes CKMT1A and CKMT1B encode identical CKMT1 proteins.

nodes.name: Dual oxidase maturation factor family
nodes.description: The dual oxidase maturation factor genes (DUOXA1 and DUOXA2) are arranged head-to-head to and co-expressed with their respective dual oxidase genes (DUOX1 and DUOX2). The genomic rearrangement leading to linkage of ancient DUOX and DUOXA genes can be traced back before the divergence of echinoderms. Dual oxidase maturation factors allow ER-to-Golgi transition, maturation, and translocation to the plasma membrane of functional DUOXs.

nodes.name: Phosphorylase kinase catalytic subunit gamma family
CASK family
nodes.description: CASK is a unique MAGUK protein that contains an N-terminal CaM-kinase domain besides the typical MAGUK domains. The CASK CaM-kinase domain was presumed to be a catalytically inactive pseudokinase because it lacks the canonical DFG motif required for Mg2+ binding that was thought to be indispensable for kinase activity. However, it has been shown that CASK functions as an active protein kinase even without Mg2+ binding. High-resolution crystal structures revealed that the CASK CaM-kinase domain adopts a constitutively active conformation that binds ATP and catalyzes phosphotransfer without Mg2+. The CASK CaM-kinase domain phosphorylates itself and at least one physiological interactor, the synaptic protein neurexin1 (NRXN1), to which CASK is recruited via its PDZ domain.

nodes.name: Insulin receptor family
nodes.description: Insulin receptors and the related receptor family members, IGF1 receptors and insulin receptor-related receptors are expressed at the cell surface as preformed heterotetramers, each comprising two hemi-receptors composed of one α- and one β-subunit. Each α- and β-subunit and the two α-subunits are cross-linked by disulphide bridges. The extracellular α subunits bind insulin or IGFs. The β-subunits have a tyrosine kinase domain. INSR and IGF1R have high sequence homology in the cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase domain, with greater divergence in the extracellular ligand-binding α-subunits. INSRRs have high homology with INSRs and IGF1Rs in the tyrosine kinase domain, but the extracellular α-subunit is divergent and does not bind insulin or IGFs. INSRRs operate as alkali sensors: exposure to extracellular alkaline pHo (pHo>8.0) causes a conformational change in the α subunit that activates the intracellular tyrosine kinase resulting in Tyr-phosphorylation of the β-subunit with activation of downstream signalling.

nodes.name: Phosphofructokinase family
nodes.description: Phosphofructokinase (PFK) catalyses the phosphorylation of fructose 6-phosphate (F6P) to fructose 1,6-bisphosphate (F1,6BP) and plays a central role in the glycolytic pathway. The human enzymes are encoded by 3 paralogous genes: PFKM, PFKL and PFKP. While the isoforms were named for the tissue that they are prevalent or originally found (muscle, liver and platelet respectively) they are not limited to these tissues. The functional enzyme is a tetramer and can be formed from one or more isoforms. The kinetic/regulatory properties vary with subunit composition.

nodes.name: Vitamin/cofactor kinases
nodes.description: This group contains genes encoding kinases that act on vitamin or metabolic cofactors substrates.

nodes.name: D-lactate dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: Lactate exists in the human body as two optical isomers: L-lactate and D-lactate. L-lactate is produced from pyruvate during anaerobic glycolysis and present in blood at concentrations 100 times greater than D-lactate. D-lactate is acquired exogenously by consumption of foods, by metabolism of chemicals such as propylene glycol, by intestinal bacteria production, or endogenously by methylglyoxal metabolism—a toxic product that is converted to D-lactate. Different classes of lactate dehydrogenase act on the different isomers. LDHD is specific for D-lactate metabolism.

nodes.name: Lactate dehydrogenases
nodes.description: Lactate exists in the human body as two optical isomers: L-lactate and D-lactate.  The term lactate dehydrogenase usually refers to the enzymes that are involved in the metabolism of L-lactate however there is also a single, unrelated, enzyme that can act on D-lactate.

nodes.name: Malate dehydrogenases
nodes.description: Malate dehydrogenase (MDH) catalyzes the oxidation of L-malate to oxaloacetate in a reversible, NADH-dependent manner. MDH1 encodes a cytosolic protein that functions in multiple pathways, including the malate-aspartate shuttle and gluconeogenesis. MDH2 encodes a mitochondrial protein that catalyzes an essential step in the citric acid cycle. The main isoforms of MDH1 and MDH2 have been well characterized biochemically; both function as dimers. Domains for substrate binding, nucleotide binding, and dimer formation are highly conserved. MDH1B is predicted to have malate dehydrogenase activity but has not been tested to date. MDH1 and MDH2 are widely expressed, while MDH1B is only expressed in a small subset of tissues.

nodes.name: Endoplasmic reticulum to nucleus signaling family
nodes.description: ERN1 and ERN2 are paralogs encoding proteins with a similar overall structure, containing a luminal sensor domain, a transmembrane and juxtamembrane domain and cytoplasmic enzymatic kinase and endonuclease domains. ERN1 functions as a ubiquitous ER stress sensor and mediator of the unfolded protein response. The function of ERN2 is less clear but its expression is restricted to epithelial cells lining mucosal surfaces, such as the respiratory and gastrointestinal tracts, suggesting a role in mucosal homeostasis.

nodes.name: BUB1 mitotic checkpoint serine/threonine kinase family
GTPases
nodes.description: The group represents genes encoding enzymes of the class 3.6.5.-, hydrolases that act of GTP.

nodes.name: Dynamin superfamily
nodes.description: The dynamin superfamily comprises an assortment of multi-domain GTPases, found from bacteria to man, that are distinguished from typical GTPases of the Ras, Rab and G-protein families by their modular structure, relatively large size (>70 kDa), and low affinity for guanine nucleotides. In addition, they display a conserved propensity to self-assemble into polymeric arrays, the dynamics of which are regulated by an autonomous, assembly-stimulated GTPase activity.

nodes.name: MX dynamin like GTPase family
nodes.description: Mx proteins are interferon-induced GTPases that belong to the dynamin superfamily of large GTPases. Similarities include a high molecular weight, a propensity to self-assemble, a relatively low affinity for GTP, and a high intrinsic rate of GTP hydrolysis. A unique property of Mx GTPases is their antiviral activity against a wide range of RNA viruses, including bunya- and orthomyxoviruses.

nodes.name: Dynamins
nodes.description: Based on domain architecture, the dynamin superfamily is broadly divided into two groups, classical dynamins and dynamin-related proteins. The common features shared by all dynamins and Drps are the presence of a large N-terminal GTPase domain, a middle domain (MD) and a GTPase effector domain (GED). While GTPase domain binds and hydrolyses GTP, MD and GED play important roles in oligomerization and regulation of GTPase activity. Classical dynamins contains two additional domains namely, pleckstrin homology domain (PHD) involved in membrane binding and a proline-rich domain (PRD) containing several SH3-binding sites important for protein–protein interactions.

nodes.name: Par-3 family cell polarity regulators
nodes.description: PAR-3/Baz family proteins can have distinct roles at the apical domain (in polarity) and at adherens junctions (in signalling). In mammals, these roles are separately performed by PAR-3 (PARD3; apical) and PAR-3-like (PARD3B; junctional). In Drosophila, there is a single PAR-3/Baz homolog (Baz) which performs both of these functions by localising apically yet having a fractional pool that can localise to adherens junctions. In C. elegans, the PAR-3 protein appears to be solely dedicated to cell polarity, rather than signalling from adherens junctions.

nodes.name: Translational GTPases
nodes.description: Translational GTPases (trGTPases) play key roles in facilitating protein synthesis on the ribosome. Despite the high degree of evolutionary conservation in the sequences of their GTP-binding domains, the rates of GTP hydrolysis and nucleotide exchange vary broadly between different trGTPases.

nodes.name: Signal recognition particle GTPases
nodes.description: This group represents the three GTPases (EC 3.6.5.4) that are associated with the signal recognition particle (SRP) and its receptor (SR). The alpha subunit of SR (SRPRA) and SRP54 contain related GTPase domains whereas the GTPase domain in the SR beta subunit of (SRPRB) defines its own GTPase subfamily.

nodes.name: Zn regulated GTPase metalloprotein activator 1 family
Insulin/relaxin superfamily
nodes.description: The insulin superfamily proteins (ISPs), in particular, insulin, IGFs and relaxin proteins are key modulators of animal physiology. They are known to have evolved from the same ancestral gene and have diverged into proteins with varied sequences and distinct functions, but maintain a similar structural architecture stabilized by highly conserved disulphide bridges.

nodes.name: Insulin family
nodes.description: The insulin/insulin-like growth factor family of ligands (IGF1, IGF1, and INS) play critical roles in normal human physiology and disease states. IGF1 and IGF1 share considerable amino acid sequence similarity with INS. These three peptides adopt similar structures including 3 disulfide bonds that maintain the correct peptide fold.

nodes.name: Plastin family
nodes.description: The plastin family of actin-bundling proteins is evolutionarily conserved and expressed in yeast, plant, and animal cells. Plastins are characterized by EF-hand Ca(2+)-binding domains and actin-binding domains and can cross-link actin filaments into higher-order assemblies like bundles.

nodes.name: Catalase family
nodes.description: Catalases are heme-containing anti-oxidative enzymes. Although classed as peroxidases by the enzyme commission they are distinct from other heme peroxidases. Both use H2O2 as an oxidant as a first step; however, catalases specifically oxidize H2O2 in the next step, thereby generating two molecules of water and oxygen by consuming two molecules of H2O2, while peroxidases oxidize other organic and inorganic substrates. Catalases have a distinct fold and evolutionary origin from the animal heme peroxidase family. There is only one catalase gene in the human genome.

nodes.name: Piezo type mechanosensitive ion channel components
nodes.description: Piezos are the largest known pore-forming multimeric (individual subunits arranged as trimers) ion channels, with each subunit composed of ∼2,500 amino acids and containing 30–40 potential transmembrane domains. Mechanical activation of the channel results in influx of sodium and calcium, which can lead to the propagation of electrical signals and initiate intracellular secondary messenger pathways. Vertebrates have two Piezo genes, PIEZO1 and PIEZO2, and the resulting proteins share ∼50% identity at the amino acid level. It is likely that they evolved to take on specialized roles in the particular tissues in which they are expressed: PIEZO1 is expressed mainly in non-neuronal cells, whereas PIEZO2 is expressed in sensory neurons and in some specialized mechanosensory structures.

nodes.name: Tyrosine protein kinase families
nodes.description: A tyrosine kinase is an enzyme that transfers a phosphate group from ATP to the hydroxyl group of tyrosine residues on target proteins.

nodes.name: SPHK, AGK, CERK lipid kinase family
nodes.description: The sphingosine kinases (SPHK1 and SPHK2), acylglycerol kinase (AGK) and ceramide kinase (CERK) are a group of lipid-signaling kinases encoded by paralogous genes. CERKL (CERK like autophagy regulator) is also paralogous but no kinase activity is been detected for CERKL.

nodes.name: Phosphoinositide kinases
nodes.description: Phosphoinositide kinases can be broadly split into three general families: one family contains all classes of the phosphoinositide 3-kinases (PI3Ks; also known as phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases) and the type III PI4Ks, another family contains the PIP kinases, with the last family containing the type II PI4Ks.

nodes.name: Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinases
nodes.description: Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinases (PI4Ks) have two major types, the type 3 and type 2 enzymes [the type 1 enzyme(s) turned out to be the Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases]. The type 3 enzymes are comprised of two proteins: the larger PI4KA and the smaller PI4KB. These enzymes are relatives of Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases and the PIK-related protein kinases, with a highly conserved COOH-terminal catalytic domain. They also have lipid-kinase unique (LKU) domains also found in Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinases. Other domains include proline-rich sequences (PR) and a frequennin-binding (Fq) domain in the PI4KB form. The smaller sized type 2 PI4Ks exist in two forms in vertebrates: PI4K2A and PI4K2B that are highly homologous except at their very NH2 termini.

nodes.name: Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase type 2 family
nodes.description: Phosphatidylinositol 4-kinases (PI4Ks) are responsible for biosynthesis of the membrane phospholipid phosphatidylinosyl 4-phosphate (PI4P). In humans, the PI4K family includes four different isoforms, which may be classified in two types, type II (PI4K2A, PI4K2B) and type III (PI4KA, PI4KB), on the basis of structural homologies and sensitivities to adenosine and wortmannin. Type III PI4Ks are structurally homologous to the better characterized PI3Ks. In contrast, type II PI4Ks possess an atypical kinase fold with a limited number of relatives in the kinome. PI4K2A and PI4K2B share a highly conserved catalytic domain, substrate specificity and sensitivity to inhibitors, which significantly differentiate them from PI3Ks and other kinases. While in mammals PI4K2A is abundantly expressed and catalytically active, the function of PI4K2B remains less clear. Type II PI4Ks are activated and recruited to the membranes via palmitoylation, after which they are mainly localized in the trans-Golgi network (TGN) and endosomes.

nodes.name: Phosphoinositide kinase, FYVE-type zinc finger containing family
Inositol phosphate kinases
nodes.description: Inositol phosphate encompasses a large multifaceted family of signalling molecules that originate from the combinatorial attachment of phosphate groups to the inositol ring. To date, four distinct inositol phosphate kinases have been identified, namely, IPK, ITPK1, IPPK (IP5-2K), and PPIP5K. The IPK family comprises three sub-types IPMK, IP6K, and ITPK (IP3-3K) each with dedicated enzymatic specificity.

nodes.name: Protein kinase AMP-activated subunits
nodes.description: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a heterotrimeric alpha/beta/gamma subunit complex that functions as a central regulator of energy homeostasis. In mammals, it is encoded by two alternative alpha subunit genes (PRKAA1 and PRKAA2), two alternative beta subunit genes (PRKAB1 and PRKAB2), and three alternative gamma subunit genes (PRKAG1, PRKAG2, and PRKAG3) the products of which can form up to 12 different alpha/beta/gamma isoforms. The alpha subunits contain a canonical Ser/Thr kinase domain.

nodes.name: PLAC8 family
nodes.description: This group contains the human PLAC8 paralog set that encode the cysteine-rich Pfam domain PF04749.

nodes.name: MIF family
nodes.description: The MIF family is encoded by a set 3 paralogs located in the same region of chromosome 22. Both MIF and DDT have been shown to have cytokine activity.

nodes.name: Pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase family
nodes.description: PYCR1, PYCR2, and PYCR3 are members of the pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase family of enzymes. They catalyze the final step of proline synthesis by converting pyrroline-5-carboxylate (P5C) into proline (EC 1.5.1.2). PYCR1 and PYCR2 localize to mitochondria, where their P5C substrate is generated from glutamate by P5C Synthase (P5CS), whereas PYCR3 is found in the cytosol and its P5C substrate is generated from ornithine by ornithine aminotransferase (OAT). PYCR1 and PYCR2 are both associated with human diseases, but with very different clinical manifestations. PYCR1 mutations cause Cutis Laxa (CL, MIM #612940 and 614438). In contrast, PYCR2 mutations cause hypomyelinating leukodystrophy type 10 (HLD10, MIM #616420). There are no diseases yet associated with PYCR3.

nodes.name: N-Ank proteins
nodes.description: N-Ank proteins are characterised by an N-Ank module (N-terminal amphipathic helix followed by ankyrin repeats) and coiled-coil domains. Despite the low sequence conservation between different N-Ank superfamily members, several have been shown to be share the ability to bind and shape membranes. The amphipathic helix is required for membrane binding while the ankyrin repeats sense membrane curverture. Coiled-coil domains allow for self-assembly.

nodes.name: Serine palmitoyltransferase complex subunits
nodes.description: The first step of de novo sphingolipid biosynthesis is catalyzed by the serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) complex, which uses serine and palmitoyl-coenzyme A (CoA) as substrates to produce an 18-carbon sphingoid base. The constitutive SPT complex is a multi-subunit complex most commonly consisting of two large subunits, SPTLC1 and SPTLC2, and one or more small subunits (SPTSSA/SPTSSB) and the ORMDL regulatory subunits. By far the most abundant sphingolipids incorporate the 18-carbon dihydrosphingosine (DHS), of which the fatty chain includes the 16 carbons from palmitate plus 2 carbons from serine. Substitution of SPTLC2 with the inducible isoform SPTLC3 causes production of alternative sphingoid bases.

nodes.name: Serine palmitoyltransferase long chain base subunits
nodes.description: Mammalian serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) has three core subunits: SPTLC1, SPTLC2, and SPTLC3. Whereas SPTLC1 and SPTLC2 are ubiquitously expressed, SPTLC3 expression is restricted to certain tissues only. SPTLC1 is essential for activity, whereas SPTLC2 and SPTLC3 are partly redundant but differ in their enzymatic properties.

nodes.name: Serine palmitoyltransferase small subunits
nodes.description: Serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) catalyzes the first committed step in sphingolipid biosynthesis. The SPT complex includes small stimulatory subunits encoded by the paralogs SPTSSA and SPTSSB that are required for maximal enzyme activity and also confer distinct acyl-CoA substrate specificities. These are functionally equivalent, but not homologous, to yeast TSC3. The 2 SPTSS isoforms share a conserved hydrophobic central domain predicted to reside in the membrane, and each interacts with the large core subunits.

nodes.name: ORMDL sphingolipid biosynthesis regulators
nodes.description: Serine palmitoyltransferase (SPT) is the first and rate-limiting enzyme required for the synthesis of all sphingolipids. SPT is a multi-subunit enzyme, the level of activity of which is controlled by the regulatory subunits known as the ORMDLs. There are three isoforms (ORMDL1-3) in mammalian cells and tissues.

nodes.name: Zinc fingers NFX1-type
nodes.description: The following pattern describes the NFX1-type zinc finger:  C-X(1-6)-H-X-C-X3-C(H/C)-X(3-4)-(H/C)-X(1-10)-C  where X can be any amino acid, and numbers in brackets indicate the number of residues. The two position can be either His or Cys. This central cysteine-rich portion encodes the DNA-binding domain which is highly conserved in eukaryotes.

nodes.name: Elastases
nodes.description: Elastases are proteases capable of degrading mature cross-linked elastin. Elastases are found in different classes of protease: the matrix metalloproteinases (MMPs), aspartic proteases, serine proteases and cysteine proteases. Elastin cleavage by certain enzymes requires pre-damage of elastin, occurring as a result of aging processes, as has for instance been described for the serine protease human leukocyte elastase (ELANE) or metalloendopeptidase neprilysin (MME).

nodes.name: Colony stimulating factors
nodes.description: Colony stimulating factors (CSFs) are a group of cytokines that play crucial roles in the development, survival, and function of myeloid cells. Originally identified for their ability to promote the growth and differentiation of hematopoietic progenitor cells in vitro, these factors have since been shown to have broader functions in regulating myeloid cell numbers and activities in both homeostatic and inflammatory conditions.

nodes.name: Protein kinase AMP-activated non-catalytic subunit beta family
nodes.description: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a heterotrimeric alpha/beta/gamma subunit complex that functions as a central regulator of energy homeostasis. Alternative isoforms of the non-catalytic beta subunit are encoded by PRKAB1 and PRKAB2. The beta subunits are composed of a myristoylated, unstructured N-terminus, a glycogen-binding carbohydrate-binding module (CBM), a scaffolding C-terminal domain (beta-CTD) that interacts with both the gamma subunit, and the alpha-CTD, and the extended beta-linker loop that connects the CBM with the beta-CTD.

nodes.name: Protein kinase AMP-activated non-catalytic subunit gamma family
nodes.description: Adenosine monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase (AMPK) is a heterotrimeric alpha/beta/gamma subunit complex that functions as a central regulator of energy homeostasis. Three isoforms of the non-catalytic gamma subunit are encoded by PRKAG1, PRKAG2 and PRKAG3. The three alternative gamma subunits consist of N-termini of different lengths, followed by a conserved adenine nucleotide-binding domain that contains four cystathione beta-synthetase (CBS) AMP/ADP/ATP binding sites. CBS1, 3, and 4 are functional, whereas in CBS2, the ribose-binding Asp residue is replaced by an Arg, and no nucleotide binding has been observed for CBS2 in heterotrimer structures.

nodes.name: Cytokines
nodes.description: This grouping includes families that fit the classical definition of cytokines as low-molecular-weight secreted proteins that act via specific receptors to coordinate immune and inflammatory responses.

nodes.name: Interleukin 1 family
nodes.description: Interleukin 1 was the first interleukin identified in the 1980s and is characterized as a potent proinflammatory molecule that contributes to innate immune responses against microbes and is involved in tissue injury. On the basis of sequence homology and genetic studies, several other IL1-related ligands have been subsequently identified. IL-1 family ligands include 7 agonists (IL1A, IL1B, IL18, IL33, IL36A, IL36B, IL36G), 3 receptor antagonists (IL1RN, IL36RN, and IL1F10), and an anti-inflammatory cytokine (IL37).

nodes.name: DIP2 family
nodes.description: Members of the DIP2 family share the structural domains of one DNA methylation 1–associated protein 1 (DMAP1) binding, along with two adenylate-forming domains (AFDs), which are involved in acetylated coenzyme A (Ac-CoA) synthesis.

nodes.name: Gamma-secretase complex subunits
nodes.description: Gamma-secretase was first used to describe the proteolytic activity that cleaves amyloid beta precursor protein (APP) within the transmembrane (TM) domain. Gamma-secretase is a complex that consists of four essential subunits: a catalytic presenilin subunit (encoded by the paralogs PSEN1 and PSEN2), nicastrin (NCSTN), a homolog of anterior pharynx defective 1 (encoded by the paralogs APH1A and APH1B), and the presenilin enhancer (PSENEN).

nodes.name: Protein prenyltransferases
nodes.description: Protein prenylation is a post-translational modification controlling the localization, activity, and protein-protein interactions of small GTPases, including the Ras superfamily. This covalent attachment of either a farnesyl (15 carbon) or a geranylgeranyl (20 carbon) isoprenoid group is catalyzed by four prenyltransferases, namely farnesyltransferase (FTase), geranylgeranyltransferase type I (GGTase-I), Rab geranylgeranyltransferase (GGTase-II), and geranylgeranyltransferase type III (GGTase-III).

nodes.name: Farnesyltransferase, CAAX box, subunits
nodes.description: The CAAX farnesyltransferase is a heterodimeric enzyme that attaches a farnesyl group to a single cysteine in several cellular proteins. Substrates include the p21ras proteins, nuclear lamins, and several retinal proteins, all of which end with a 'CAAXbox,' where C is cysteine, A is an aliphatic amino acid, and X is methionine or serine.

nodes.name: Protein geranylgeranyltransferase type I subunits
nodes.description: Protein geranylgeranyltransferase type I (GGTase-I) transfers a geranylgeranyl group to the cysteine residue of candidate proteins containing a carboxyl-terminal CAAX (C, cysteine; A, aliphatic amino acid; X, any amino acid) motif in which the 'X' residue is leucine. The enzyme is composed of a 48-kilodalton alpha subunit and a 43-kilodalton beta subunit. Peptides isolated from the alpha subunit of GGTase-I were shown to be identical with the alpha subunit of a related enzyme, protein farnesyltransferase.

nodes.name: Rab geranylgeranyltransferase subunits
nodes.description: Rab proteins comprise a family of small GTPases that serve a regulatory role in vesicular membrane traffic. Geranylgeranylation of these proteins on C-terminal cysteine motifs is crucial for their membrane association and function. This post-translational modification is catalysed by rab geranylgeranyl transferase (Rab-GGTase), a multisubunit enzyme consisting of a catalytic heterodimer of alpha and beta subunits and a substrate binding subunit encoded CHM or CHML (also known as REP-1 and REP-2).

nodes.name: Protein geranylgeranyltransferase type III subunits
nodes.description: The prenyltransferase GGTase3 consists of the alpha subunit, PTAR1, and the beta subunit of GGTase2, RABGGTB. GGTase3, geranylgeranylates FBXL2 to allow its localization at cell membranes, where this ubiquitin ligase mediates the polyubiquitylation of membrane-anchored proteins.

nodes.name: Spectrin repeat containing
nodes.description: The spectrin superfamily of proteins function to connect cytoskeletal elements to each other, the cell membrane, and the nucleus. The signature domain is the spectrin repeat, a 106–122-amino-acid segment comprising three α-helices. α-actinin is considered to be the ancestral protein and functions to cross-link actin filaments. It then evolved to generate spectrin and dystrophin that function to link the actin cytoskeleton to the cell membrane, as well as the spectraplakins and plakins that link cytoskeletal elements to each other and to junctional complexes. A final class comprises the nesprins, which are able to bind to the nuclear membrane.

nodes.name: AEBS complex subunits
nodes.description: The microsomal antiestrogen binding site (AEBS) comprises enzymes involved in the last stages of cholesterol biosynthesis.

nodes.name: ADCK family
nodes.description: The AarF domain-containing kinase (ADCK) family of proteins is a group of putative mitochondrial kinases believed to play a pivotal role in regulating mitochondrial functions and cellular metabolism. Currently, five isoforms of ADCK proteins have been identified. Although the precise functions of each isoform remain largely undefined, the ADCK kinase family is involved in coenzyme Q (CoQ) biosynthesis, maintenance of mitochondrial homeostasis, and tumorigenesis.

nodes.name: Atypical protein kinase families
nodes.description: Most protein kinases belong to a single superfamily containing a eukaryotic protein kinase (ePK) catalytic domain. This group contains atypical protein kinase (aPK) families. The atypical kinases contain proteins reported to have biochemical kinase activity, but which lack sequence similarity to the ePK domain, and their close homologs. Some aPKs have structural similarity to ePK domains. New aPKs were also identified with the use of additional HMMs and Psi-Blast.

nodes.name: Alpha kinases
nodes.description: Alpha kinases are a family of protein kinases that have no detectable sequence homology to conventional protein kinases (CPKs). Mammals have six alpha kinases, including two channel-kinases—novel signaling molecules that contain an alpha kinase domain fused to an ion-channel. Analysis of all known alpha kinase sequences reveals the presence of several highly conserved motifs. Despite the fact that alpha kinases have no detectable sequence identity with CPKs, the three-dimensional structure of the channel-kinase TRPM7/ChaK1 kinase domain revealed that alpha kinases have a fold very similar to CPKs.

nodes.name: Phosphatidylinositol 3-kinase-related kinase family
nodes.description: Phosphatidylinositol-3 kinase-related kinases (PIKKs) comprise a family of Ser/Thr protein kinases that respond to various stresses, including DNA damage, blocks in DNA replication, availability of nutrients and errors in mRNA splicing. PIKKs are characterized by the presence of a conserved kinase domain (KD), whose activity is regulated by two C-terminal regions, referred to as PIKK-regulatory domain (PRD) and FRAP-ATM-TRRAP-C-terminal (FATC), respectively. It should be noted that TRRAP, unlike the other PIKKs, does not possess kinase activity, because the amino acids required for such activity are absent in its kinase-like domain. Nevertheless, TRRAP has high sequence similarity with the other PIKKs and is considered as a true member of this family.

nodes.name: RIO kinase family
nodes.description: The RIO family was first identified as a group of proteins containing the conserved RIO domain, named based on the founding member of the family, yeast Rio1 (right open reading frame 1). The RIO domain contains a discernible kinase signature, but otherwise exhibits little sequence similarity with conventional protein kinases.

nodes.name: Pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase family
nodes.description: Activity of the mammalian pyruvate dehydrogenase complex is regulated by phosphorylation-dephosphorylation of three specific serine residues of the alpha subunit of the pyruvate dehydrogenase (E1) component. Phosphorylation is carried out by four pyruvate dehydrogenase kinase (PDK) isoenzymes. BCKDK is also a member the PDK gene family but has a different mitochondrial dehydrogenase substrate — in its case, the branched-chain α-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex (BCKDH).

nodes.name: Arginine vasopressin/oxytocin peptide family
nodes.description: Across many species, signaling mediated by oxytocin- and vasopressin-related neuropeptides provides a global, biologically conserved organizing role in sexual reproduction and social behavior. The neurohypophyseal peptide hormones oxytocin and vasopressin differ only in two of their nine amino acids, but they are structurally distinct from other neuropeptides in being cyclized through a disulfide bond between two cysteines at positions 1 and 6 of the peptide chain. Oxytocin and arginine vasopressin orchestrate their biological role through binding and activation of closely related G protein–coupled receptors (GPCRs).

nodes.name: Ficolin family
nodes.description: Ficolins are a family of oligomeric proteins consisting of an N-terminal collagen-like domain and a C-terminal globular fibrinogen-like domain. They are novel lectins that employ the fibrinogen-like domain as a functional domain. Ficolins specifically recognize N-acetyl compounds such as N-acetylglucosamine, components of bacterial and fungal cell walls, and certain bacteria. Like mannose-binding lectin (MBL), ficolins circulate in complexes with MBL-associated serine proteases (MASPs). MASP complexes form with ficolins and MBL, thereby activating the complement through the lectin pathway. Upon binding of ficolins and MBL to carbohydrates on pathogens, MASPs convert to active forms, and subsequently activate the complement. The activated complements lead to pathogen phagocytosis, aggregation and lysis. In humans, three ficolins have been identified, which exhibit differences in tissue expression, protein location site, ligand-binding and bacteria-recognition, suggesting a specific role of each ficolin.

nodes.name: Gonadotropin releasing hormone family
nodes.description: Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GNRH) is secreted in a pulsatile fashion from hypothalamic neurons into the portal circulation, where GNRH receptors on the anterior pituitary are activated with subsequent secretion of follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) and luteinizing hormone (LH). FSH and LH target the gonads and regulate the secretion of steroid hormones. In mammals, two types of GNRH have been found: GNRH1 and GNRH2. GNRH1 is secreted from the hypothalamus, whereas both types are present in several organs and tissues of the body, e.g., neural tissue, where they exert neuroendocrine, paracrine, and autocrine functions in the central and peripheral nervous system. TBoth GNRH1 and GNRH2 act through the same receptor, GNRHR.

nodes.name: Eotaxins
nodes.description: The CC chemokines CCL11 (eotaxin-1), CCL24 (eotaxin-2) and CCL26 (eotaxin-3) are potent chemoattractants for eosinophils and often described as eotaxins. They are mainly produced by epithelial and endothelial cells and mainly activate the GPCR CCR3 that is highly expressed on eosinophils.

nodes.name: Interleukin 17 family
nodes.description: IL17A is the prototypic member of this family. The other members, IL17B to IL17F were subsequently identified based on their homology to IL17A. These proteins are highly conserved at the C terminus, and contain five spatially conserved cysteine residues that mediate dimerization. Members of the IL17 receptor family, IL17RA to IL17RE, mediate the biological functions of these cytokines.

nodes.name: Natriuretic peptides
nodes.description: The natriuretic peptides are a family of structurally related peptides which share a common, 17-membered, internal disulfide ring. Three major subtypes (A-, B-, and C-type natriuretic peptides) exist, and each is present in various tissues in multiple N- and C-terminally extended or shortened forms.

nodes.name: Branched chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase complex subunits
nodes.description: Leucine, isoleucine, and valine are collectively known as branched chain amino acids (BCAAs). Muscular proteins are dominantly built with BCAAs, which make up 20% to 25% of all amino acids in dietary proteins and play primary roles in muscular function. BCAT aminotransferases transfer the amino group of BCAAs to 2-ketoglutarate, which results in corresponding branched chain 2-keto acids (BCKAs) and glutamate. BCKDH performs an oxidative decarboxylation of BCKAs, which produces their coenzyme A-conjugates and NADH.

nodes.name: XTBD family
nodes.description: The XTBD domain folds into a globular four-helix bundle (H1-H4) connected by three loops (L1-L3). H1-H3 form an antiparallel helical array and H4 folds back on top of H2 and H3 at a 90degree angle. The four-helical bundle is mainly stabilized by hydrophobic helix-helix interactions together with additional polar interactions between side chains located on neighbouring helices. The four-helix bundle of XTBD represents a structurally unique arrangement for XRN2 binding.

nodes.name: Kringle domain containing
nodes.description: Kringles are autonomous structural domains, found throughout the blood clotting and fibrinolytic proteins. Kringle domains are believed to play a role in binding mediators (e.g., membranes, other proteins or phospholipids), and in the regulation of proteolytic activity. Kringle domains are characterised by a triple loop, 3-disulphide bridge structure, whose conformation is defined by a number of hydrogen bonds and small pieces of anti-parallel β-sheet. They are found in a varying number of copies in some plasma proteins including prothrombin and urokinase-type plasminogen activator, which are serine proteases belonging to MEROPS peptidase family S1A.

nodes.name: Adhesion molecule with Ig like domain family
nodes.description: The AMIGOs form a novel family of genes coding for type I transmembrane proteins which contain a signal sequence for secretion and a transmembrane domain. The deduced extracellular parts of the AMIGOs contain six leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) flanked by cysteine-rich LRR NH2- and COOH-terminal domains and by one immunoglobulin domain close to the transmembrane region. A homophilic and heterophilic binding mechanism is shown between the members of the AMIGO family.

nodes.name: EGF-CFC family
nodes.description: The family of EGF-CFC proteins got its name from a conserved domain, composed of an EGF-like motif and a novel CFC sequence, first identified in mouse Cripto, frog FRL-1, and mouse Cryptic/Cfc1. The EGF-CFC domain that mediates binding to the Type I receptor and Nodal protein. These; proteins also contain a signal peptide that mediates protein secretion and a glycosylphosphatidylinositol-anchor signal sequence (GPI) that mediates membrane anchoring. EGF-CFC proteins enhance Nodal binding to Type I/II receptors, which is required for phosphorylation of Smad2 and activation of the Nodal signaling pathway.

nodes.name: Pyruvate kinase family
nodes.description: In human, two distinct genes encode PK enzymes [EC:2.7.1.40] pyruvate kinase M (PKM) and pyruvate kinase L/R (PKLR). The PKM gene encodes for PK-M1 (muscle) and PK-M2 (fetal) isoenzymes by alternative splicing. PKLR codes for both the PK-L (Liver-type) and PK-R (Red Blood Cells-Type) isoenzymes using two alternative promoters.

nodes.name: Tubulin alpha family
nodes.description: Alpha-tubulins are globular GTP-binding proteins that, together with beta-tubulins, form the alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimer, the fundamental building block of microtubules in eukaryotic cells. Unlike beta-tubulin, alpha-tubulin binds GTP non-exchangeably.

nodes.name: Tubulin beta family
nodes.description: Beta tubulins are globular GTP-binding proteins that, together with alpha tubulins, form the alpha/beta-tubulin heterodimer, the fundamental building block of microtubules in eukaryotic cells. Unlike alpha tubulin, beta tubulin hydrolyses GTP.

nodes.name: Uridine-cytidine kinase family
nodes.description: Uridine-cytidine kinase (UCK) is a pyrimidine ribonucleoside kinase that catalyzes the phosphorylation of uridine and cytidine to their monophosphate forms, UMP and CMP, respectively. This is the first step in the pyrimidine salvage pathway and is thought to be rate-limiting. There are three human genes that encode UCK activity [EC 2.7.1.48].

nodes.name: Galactokinase family
nodes.description: The two genes of the Galactokinase family (GALK1 and GALK2) encode enzymes that share 35% amino acid identity and are capable of galactokinase activity (EC:2.7.1.6). However GALK2 only acts as a acts as a galactokinase when galactose is present at high concentrations. GALK2 prefers to act on GalNAc as a N-acetylgalactosamine kinase (EC:2.7.1.157).

nodes.name: Tubulin gamma family
nodes.description: Gamma-tubulin is an essential component of the microtubule organizing centers of eukaryotes. It is required for the nucleation of microtubule assembly from microtubule organizing centers in animal and fungal cells, and it is, consequently, essential for mitosis and for the organization of the microtubule cytoskeleton in these organisms. The two human genes encoding gamma-tubulin (TUBG1 and TUBG2) share 97.3% amino acid identity.

nodes.name: Vasohibin family
nodes.description: Vasohibins (VASH1 and VASH2) were originally identified as angiogenesis regulators. They have since been shown to act as SVBP-dependent tubulin detyrosinating enzymes.

nodes.name: Tubulin carboxypeptidase families
nodes.description: Microtubules are a major component of the cytoskeleton and can accumulate a plethora of modifications. The microtubule detyrosination cycle is one of these modifications; it involves the enzymatic removal of the C-terminal tyrosine of α-tubulin on assembled microtubules and the re-ligation of tyrosine on detyrosinated tubulin dimers. This modification cycle has been implicated in cardiac disease, neuronal development, and mitotic defects. The vasohibin and microtubule-associated tyrosine carboxypeptidase enzyme families are responsible for microtubule detyrosination. The two enzyme families are evolutionary unrelated. The vasohibins have a catalytic domain that belongs to the cysteine peptidases family, while the MATCAPs catalytic domain belongs to the Gluzincin clan of zinc metalloproteases, bearing a degenerate version of the family signature motif (HExxxH instead of HExxH).

nodes.name: Tubulin delta family
nodes.description: The tubulin delta family has a single member, TUBD1. Delta tubulin has functions in common with epsilon tubulin but is classed as a separate subfamily. Delta and epsilon tubulin are required for triplet microtubule stability in centrioles and basal bodies. Mutations in these tubulins result in compromised triplet microtubule structures, wherein the centriole loses its ability to facilitate efficient mitosis and the basal body has a reduced ability to form cilia. Delta and epsilon tubulin can interact with each other and are posited to interact with both alpha/beta tubulin and non-tubulin proteins. Delta and epsilon tubulin have shown localization to non-centriolar structures, indicative of a potential function outside the centriole.

nodes.name: Tubulin epsilon family
nodes.description: The tubulin epsilon family has a single member, TUBE1. Epsilon tubulin has functions in common with delta tubulin but is classed as a separate subfamily. Epsilon and delta tubulin are required for triplet microtubule stability in centrioles and basal bodies. Mutations in these tubulins result in compromised triplet microtubule structures, wherein the centriole loses its ability to facilitate efficient mitosis and the basal body has a reduced ability to form cilia. Delta and epsilon tubulin can interact with each other and are posited to interact with both alpha/beta tubulin and non-tubulin proteins. Delta and epsilon tubulin have shown localization to non-centriolar structures, indicative of a potential function outside the centriole.

nodes.name: TKL kinase families
nodes.description: TKL (tyrosine kinase–like) is a diverse group of families that resemble both tyrosine and serine-threonine kinases.

nodes.name: STE kinase families
nodes.description: The STE kinase group consists of MAPK cascade families (Ste7/MAP2K, Ste11/MAP3K, and Ste20/MAP4K).

nodes.name: ZNF804 family
nodes.description: These three paralogs all have a C2H2 zinc finger and a small beta-sheet domain but only GPATCH8 has a GPATCH domain.

nodes.name: STE20 kinase family
nodes.description: These serine/threonine kinases are grouped within the Ste20 or Ste20-related family of mammalian protein kinases due to their shared homology to the budding yeast kinase Ste20. Despite their grouping within one family, these kinases are rather diverse and serve a wide range of functions in a variety of physiological settings. These proteins contain the characteristic sequence GTP(Y/F/C)WMAPE in subdomain VIII of the kinase or catalytic domain. The kinases are first divided into two major groups, based on the location of the catalytic domain: 3′ or C-terminal for the p21-activated kinases (PAKs) and 5′ or N-terminal for the germinal center-like kinases (GCKs).

nodes.name: OXSR1/STK39 kinase family
nodes.description: Serine/threonine kinase 39 (STLK39; also known as SPAK) and oxidative stress responsive kinase 1 (OXSR1; also known as OSR1) are two serine/threonine protein kinases that regulate the function of ion co-transporters through phosphorylation. The highly conserved C-terminal (CCT) domains of STLK39 and OXSR1 bind to RFx[V/I] peptide sequences from their upstream WNK lysine deficient protein kinases, facilitating their activation via phosphorylation.

nodes.name: STK3/STK4 kinase family
nodes.description: Serine/threonine kinases 3 (STK3/MST2) and 4 (STK4/MST1) are principal upstream kinases of the Hippo signaling pathway, which regulates cell proliferation, differentiation, and apoptosis.

nodes.name: p21 (RAC1) activated kinase family
nodes.description: The p21-activated kinases (PAKs) are serine/threonine kinases and were initially discovered as binding proteins of small GTPases. PAKs soon emerged as effectors of Cdc42 and Rac1 small GTPases. The PAK family consists of six members and divided into two groups, group I (PAK1, PAK2, and PAK3) and group II (PAK4, PAK5, and PAK6). PAK5 is sometimes referred to as PAK7. The PAK gene sequences and their structures are conserved from amoeba, yeast, Caenorhabditis elegans, Xenopus, to human. The PAK family represents a converging junction for discrete cell surface triggers and affects cytoskeleton remodeling, intracellular signaling, and gene expression.

nodes.name: SLK/STK10 kinase family
nodes.description: SLK (STE20 like kinase) and STK10 (serine/threonine kinase 10) are closely related kinases whose enzymatic activity is linked to the regulation of ezrin, radixin, and moesin function and to the regulation of lymphocyte migration and the cell cycle.

nodes.name: TMEM63 family
nodes.description: OSCA/TMEM63 mechanosensitive ion channels bear structural homology to the dual functional TMEM16 family. Phospholipids can be translocated through the open pores of TMEM63A/B proteins, suggesting a dual ion channel and lipid scramblase function for members of this protein family. Lipid scrambling in TMEM63 proteins can be activated by mechanical forces in the membrane, making these mechanically activated lipid scramblases. This activity is important for the mechanically induced morphological remodeling of biological membranes and the resilience of cells to high mechanical forces.

nodes.name: TCS superfamily
nodes.description: The calcium-activated TMEM16 proteins and the mechanosensitive/osmolarity-activated OSCA/TMEM63 proteins belong to the Transmembrane Channel/Scramblase (TCS) superfamily. Within the superfamily, OSCA/TMEM63 proteins, as well as TMEM16A and TMEM16B, are thought to function solely as ion channels. However, most TMEM16 members, including TMEM16F, maintain an additional function as scramblases, rapidly exchanging phospholipids between leaflets of the membrane.

nodes.name: TAO kinase family
nodes.description: TAO kinases were identified while searching for a mammalian ortholog of STE20, a serine/threonine kinase that acts upstream of MAP kinases in the MAPK cascade of the yeast pheromone response pathway. TAOKs are involved in various cellular signaling pathways including the p38/MAPK14 stress-activated MAPK cascade, the JNK/SAPK cascade, and the Salvador–Warts–Hippo cascade. In addition, TAOKs are found to interact with other cellular proteins both dependent and independent of their kinase activity. Through these interactions, TAOKs regulate the DNA damage responses, cytoskeleton stability, apoptosis, and other physiological and pathophysiological responses.

nodes.name: WEE kinase family
nodes.description: Members of the Wee family of protein kinases, WEE1 (WEE1A), WEE2 (WEE1B), and PKMYT1 (MYT1), function as negative regulators of the cell cycle by inhibiting the CDK1-cyclin B complex. WEE1 is a tyrosine kinase first identified in fission yeast which inactivates the CDK1-cyclin B complex through phosphorylation of Tyr15, thereby preventing entry into mitosis at the G2-M transition. Unlike the ubiquitously expressed WEE1, WEE2 expression is germ-cell-specific and inhibits meiosis by phosphorylating Tyr15 of the CDK1-cyclin B complex. PKMYT1 is a dual specificity protein kinase localized to the ER-Golgi complex which in vitro inhibits CDK1-cyclin B by phosphorylating Thr14 and Tyr15.

nodes.name: Tousled like kinase family
nodes.description: The Tousled like kinases (TLKs) are an evolutionarily conserved family of serine-threonine kinases that have been implicated in DNA replication, DNA repair, transcription, chromatin structure, viral latency, cell cycle checkpoint control and chromosomal stability in various organisms.

nodes.name: Nuclear receptor binding protein family
nodes.description: Nuclear receptor-binding proteins (NRBP1 and NRBP2) are evolutionarily conserved pseudokinases that can act as regulators of L1 retrotransposition.

nodes.name: TTK protein kinase family
nodes.description: TTK, a central component of the mitotic spindle assembly checkpoint, is classed as a dual-specificity kinase as it can phosphorylate serine, threonine, and tyrosine residues but thus far, no biologically relevant substrate is known to be phosphorylated on tyrosine by TTK.

nodes.name: LMBR family
nodes.description: The LMBR family encode SLC-like proteins. LMBR1 is a probable lysosomal cobalamin transporter.

nodes.name: Biorientation of chromosomes in cell division family
Twinfilin actin binding protein family
nodes.description: Twinfilins are evolutionarily conserved actin-binding proteins initially mischaracterized as tyrosine kinases but later recognized as key regulators of cellular actin dynamics.

nodes.name: Actin-depolymerising factor homology domain containing
nodes.description: The actin-depolymerizing factor homology (ADF-H) domain is a structurally conserved protein motif, which promotes cytoskeletal dynamics by interacting with monomeric and/or filamentous actin, and with the Arp2/3 complex. Despite their structural homology, the five classes of ADF-H domain proteins display distinct biochemical activities and cellular roles.

nodes.name: Cofilin family
nodes.description: Members of the Cofilin family are among the most abundant actin-binding proteins in cells, and appear to be present in all eukaryotes from mammals to plants. They are entirely composed of a single actin-depolymerising factor homology (ADF-H) domain. The most important physiological function of destrin/cofilins is to induce the disassembly of actin filaments.

nodes.name: Glia maturation factor family
nodes.description: Glia Maturation Factor (GMF) was first identified as a factor in brain extracts that could induce the differentiation of cultured glioblasts, gliomas, and neuroblastoma cells. Thus, GMF was studied for decades as a signaling factor controlling brain cell differentiation and function. GMF is now established as a regulator of the actin cytoskeleton with a unique role in remodeling actin network architecture. Conserved from yeast to mammals, GMF (encoded in human by the paralogs GMFB and GMFG) is a member of the ADF-H family of actin regulatory proteins. GMF does not bind actin, but does bind the Arp2/3 complex with high affinity. Through this association, GMF catalyzes the debranching of actin filament networks and inhibits actin nucleation by Arp2/3 complex.

nodes.name: Drebrin family
nodes.description: Drebrin and drebrin like (often called actin-binding protein 1, ABP1) encode multidomain proteins that includes an actin-depolymerising factor homology (ADF-H) domain in their N-terminus. They interact with actin filaments and regulate the activities of other proteins during various actin-dependent processes.

nodes.name: Coactosin like F-actin binding protein family
nodes.description: Human COTL1 shares significant homology with coactosin, an F-actin binding protein from Dictyostelium discoideum. Coactosin consists of single actin-depolymerising factor homology (ADF-H) domain. In a phylogenetic analysis, COTL1 forms separate branch from other ADF-H domain family members so is the sole member of this group.

nodes.name: TATA-box binding protein associated factor 1 family
nodes.description: TATA-box binding-protein associated factor 1 (TAF1) plays a key role in the initiation of RNA polymerase II (pol II)-dependent transcription. TAF1 is best known for being part of a protein complex with TBP and other TAFs, forming the basal transcription factor IID (TFIID), which is an essential component of the RNA pol II initiation complex. Similarly to all other TAFs, TAF1 is a highly conserved protein, which has undergone only limited changes throughout eukaryotic evolution. This testifies to the central role TAF1 plays in eukaryotic transcription regulation. TAF1L is a intronless paralog of TAF1 that probably arose from a retrotransposon gene insertion. It can be translated into an intact protein which shows approximately 95% amino acid homology with TAF1. TAF1L has been proposed to compensate for TAF1 in spermatocytes, where TAF1L is exclusively expressed.

nodes.name: DOP1 leucine zipper like protein family
nodes.description: The DOP1 family encode large proteins with leucine zipper like domains that are conserved from yeast to human. DOP1 proteins act in multiple cellular processes that involve membrane trafficking. Dysregulation of DOP1 family proteins is linked to developmental defects during gastrulation, as well as to neurological conditions and diseases like Down syndrome and Peters anomaly.

nodes.name: Jade family PHD fingers
nodes.description: The Jade family are paralogs that encode proteins with PZP (PHD1-zinc-knuckle-PHD2) domain. JADE proteins are subunits of the KAT7 (also known as HBO1) acetyltransferase complex where they facilitate recruitment of the complex to chromatin and mediate its enzymatic activity.

nodes.name: TSC22 domain family
nodes.description: The TSC22 domain family encode a group of transcriptional regulators with multifaceted roles in cellular physiology. The encoded proteins are characterized by a conserved leucine zipper domain, which facilitates protein–protein interactions essential for their function as transcriptional modulators.

nodes.name: ZFX transcription factor family
nodes.description: The ZFX family is a family of closely related transcription regulators that includes ZFX and ZNF711 encoded on the X-chromosome, and ZFY on the Y-chromosome. All encoded proteins have an acidic domain at the N-terminus thought to be an activation domain that interacts with other proteins that regulate transcription, a nuclear localization signal (NLS), and an array of ZNF domains containing a DNA-binding region. The ZNF domains beyond domain Z3 are arranged in even/odd two-finger repeats that have distinctive sequence signatures.

nodes.name: ABI family
nodes.description: The ABI family of adaptor proteins play significant roles in actin cytoskeleton organization through participation in the WAVE complex. ABI1 and ABI2, were originally identified as proteins that bind to ABL1 and negatively modulate its transforming activity. The third paralog, ABI3 is more distantly related and does not interact with ABL1.

nodes.name: Protamine family
nodes.description: The protamines are a diverse family of small arginine-rich proteins that are synthesized in the late-stage spermatids of many animals and plants and bind to DNA, condensing the spermatid genome into a genetically inactive state. Humans have two functional protamine genes (PRM1 and PRM2), which are adjacent on chromosome 16. Even though it is likely that the PRM2 gene derives from a duplication of the PRM1 gene, the two proteins appear to be rapidly diverging in amino-acid sequence. Comparison of protamine gene and amino-acid sequences suggests that the family evolved from specialized histones through protamine-like proteins to the true protamines. Structural elements present in all true protamines are a series of arginine-rich DNA-anchoring domains (often containing a mixture of arginine and lysine residues in non-mammalian protamines) and multiple phosphorylation sites. The protamine cluster also contains PRM3 - the predicted amino acid sequence for this protein, which would be approximately the same size as PRM2, contains stretches of repeating glutamic and aspartic acid residues similar in number and distribution to the clusters of arginine and lysine residues found in the DNA-binding domains of protamines. This difference in composition (a high content of negatively charged amino acids compared with the high content of positively charged amino acids in protamines) suggests that the PRM3 protein, which is not likely to bind to and condense DNA, may instead bind to and interact with the protamines and perform some other function related to chromatin repackaging.

nodes.name: Muscleblind like splicing regulator family
nodes.description: As RNA-binding proteins, MBNL family members interact with pre-mRNAs through evolutionarily conserved tandem zinc finger domains and play critical roles in various RNA metabolic processes, including alternative splicing, mRNA stability, trafficking, regulation of subcellular localization, and alternative polyadenylation. Dysregulation of MBNL proteins can lead to severe consequences. Initially, research primarily associated MBNL proteins with myotonic dystrophy. However, subsequent studies have revealed their involvement in a broad spectrum of physiological and pathological processes, such as embryonic tissue differentiation and circulatory disorders.

nodes.name: CD79 molecule family
nodes.description: CD79A and CD79B are paralogs that encode proteins sharing 25% identity. Together these proteins form a disulfide-linked heterodimer that acts as the signaling subunit of the B cell receptor (BCR) transmembrane immunoglobulin complex. Each subunit of the heterodimer contains a cytoplasmic immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activation motif (ITAM), characterized by two conserved tyrosine residues within a consensus sequence, which serves as a docking site for SH2 domain-containing effector proteins. These subunits are essential for BCR assembly, stabilization, and the transport of IgM to the cell surface.

nodes.name: Inversin complex subunits
nodes.description: Primary cilia in many cell types contain a periaxonemal subcompartment called the inversin compartment. The function of the inversin compartment is unknown, but it appears to be critical for normal development, including left-right asymmetry and renal tissue homeostasis.

nodes.name: Ubiquitin-binding zinc fingers
nodes.description: The ubiquitin-binding zinc finger (UBZ) is a type of zinc-coordinating β-β-α fold domain found mainly in proteins involved in DNA repair and transcriptional regulation.

nodes.name: Pattern recognition molecules
nodes.description: The innate immunity receptors have been called pattern recognition molecules (PRMs) since they recognize motifs expressed by microorganisms and called pathogen associated molecular patterns (PAMP). In addition, PRMs can recognize a set of motifs expressed by dying cells (i.e. apoptotic cell-associated motifs (ACAMP)) and a set of alarmins, such as endogenous molecules released by necrotic cells. Based on their localisation, PRMs have been divided between cell-associated PRMs and soluble PRMs. Cell-associated PRMs include endocytic receptors, such as scavenger receptors, and signalling receptors, which can be both membrane-associated (e.g. Toll TLRs) or cytoplasmic molecules (e.g. RIGI and NLRs). Fluid phase PRMs are heterogeneous in terms of structure, expression and specificity and include collectins, ficolins and pentraxins.

nodes.name: Pattern recognition pentraxins
nodes.description: This group contains the members of the pentraxin superfamily that are components of the humoral arm of innate immunity.

nodes.name: Soluble pattern recognition molecules
nodes.description: Soluble pattern recognition molecules (PRMs), including collectins, ficolins, and pentraxins, are specialised in the discrimination of self versus non-self and modified-self and share basic multifunctional properties including recognition and opsonisation of pathogens and apoptotic cells, activation and regulation of the complement cascade and tuning of inflammation.

nodes.name: C-type lectin receptors
nodes.description: Transmembrane C-type lectin receptors (CLRs) are one group of pattern recognition receptors expressed by immune cells that contribute to the recognition of both microbial components, known as pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs), and endogenous host-derived molecules, known as damage-associated molecular patterns (DAMPs). Upon recognition of their ligands, these CLRs can trigger various intracellular signaling pathways that broadly result in the activation or inhibition of cellular function, modulating innate and adaptive immune responses.

nodes.name: CD3 subunits of T-cell receptor complex
nodes.description: CD3 is the invariant signaling complex that associates with the T cell receptor (TCR) on T cells and converts antigen recognition into intracellular activation signals. CD3 contains three dimers: CD3E forms heterodimers with CD3G and CD3D while CD247, also known as CD3Z, forms a homodimer. The CD3G, CD3D, and CD3E subunits are genetically related to each other, belonging to the C-type immunoglobulin superfamily. CD247 is genetically unrelated to the other CD3 subunits. All CD3 subunits display signal transduction motifs also present in other immune receptors, e.g., B cell and Fc receptors. These motifs, named immune receptor tyrosine-based activation motifs (ITAMs), are present as a single copy in CD3G, CD3D, and CD3E and three copies in CD247.

nodes.name: Multi-pass translocon complex subunits
nodes.description: Most membrane proteins are synthesized on ER-bound ribosomes docked at the translocon, a heterogeneous ensemble of transmembrane factors operating on the nascent chain. The 'multipass translocon' is distinguished by three components that selectively bind the ribosome-Sec61 complex during multipass protein synthesis: the GET- and EMC-like (GEL), protein associated with translocon (PAT) and back of Sec61 (BOS) complexes.

nodes.name: BOS complex subunits
nodes.description: The function of the BOS complex remains unknown, but is thought to act as a scaffold for recruitment of the remaining multipass components. Together, these factors create a protected lipid cavity behind Sec61 to facilitate multipass membrane protein insertion and folding.

nodes.name: PAT complex subunits
nodes.description: The PAT complex engages nascent transmembrane domains that contain unshielded hydrophilic side chains within the lipid bilayer, and it disengages concomitant with substrate folding. Cells that lack either subunit of the PAT complex show reduced biogenesis of numerous multi-spanning membrane proteins. Thus, the PAT complex is an intramembrane chaperone that protects TMDs during assembly to minimize misfolding of multi-spanning membrane proteins and maintain cellular protein homeostasis.

nodes.name: GEL complex subunits
nodes.description: The GEL complex inserts proteins into the reticulum membrane.

nodes.name: Sec61 complex subunits
nodes.description: The Sec61 complex provides a ribosome docking site, houses a channel across the membrane, and contains a lateral gate that opens toward the lipid bilayer. Model multipass proteins can be stitched into the membrane by iteratively using Sec61's lateral gate for transmembrane domain insertion and its central pore for translocation of flanking domains.

nodes.name: Translocon associated protein complex subunits
nodes.description: The TRAP complex regulates glycosylation for a subset of ER-translated proteins under conditions of ER stress.

nodes.name: NDFIP family
nodes.description: NDFIP1 and NDFIP2 are homologous adaptors of NEDD4 family E3 ubiquitin ligases. NDFIPs contain three N-terminal PY motifs, three TM domains and a short C-terminal region. They localise to the Golgi, endosomes and MVBs. Both NDFIP1 and NDFIP2 interact with multiple members of the NEDD4 family E3s. NDFIPs have been shown to mediate autoubiquitination of E3s while simultaneously also relieving their autoinhibition by binding to WW domains resulting in enhanced catalytic activity. They use the PY motifs to interact with WW domains of HECT E3s to relieve their autoinhibition and this facilitates ubiquitination of substrates.

nodes.name: Nedd4 family E3 ubiquitin protein ligases
nodes.description: NEDD4 encodes a ubiquitin-protein ligase with a catalytic domain of the HECT (homologous to E6-AP carboxyl terminus) class). NEDD4 is the prototypic member of a family of proteins that is conserved from yeast to mammals. NEDD4 family proteins are modular proteins consisting of three or four WW domains, which are protein–protein interaction domains, a carboxyl terminal HECT domain and an amino terminal C2 domain, which is a calcium/lipid-binding domain.
