nodes.description: CMPK1 and CMPK2 encode the two human cytidine/uridine monophosphate kinases [EC 2.7.4.14]. CMPK1 is the cytosolic isoform and CMPK2 is mitochondrial.

nodes.name: Isoprenoid biosynthesis kinases
nodes.description: In the isoprenoid biosynthesis pathway, mevalonate is phosphorylated in 2 subsequent enzyme steps by MVK and PMVK to generate mevalonate pyrophosphate that is further metabolized to produce sterol and nonsterol isoprenoids.

nodes.name: RNA kinases
nodes.description: This group contains genes encoding kinases have act on substrates that include RNA. CLP1 phosphorylates the 5′-hydroxyl of an RNA molecule. NOL9 phosphorylates the 5′-hydroxyl of both RNA and DNA molecules. Note PSTK does not phosphorylate the RNA directly but phosphorylates a seryl amino acid attached to tRNA.

nodes.name: Small molecule kinases
nodes.description: This group contains genes that encode kinases that act of small molecules, typically metabolites.

nodes.name: Fructosamine 3 kinase family
nodes.description: Glycation of proteins by glucose and other sugars naturally occurs in vivo and is elevated in diabetes mellitus. Amadori compounds such as fructosamines are formed during the early stage of glycation and represent the main products. This protein modification may lead to altered function, e.g., decreased activity of 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate mutase. The two ketosamine kinases, fructosamine-3-kinase (FN3K) and fructosamine-3-kinase-related protein (FN3KRP), can deglycate free and protein-bound Amadori compounds and are thus considered as protein repair enzymes.

nodes.name: NAD kinases
nodes.description: NADK genes are evolutionarily conserved from archaea to mammals. NADK phosphorylates the 2' position of the ribose ring connected to the adenine moiety in NAD(H). Because NADP and NADPH are membrane impermeable, the presence of organelle-specific NADP(H) synthesis systems is critical. In mammals, NADK is predominantly localized in the cytoplasm, whereas NADK2 is found in mitochondria.

nodes.name: Nucleic acid kinases
nodes.description: This group contains genes that encode kinases that act on substrates containing nucleic acids.

nodes.name: BCR kinase family
nodes.description: The normal cellular BCR gene encodes a 160,000 dalton phosphoprotein associated with a serine/threonine kinase activity, but it shows only weak dispersed homologies to protein kinases. p160c-BCR was purified to apparent homogeneity as an oligomer of greater than 600,000 daltons that contains autophosphorylation activity and transphosphorylation activity for several protein substrates. A region containing paired cysteine residues within the 426 amino acids encoded by the first exon of BCR is essential for its novel phosphotransferase activity, which overlaps with the strong SH2-binding regions.

nodes.name: DNA kinases
nodes.description: This group contains genes that encodes kinases that act on DNA substrates.

nodes.name: Globin family
nodes.description: Hemoglobins (and related heme proteins, generally referred to as 'globins') are small respiratory proteins that reversibly bind O2 by means of a Fe-containing porphyrin ring. Globins have been identified in many taxa, including bacteria, plants, fungi, and animals. Most globins augment the O2 supply to the aerobic metabolism of the respiratory chain, although they can also carry out enzymatic functions).  Four types of globin, differing in structure, tissue distribution and likely in function, have been discovered in man and other vertebrates: hemoglobin, myoglobin, neuroglobin and cytoglobin. The cooperative heterotetrameric hemoglobin (Hb), located in the red blood cells, serves to transport O2 in the circulatory system. The monomeric myoglobin (Mb), present mainly in the cardiac and striated muscle, acts as an O2 buffer, facilitates O2 diffusion and is involved in the removal of toxic NO. Neuroglobin, which is expressed predominantly in the nervous system, and cytoglobin (also named histoglobin, which is present in almost all tissue types, were the last members of the globin superfamily to be identified.

nodes.name: Laforin/Malin E3-ubiquitin ligase complex
nodes.description: Laforin and malin form a functional complex that is involved in the regulation of glycogen synthesis. Thus, in the absence of a functional complex glycogen accumulates in Lafora bodies (LBs). In addition, it has been suggested that the laforin-malin complex participates in alternative physiological pathways, such as intracellular protein degradation, oxidative stress, and the endoplasmic reticulum unfolded protein response.

nodes.name: MORN repeat containing
nodes.description: MORN repeats are an example of single-layered beta sheet formed by beta-hairpin tandem repeats. They were first identified in junctophilins, a protein family that functions as a tether between plasma membranes and sarcoplasmic/ER membranes in excitable cells. The MORN repeats were named after their proposed function as 'Membrane Occupation and Recognition Nexus.' MORN repeats were later found in a number of other proteins including MORN1-5, SETD7, and plant PIPK, among others. When initially discovered, MORN repeats were suggested to bind to lipid membranes but evidence now suggests they are versatile protein-protein interaction modules.

nodes.name: Sine oculis binding protein homologs
nodes.description: SOBP and RAI2 are paralogs that are homologous to Drosophila Sobp (Sine oculis-binding protein). RAI2 is truncated at the N-terminus relative to SOBP and encodes a protein of 530aa rather than 873aa. The extended N-terminal region of SOBP contains a MYM-type zinc finger that is absent from RAI2. SOBP is considered the ortholog of Sobp.

nodes.name: TCF20 family
nodes.description: TCF20 (also known as  SPBP) and RAI1 are two nuclear chromatin binding multidomain proteins containing seven regions with strong sequence similarity, in addition to similar domain organization. Their genome structures suggest that they probably have evolved by gene duplication. Both proteins are involved in modulation of transcriptional activity.

nodes.name: Syntrophin family
nodes.description: Syntrophins are a family of 59 kDa peripheral membrane-associated adapter proteins, containing multiple protein-protein and protein-lipid interaction domains. The syntrophin family consists of five isoforms that exhibit specific tissue distribution, distinct sub-cellular localization and unique expression patterns implying their diverse functional roles. These syntrophin isoforms form multiple functional protein complexes and ensure proper localization of signalling proteins and their binding partners to specific membrane domains and provide appropriate spatiotemporal regulation of signalling pathways. Syntrophins consist of two PH domains, a PDZ domain and a conserved SU domain. The PH1 domain is split by the PDZ domain. The PH2 and the SU domain are involved in the interaction between syntrophin and the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex (DGC). Syntrophins recruit various signalling proteins to DGC and link extracellular matrix to internal signalling apparatus via DGC. The different domains of the syntrophin isoforms are responsible for modulation of cytoskeleton. Syntrophins associate with cytoskeletal proteins and lead to various cellular responses by modulating the cytoskeleton. Syntrophins are involved in many physiological processes which involve cytoskeletal reorganization like insulin secretion, blood pressure regulation, myogenesis, cell migration, formation and retraction of focal adhesions.

nodes.name: DPY30 domain containing
nodes.description: DYDC1 and DYDC2 are paralogs that both encode 177aa proteins with overall identity of 26%. The N-terminal half of DYDC1 and DYDC2 are well conserved and this domain is also found in the C-terminus of DPY30.

nodes.name: Regulation of nuclear pre-mRNA domain containing
nodes.description: RPRD1A, RPRD1B and RPRD2 co-precipitate with phosphorylated RNA polymerase II (RNAP II). The proteins are homologous, sharing an RNAP II C-terminal domain (CTD) interaction domain (CID) followed by a coiled-coil region. However, RPRD2 is much larger than RPRD1A and RPRD1B and contains compositionally biased serine- and proline-rich regions in its extended C-terminus. RPRD1A and RPRD1B form homodimers and heterodimers through their coiled-coil domains and interact preferentially via CIDs with CTD repeats phosphorylated at S2 and S7.

nodes.name: Dynein light chains
nodes.description: The dynein light chains can be divided into three subfamilies: the t-complex associated (Tctex)–type family (encoded by DYNLT1, DYNLT2, DYNLT2B, DYNLT3, DYNLT4, and DYNLT5), the LC8-type family (encoded by DYNLL1, DYNLL2, and DNAL4), and the roadblock-type family (encoded by DYNLRB1 and DYNLRB2). Most of these protein chains can be found in both cytoplasmic dynein complexes: the exceptions are DYNLT2, which is an axonemal dynein subunit; DYNLT2B, which is found in the dynein 2 complex and the I1/f inner dynein arm (IDA); DYNLT4 and DYNLT5, which are not well characterized; and DNAL4, which is present only in outer dynein arms (ODAs).

nodes.name: Dynein heavy chains
nodes.description: Dynein-based movement is powered by the ATP-driven dynein heavy chain subunits. A family of 15 genes in the human genome encode dynein heavy chains: 1 for each of the 2 cytoplasmic dynein complexes and 13 that encode heavy chain components of the various axonemal dynein complexes.

nodes.name: Dyneins grouped by chain type
nodes.description: Dynein subunits are classified by mass into four categories: heavy (∼520 kD), intermediate (∼70 –140 kD), light intermediate (∼53–59 kD), and light (∼10–30 kD) chains. The heavy and intermediate chains are specific to certain dynein complexes, while the light chains may be components of both cytoplasmic and axonemal dynein machinery, and in some cases, nondynein complexes. The light intermediate chains are present only in the cytoplasmic dynein class.

nodes.name: Dyneins grouped by location
nodes.description: Dynein motor proteins form multiple different dynein complexes in mammals, with important roles in a wide range of cellular functions. Dyneins can be broadly classified into two groups: cytoplasmic and axonemal.

nodes.name: NFKB inhibitor family
nodes.description: The NFKB inhibitor proteins (NFKBIs or IκBs) can be classified into three subfamilies: prototypical (NFKBIA, NFKBIB and NFKBIE); atypical (IκBs (BCL3, NFKBID and NFKBIZ); and the p105 and p100 precursors of NFKB1 (p50) and NFKB2 (p52). These proteins are also categorized into two groups on the basis of their localization either in the cytoplasm (NFKBIA, NFKBIB, NFKBIE, NFKB1 (p105) and NFKB2 (p100)) or nucleus (BCL3, NFKBID and NFKBIZ). All seven members share a common feature: ankyrin-repeats (ANKs) in the COOH-terminal region, and these repeats are believed to inhibit the activities of the NH2 -terminal region via molecular mechanisms. Notably, ANKs cover the nuclear localization sequence (NLS) in the Rel homologous domain of NF-κB to inhibit NF-κB activity.

nodes.name: CD300 molecule family
nodes.description: The CD300 receptors are type I transmembrane proteins expressed in both myeloid and lymphoid lineages and modulate immune responses by their stimulatory and inhibitory capabilities. These molecules have an IgV-like extracellular domain, a transmembrane domain and a cytoplasmic tail that could be short or long depending on their functionality. In humans, the CD300 family consists of eight members divided into two groups. Most of them (CD300BL, CD300C, CD300DL, CD300E, and CD300H) have a short cytoplasmic tail with a basic transmembrane residue or a leucine zipper-like sequence. These transmembrane domains facilitate the association with adaptor proteins containing immunoreceptor tyrosine-based activating motifs (ITAMs) which enable their activating function. By contrast, other members of this family (CD300A and CD300LF) exhibit an inhibitory capacity due to their long cytoplasmic tail containing immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitory motifs (ITIMs). CD300LF is also able to deliver activating signals through motifs reported to bind the p85α regulatory subunit of PI3K and growth factor receptor-bound protein 2 (GRB2). The exception is the CD300G receptor, which has an additional extracellular mucin-like domain and lacks structural motifs indicative of stimulatory or inhibitory potential in the intracellular tail. Furthermore, CD300G is mostly expressed on the vascular endothelial cells of high endothelial venules of lymph nodes.

nodes.name: Retinoic acid early transcript 1 family
nodes.description: The RAET1 (or ULBP) family is a group of stress-inducible major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I-like molecules that act KLRK1 (NKG2D) ligands, alerting the immune system to the presence of abnormal cells. The RAET1 family of KLRK1 ligands is encoded outside the MHC region in most species, while the related MIC family is encoded in the MHC region.

nodes.name: KLRK1 ligand family
nodes.description: KLRK1 (NKG2D) ligands are a group of stress-inducible major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I-like molecules that act as a danger signal alerting the immune system to the presence of abnormal cells. In mammals, two families of KLRK1 (NKG2D) ligands genes have been identified: the MIC gene family encoded in the MHC region and the RAET1 (or ULBP) gene family encoded outside the MHC region in most species.

nodes.name: MIC family
nodes.description: The MIC family is a group of stress-inducible major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I-like molecules that act KLRK1 (NKG2D) ligands, alerting the immune system to the presence of abnormal cells. The MIC family is encoded in the MHC region while the related RAET1 (or ULBP) family of KLRK1 ligands is encoded outside the MHC region in most species.

nodes.name: SEC16 endoplasmic reticulum export factor family
nodes.description: Budding yeast Sec16 is a large peripheral endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane protein that functions in generating COPII transport vesicles and in clustering COPII components at transitional ER (tER) sites. Sec16 interacts with multiple COPII components. Mammalian cells contain two distinct Sec16 homologues: a large protein encoded by SEC16A and encoded by SEC16B. These proteins localize to tER sites, and an N-terminal region of each protein is necessary and sufficient for tER localization. The SEC16A and SEC16B genes are both expressed in every tissue examined, and both proteins are required in HeLa cells for ER export and for normal tER organization. SEC16A resembles yeast Sec16 in having a C-terminal conserved domain that interacts with the COPII coat protein Sec23, but SEC16B lacks such a C-terminal conserved domain.

nodes.name: RUN and SH3 domain containing family
nodes.description: RUSC1 and RUSC2 both contain a RUN domain and a C-terminal SH3 domain. They have been reported to have various roles as adaptor proteins. Both RUSC1 and RUSC2 were identified as accessory proteins of membrane trafficking complex AP-4. They have also been implicated in inhibition of hedgehog signaling through interaction with SUFU. RUSC1 (also known as NSECA) links the molecular motor kinesin with the pre-synaptic membrane protein, syntaxin 1.

nodes.name: DTW motif tRNA-uridine aminocarboxypropyltransferases
nodes.description: Human tRNAs contain 3-(3-amino-3-carboxypropyl)uridine (acp3U) modification. DTWD1 and DTWD2 encode the tRNA aminocarboxypropyltransferases responsible for acp3U formation. DTWD1 is responsible for acp3U20 formation in tRNAs for Cys(GCA) and Tyr, whereas DTWD2 is responsible for acp3U20a formation in tRNAs for Asn(GTT), Ile(AAT), and Ile(TAT). DTWD2 also has a weak activity to form acp3U20.

nodes.name: Musashi RNA binding protein family
nodes.description: The Musashi RNA-binding proteins form a subgroup within the heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein (hnRNP) A/B class of proteins. The hnRNPs are generally composed of one or more RNA-binding modules and at least one other auxiliary domain that often mediates protein-protein interaction. Like other hnRNPs of the A/B class, Musashi proteins have two RNA recognition motifs (RRMs) separated by a short linker region. Musashi proteins modulate translation through their RNA binding domains. Both proteins play a necessary role in stem cell self-renewal and maintenance.

nodes.name: Microtubule associated protein 7 family
nodes.description: MAP7 family members are positive regulators of kinesin-1, the major microtubule (MT) plus-end–directed motor involved in a broad variety of transport processes. All MAP7 family members have a similar organization, with two conserved domains that are predicted to be helical, connected by an unstructured linker. The N-terminal domain of MAP7 proteins strongly interacts with MTs, while the C-terminal domain binds to the stalk region of kinesin-1.

nodes.name: SH2B adaptor protein family
nodes.description: The SH2B family of adaptor proteins consists of three members – SH2B1 (SH2B/PSM), SH2B2 (APS) and SH2B3 (Lnk) – that share a common protein structure with an N-terminal proline-rich stretch, a PH domain, an SH2 domain and a highly conserved C-terminal Cbl recognition motif. They have been shown to regulate signal transduction by receptor tyrosine kinases such as the INSR, IGF1 receptor and receptors for nerve growth factor, hepatocyte growth factor, platelet-derived growth factor and fibroblast growth factor, as well as by the JAK family of tyrosine kinases

nodes.name: EFR3 family
nodes.description: EFR3 proteins act as membrane localization signals for the PI4KA complex, with a palmitoylation code controlling their spatial organization between liquid-ordered and disordered regions of the plasma membrane. ERB3A interacts directly with both the TTC7B and FAM126A components of the PI4KA complex through an evolutionarily conserved region within the ERB3A C-terminus. The C-terminus has a 67% sequence similarity between EFR3A and EFR3B, with most of the interfacial residues being strongly conserved.

nodes.name: Small glutamine rich tetratricopeptide repeat co-chaperone family
nodes.description: SGTA and SGTB are closely related small glutamine-rich tetratricopeptide repeat-containing proteins. SGTA is a well characterised co-chaperone.

nodes.name: RIB43A domain with coiled-coils family
nodes.description: The paralogs RIBC1 and RIBC2 encode microtubule inner proteins (MIPs) associated with the A-tubule of the ciliary axenome.

nodes.name: LRPPRC:SLIRP complex subunits
nodes.description: In mammals, the leucine-rich pentatricopeptide repeat protein (LRPPRC) and the stem-loop interacting RNA-binding protein (SLIRP) form a complex in the mitochondrial matrix that is required throughout the life cycle of most mitochondrial mRNAs. The LRPPRC/SLIRP protein complex is critical for maintaining normal complex I levels and also coordinates mitochondrial translation in a tissue-specific manner.

nodes.name: EFHC family
nodes.description: Paralogs EFHC1 and EFHC2 encodes microtubule inner proteins (MIPs) associated with the A-tubule of the ciliary axoneme. EFHC1 and EFHC2 span protofilaments A01 to A05. Each protein contains three DM10 domains that interact with protofilaments A01, A03 and A05 and a C-terminal EF-hand domain. These two MIPs form a 16-nm periodicity, alternating at every tubulin dimer interface along the microtubule lattice.

nodes.name: Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily C
nodes.description: TRPCs are a family of nonselective, calcium-permeable cation channels, which cause both a collapse of the cell's membrane potential and entry of calcium. The family comprises 7 members and is widely expressed. Unlike the other TRPCs that are widely expressed in vertebrates, TRPC2 is unique in that it exists only as a pseudogene in the genomes of Old World monkeys and humans. TRPCs have been shown to assemble both as homomeric and heteromeric complexes.

nodes.name: Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily A
nodes.description: TRPA1 is the sole member of mammalian Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily A. Predominantly expressed in nociceptive neurons, TRPA1 functions as a polymodal receptor that integrates environmental irritants, oxidative insults, and cellular stress signals to regulate sensory signaling and neurogenic inflammation. Beyond sensory neurons, TRPA1 expression has also been reported in several nonneuronal cell types, including Schwann cells, keratinocytes, lung fibroblasts, and enterochromaffin cells, suggesting broader physiological roles beyond sensory functions. A functional TRPA1 channel is a homotetramer, with each subunit comprising six transmembrane segments (S1–S6), flanked by intracellular N terminus (~700 residues) and C terminus (~90 residues). The S1–S4 helices form a peripheral voltage sensor-like domain (VSLD), while S5 and S6, along with intervening pore helices (PH1 and PH2), form the ion conduction pore. The N terminus of TRPA1 is notable for its numerous ankyrin repeats (16 in human and 14 in mouse TRPA1), while the C terminus contains a TRP-like domain and ends in a tetrameric coiled-coil structure that is important for channel assembly.

nodes.name: Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M
Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily V
Transient receptor potential cation channel group 1
nodes.description: The TRP superfamily is broadly divided into two groups based on sequence and topological differences. The group 1 TRPs consist of five subfamilies, which bear the strongest sequence homology to the founding member of the superfamily, Drosophila TRP. Those channels most related to Drosophila TRP are referred to as the classical or TRPC channels. The TRPV, TRPM, TRPA, and TRPN subfamilies are so named based on the original name of the initially described member of each subfamily. The TRPN proteins are not found in mammals, although they are expressed in some vertebrates, such as zebrafish. The group 1 TRPs include several notable sequence elements and domains. The largest region of sequence homology spans the six transmembrane segments, including the pore loop situated between the fifth and sixth transmembrane segments. TRPC, TRPM, and TRPN channels also contain a TRP domain, which follows the sixth transmembrane segment. With the exception of the TRPM channels, the TRPs in group 1 have multiple N-terminal ankyrin repeats. Three TRPM proteins are so-called chanzymes, with C-terminal enzyme domains.

nodes.name: Transient receptor potential cation channel group 2
nodes.description: The TRP superfamily is broadly divided into two groups based on sequence and topological differences. The two subfamilies TRPP and TRPML comprise the group 2 TRPs, which are distantly related to the group 1 TRPs. The TRPP and TRPML proteins share sequence homology over the transmembrane segments and contain a large loop separating the first two transmembrane domains. The TRPP subfamily may be the most ancient, as members of this subfamily extend from yeast to mammals. The founding TRPP and TRPML proteins were discovered as gene products mutated in autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD) and mucolipidosis type IV (MLIV), respectively.

nodes.name: Mucolipin TRP cation channel family
nodes.description: One subfamily of the TRP channels, the mucolipin or MCOLN/TRPML subfamily comprises three members in mammalian genomes, MCOLN1 (TRPML1), MCOLN2 TRPML2), and MCOLN3 (TRPML3) which are all found to be expressed in the endolysosomal system, i.e., in early and late endosomes, in recycling endosomes and in lysosomes to various degrees. All three channels are regulated by the phosphoinositide PI(3,5)P2, a major component of endolysosomal membranes and by luminal pH.

nodes.name: Polycystin 2, transient receptor potential cation channel family
Insulin receptor substrate family
nodes.description: Insulin receptor substrate (IRS) molecules are key mediators in insulin signaling and play a central role in maintaining basic cellular functions such as growth, survival, and metabolism. They act as docking proteins between the insulin receptor and a complex network of intracellular signaling molecules containing Src homology 2 (SH2) domains. There are 3 protein coding members (IRS1, IRS2, IRS4) of this family in human. The fourth member of the family is a pseudogene in human (IRS3P) but expressed in other species including rodents. The members differ as to tissue distribution, subcellular localization, developmental expression, binding to the insulin receptor, and interaction with SH2 domain-containing proteins.

nodes.name: Growth factor receptor bound protein 7 family
Growth factor receptor bound protein 2 family
nodes.description: The Growth factor receptor bound protein 2 family consists of 4 homologous genes: GRB2, GRAP, GRAP2 and GRAPL. All four proteins share an N-terminal SH3 domain followed immediately by an SH2 domain. GRB2, GRAP and GRAP2 have a second SH3 domain at the C-terminus. GRAP2 includes an additional 100aa unstructured region between the SH2 and C-terminal SH3 domain. GRB2, GRAP and GRAP2 have all been shown to function as adaptor proteins. GRAPL is truncated within the SH2 domain and so missing second SH3 domain.

nodes.name: Src-like-adaptor family
nodes.description: SLA (SLAP-1) and SLA2 (SLAP-2) are adaptor proteins that have a prominent role in the negative regulation of several membrane bound receptors and receptor tyrosine kinases. SLA and SLA2 contain unique carboxy-terminal sequences, common SH2-SH3 domains and amino-terminals which exist in myristoylated and nonmyristoylated isoforms. SH2 domains help molecules to bind to phosphorylated tyrosine containing epitopes. The SH3 domains connect the proline and hydrophobic amino acid containing molecules.

nodes.name: Inhibitor of growth family
nodes.description: ING family proteins are evolutionary conserved co-factors of histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylase (HDAC) that mediate acetylation of essential cellular components, including core histones and the p53 tumor suppressor.

nodes.name: TM2 domain containing family
nodes.description: TM2 domain containing (TM2D) proteins are conserved in metazoans and encoded by three separate genes in each model organism species that has been sequenced. Rare variants in TM2D3 are associated with Alzheimer's disease (AD). The three members of the TM2D family (TM2D1, TM2D2, TM2D3) share a similar protein domain structure. All TM2D proteins have a predicted N-terminal signal sequence and two transmembrane domains that are connected through a short intracellular loop that are found close to the C-terminus. Within this loop, there is an evolutionarily conserved DRF (aspartate-arginine-phenylalanine) motif, a sequence found in some G-protein coupled receptors that mediates their conformational change upon ligand binding. The extracellular region between the signal sequence and first transmembrane domain is divergent in different species as well as among the three TM2D containing proteins. In contrast, the sequences of the two transmembrane domains as well as the intracellular loop is highly conserved throughout evolution as well as between the three TM2 domain containing proteins. The three proteins also have short C-terminal extracellular tails that are evolutionarily conserved within orthologs but vary among the three proteins (e.g. TM2D1 has a slightly longer C'-tail than TM2D2 and TM2D3).

nodes.name: Ral GEF with PH domain and SH3 binding motif family
nodes.description: RalGPS1 and RalGPS2 (Ral GEF with PH domain and SH3-binding motif) comprise the second family of RalGEFs to be indentifed. These two related proteins (63% identity) contain an N-terminal CDC25 homology RasGEF but lack a REM and RA domain. Instead, they contain a C-terminal pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. Additionally, they possess is a central proline-rich sequence with PxxP motifs recognized by Src homology 3 (SH3) domain-containing proteins. The absence of an RA domain uncouples these RalGEFs from direct association with Ras family small GTPases. Instead, the PH domain has been shown to be sufficient for membrane targeting and necessary for Ral activation.

nodes.name: Ral guanine nucleotide dissociation stimulator family
nodes.description: RalGDS family proteins have been identified as effectors for Ras and Ras-related proteins and as GEFs for Ral. Thanks to this double action they are able to bridge Ras and Ral signalling thus being involved in different cellular processes and cell types. RalGDS family members share three distinct domains: a central CDC25 homology domain, with an upstream Ras Exchange Motif (REM), and a C-terminal Ras Binding Domain (RBD). These domains are responsible of the ability of RalGDS proteins to mediate cross-talk between small GTPases.

nodes.name: Noggin family
nodes.description: Noggin, encoded by the NOG gene, is a secreted homodimeric glycoprotein with a molecular mass of 64 kDa. Noggin was discovered by its ability to induce secondary axis formation in Xenopus embryos. Noggin is known to regulate a major class of metabologens, so-called bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs). Noggin's primary structure consists of an acidic amino-terminal and a cysteine-rich carboxy-terminal region. The carboxy-terminal region has a cystine knot with a ten-membered ring.

nodes.name: Twisted gastrulation family
nodes.description: Twisted gastrulation BMP signaling modulator 1 (TWSG1) was initially identified as a regulator of the dorsoventral axis formation in Drosophila. The mechanism of BMP signaling modulation by TWSG1 is complex. TWSG1 inhibits BMP signaling by binding to BMP ligands including BMP4, whereas it enhances signaling by interacting with Chordin, a BMP antagonist. Therefore, TWSG1 can act as both a BMP agonist and antagonist.

nodes.name: Syntaxin binding protein 5 family
nodes.description: Paralogs STXBP5 and STXBP5L (also known as tomosyn-1 and tomosyn-2) play important roles in vesicle fusion. STXBP5 and STXBP5L share a conserved structure containing a large N-terminal WD40 repeat domain and a small C-terminal SNARE motif and can inhibit exocytosis in many secretory cell types, including mammalian central and peripheral neurons, with a few exceptions hinting at an additional positive role. Mutations in tomosyns are associated with neurodevelopmental disorders and thrombosis, suggesting an important and conserved function in different secretory tissues.

nodes.name: LLGL scribble cell polarity complex component family
nodes.description: Drosophila l(2)gl and its mammalian homologues, LLGL1 and LLGL2, are scaffolding proteins that regulate the establishment of apical–basal polarity in epithelial cells.

nodes.name: LRRC family of potassium calcium-activated channel subfamily M regulatory subunits
Potassium calcium-activated channel subfamily M regulatory subunit families
nodes.description: Large-conductance voltage- and Ca2+-activated potassium (BK) channels are essential regulators of physiological processes including smooth muscle tone, neurotransmitter release, and neuronal excitability. While the pore-forming alpha-subunit (encoded by KCNMA1) is sufficient for channel function, the remarkable diversity of BK currents in native tissues arises from its association with three structurally distinct auxiliary subunit families: beta, gamma, and LINGO, each one containing four members.

nodes.name: Cyclin dependent kinase 5 regulatory subunit family
nodes.description: Cyclin dependent kinase 5 (CDK5), is an atypical member of the CDK family of proline-directed serine/threonine kinases with no evident role in cell cycle progression. CDK5 is present in post-mitotic and terminally differentiated neuronal/glial cells and is also known to arrest cell cycle. Also atypical is the activation of CDK5 by binding of a non-cyclin activator protein, namely, the CDK5 regulatory proteins CDK5R1 (p35), truncated CDK5R1 (p25), or CDK5R2 (p39).

nodes.name: Ral guanine nucleotide exchange factors
nodes.description: Ral-selective GEFs accelerate the low intrinsic exchange and GTP hydrolysis activities to promote formation of active GTP-bound and inactive GDP-bound Ral. The RalGEFs are highly conserved across species. All RalGEFs contain a CDC25 homology domain, which is responsible for catalytic activity. There are four human isoforms of RalGEF (RALGDS. RGL1, RGL2, RGL3) that contain Ras-association (RA) domain. These isoforms also contain a Ras exchanger motif (REM) that likely stabilizes the CDC25 homology domain and is essential for RalGEF catalytic activity. The RALGPS RalGEFs lack a REM domain and do not associate with Ras, but instead contain a pleckstrin homology (PH) domain. RGL4 contains a CDC25 homology domain, but lacks a REM, RA or PH domain.

nodes.name: RGL4 family
nodes.description: RGL4, was identified originally as a RalGDS-related (Rgr) oncogene in a DMBA (7,12-dimethylbenz[α]anthracene)-induced rabbit squamous cell carcinoma. However, while RGL4 does contain a CDC25 homology domain, it lacks a well-defined RA or PH domain. Furthermore, while the other RalGEFs are highly selective activators of Ral, RGL4 has also been described to activate other Ras family small GTPases.

nodes.name: RAS-independent RalGEFs
nodes.description: The seven known RALGEFs, RALGDS, RGL1, RGL2, RGL3, RGL4, RALGPS1, and RALGPS2, can be divided into two groups. The first (RALGDS, RGL1, RGL2, RGL3) can directly bind to the effector binding region of activated RAS and hence relies on RAS activation, while the other group (RALGPS1, RALGPS2, RGL4) can be activated by RAS-independent mechanisms.

nodes.name: FMR1 family
nodes.description: The fragile X protein family comprises the multifunctional RNA-binding proteins FMR1, FXR1, and FXR2 that play an important role in RNA metabolism and regulation of translation, but also in DNA damage and cellular stress responses, mitochondrial organization, and more. These proteins are highly homologous to each other, especially in the N-terminal half, while more variation is found in the C-terminal part. Evolutionary, fragile X proteins are highly conserved and most organisms higher than insects encode all three family members in their genomes. The functional domains of the family include a tandem Agenet-like domain (TAD) at the N-terminus followed by a nuclear localization signal (NLS), three RNA-binding K-homology (KH) domains, a nuclear export signal (NES), and a mostly disordered C-terminus comprising RNA-binding RGG motifs, or variations thereof.

nodes.name: SH3 domain binding protein 5 family
nodes.description: SH3BP5 and SH3BP5L have been identified as the first 'standalone' RAB11 family GEFs, unique in directly engaging the switch I and II regions of RAB11 to catalyze nucleotide exchange. Both proteins are further controlled by tankyrase, a poly-ADP-ribose polymerase that modifies distinct sites on each paralog, thereby suppressing their GEF activity and reducing RAB11A-GTP levels. Despite these similarities, the 2 paralogs diverge significantly in both sequence and function. SH3BP5L contains an extended N-terminal region and shows substantially higher catalytic efficiency toward RAB11A. SH3BP5 has been implicated instead in negative regulation of Bruton's tyrosine kinase and in sustaining JNK activation under stress. In contrast, SH3BP5L has emerged as the paralog primarily dedicated to polarized trafficking, positioning it as a strong candidate to regulate RAB11-dependent recycling of integrins and other surface effectors whose delivery to the plasma membrane sustains directed migration.

nodes.name: RA and PH domain adapter family
MRL family adaptor proteins
nodes.description: The MRL family acronym refers to the C. elegans ortholog mig-10, and aliases for the RAPH1 (lamellipodin) and APBB1IP (RIAM) genes.

nodes.name: p53 transcription factor family
nodes.description: The p53 family members TP53, TP63 and TP73 are homologs that share a similar DNA binding domain but differ in N- and C-termini.

nodes.name: Acyl-CoA oxidase family
nodes.description: Acyl-CoA oxidase (ACOX) enzymes play a central role in primary metabolism, catalyzing the first and rate-limiting step in the peroxisomal β-oxidation cycle that shortens long-chain fatty acids, branched-chain fatty acids, and bile acid intermediates. In humans, there are at least three ACOX enzymes (ACOX1, 2, and 3) with each specializing in different types of substrates. The family containing a fourth gene, acyl-CoA oxidase like (AXOL) which has not been confirmed to have activity. The crystal structures of human ACOX1 and homologs from a variety of organisms reveal that these enzymes have a homodimeric structure with FAD cofactors noncovalently bound to each subunit at the dimeric interface. These enzymes use a two-step mechanism to install α,β-unsaturation in their acyl-CoA substrates. First, a catalytic glutamate abstracts the α-proton of the CoA-thioester, leading to hydride transfer from the β-position to FAD. Then, FADH2 is reoxidized through the reduction of molecular oxygen to form hydrogen peroxide. In contrast, the mitochondrial counterpart to the peroxisomal ACOX enzymes, the acyl-CoA dehydrogenases, transfer the electrons to FAD and ultimately the electron transport chain.

nodes.name: Oxidoreductases
nodes.description: Genes encoding Oxidoreductases (EC 1.-.-.-).

nodes.name: Lysyl oxidase family
nodes.description: The lysyl oxidase (LOX) enzyme was identified as a secreted enzyme that catalyzes the deamination of the ε-amino group of lysines in collagen and elastin monomers, resulting in the formation of covalent cross-linkages, and the stabilization of collagen and elastin fibers. This is the first step in the cross-linking reaction of collagen and elastin. Many years later, it was realized that LOX is but one member of a lysyl oxidase enzyme family that includes four additional members (LOXL1–4). The lysyl oxidases also produce hydrogen peroxide as a side product of their enzyme activity, and hydrogen peroxide, in turn, can activate signal transduction via the focal adhesion kinase (FAK) pathway. The five lysyl oxidase family members are characterized by their highly conserved C-terminal regions, which contain their catalytic domains. The catalytic domains of all lysyl oxidases contain a copper-binding domain that is required for their catalytic activity, and a unique lysyl tyrosine quinone (LTQ) covalently linked internal structure that is also essential for their catalytic function. However, the N-termini of the lysyl oxidases are much more diversified, and based upon their structure, the lysyl oxidases can be further divided into two subfamilies. The first subfamily includes LOX and LOXL1, which are synthesized as pro-enzymes that are cleaved by the bone morphogenic protein 1 (BMP1) protease, to generate the active mature enzymes. The second subdivision includes LOXL2–4, which is characterized by the presence of four scavenger receptor cysteine-rich (SRCR) domains in their N-terminal regions. It should be noted that there may be additional enzymatic functions associated with the SRCR domains of these lysyl oxidases. LOXL3 was found to associate with Stat3 in cell nuclei, and to deacetylate and deacetyliminate STAT3 on multiple acetyl–lysine sites. This activity was found to be associated with the N-terminal SRCR repeats of LOXL3, rather than with the C-terminal oxidase catalytic domain. Furthermore, when overexpressed, SRCR repeats from additional LOX family members also catalyze protein deacetylation/deacetylimination.

nodes.name: Monoamine oxidase family
nodes.description: Monoamine oxidases A and B (MAOA and MAOB) are outer mitochondrial membrane proteins that catalyze the oxidation of primary, secondary, and tertiary amines, including several neurotransmitters, to the corresponding imines; the oxidized products are hydrolyzed nonenzymatically to the respective aldehydes or ketones. The two enzymes share 70% amino acid identity, and both contain a covalently-bound FAD cofactor attached to an enzyme cysteine via the 8α-methylene of the isoalloxazine ring. MAOA metabolizes serotonin (5-hydroxytryptamine), norepinephrine, and dopamine, while MAOB preferentially oxidizes benzylamine, dopamine and phenylethylamine and only metabolizes norepinephrine and serotonin slowly. MAOB also forms the neurotoxin 1-methyl-4-phenyl-pyridinium, a causative agent of Parkinson's disease, from 1-methyl-4-phenyl-1,2,3,6-tetrahydropyridine (MPTP). Inhibitors of the monoamine oxidases have been used clinically for the treatment of depression, as well as Parkinson's, Alzheimer's and other neurodegenerative diseases

nodes.name: AIF family
nodes.description: The apoptosis-inducing factor (AIF) family is represented by three different proteins, known as AIFM1 (AIF), AIFM1 (AMID) and AIFM3 (AIFL), that have in common the mitochondrial localisation in healthy cells, the presence of FAD- and NADH-dependent domains involved in oxidoreductase function and their capability to induce programmed cell death.

nodes.name: Amine oxidase copper containing family
nodes.description: The Amine oxidase copper containing family comprises four AOC genes: AOC1 (diamine oxidase, DAO), AOC2 (retina-specific amine oxidase, RAO), AOC3 (vascular adhesion protein-1, VAP-1), and AOC4P (a pseudogene, truncated in the active site). The translated sequences of AOC2 and AOC3 share 65% identity, but AOC1 only shares ∼38% identity with either AOC2 or AOC3. The Tyr precursor for TPQ, the active-site base (i.e. Asp), three His for the copper-binding site, and a Tyr residue that has a hydrogen bond interaction with the TPQ cofactor are all conserved. AOC1 and AOC2 contain predicted secretion signals at their N-termini, while AOC3 does not contain a secretion signal, but has a helical transmembrane (type II) domain.

nodes.name: Ecto-NOX disulfide-thiol exchanger family
nodes.description: Ecto-NOX (because of their cell surface location) proteins comprise a family of NAD(P)H oxidases of plants and animals that exhibit both oxidative and protein disulfide isomerase-like activities. The two biochemical activities, hydroquinone [NAD(P)H] oxidation and protein disulfide--thiol interchange alternate, a property unprecedented in the biochemical literature. Tumor-associated ENOX2 (also known as tNOX) is cancer-specific and drug-responsive. The constitutive ENOX1 (also known as CNOX) is ubiquitous and refractory to drugs. The physiological substrate for the oxidative activity appears to be hydroquinones of the plasma membrane such as reduced coenzyme Q10. Ecto-NOX proteins are growth-related and drive cell enlargement. Also indicated are roles in aging and in neurodegenerative diseases. The regular pattern of oscillations appears to be related to alpha-helix-beta-structure transitions and serves biochemical core oscillator of the cellular biological clock. Period length is independent of temperature (temperature compensated) and synchrony is achieved through entrainment.

nodes.name: Glutamate dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: Mammalian glutamate dehydrogenase (GDH) is an NAD(P)-dependent GDH (EC: 1.4.1.3) catalyzing reversible oxidation of L-glutamate to 2-oxoglutarate and ammonia. Its function is indispensable for the metabolism of the neurotransmitter glutamate in the brain. The role of GDH as an enzyme controlling anaplerotic flux fulfilling the TCA cycle is also hard to overestimate. As an ammonia-producing/assimilating enzyme, GDH is relevant for kidney function and for the metabolism and progression of some tumors. Thus, GDH is an essential enzyme linking carbon and nitrogen metabolism, which is relevant for all tissues.  GDH is found in all living organisms, with two different structural subfamilies of small and large GDH identified. All mammalian GDHs belong to the subfamily of small GDH with subunits of ~55 kDa. These hexameric enzymes are organized as a dimer of trimers, which may form supramolecular filamentous structures of higher molecular weight. Mammalian GDH was one of the first discovered allosteric enzymes.   Although GDH is an essential enzyme for the human body, particularly necessary for brain function, its role is far from being fully understood. This is partially due to the GDH gene (GLUD1) duplication in humans. The second intronless GLUD2 gene is specific to hominoids/apes (gibbons and great apes) and emerged due to a retroposition less than 23 million years ago.

nodes.name: Iodothyronine deiodinase family
nodes.description: Thyroid hormones, produced by the thyroid gland, are crucial for regulating a variety of physiological functions in the human body. The thyroid primarily produces the prohormone L-thyroxine (T4, or 3,5,3′,5′-tetraiodothyronine), along with small amounts of the biologically active hormone, 3,5,3′-triiodothyronine (T3). However, most of the T3 in the body is generated by a group of enzymes known as DIOs, which contain the catalytically significant selenocysteine residue in the active site. There are three isoforms of DIOs known, which are homologous in nature. They share almost similar amino acid residues at their active sites, but they differ in their activity towards the deiodination of thyroid hormones and their tissue distribution.  DIO1 catalyzes the 5′ and 5-deiodination of T4 to produce the biologically active hormone T3 and its inactive metabolite reverse T3 (rT3), respectively. It is primarily expressed in the liver, kidneys, and thyroid. In contrast, DIO2, which is found in the brain, skeletal muscle, and brown adipose tissue, is mainly responsible for producing active T3 through 5′-deiodination. The third isoform, DIO3, specifically catalyzes 5-deiodination and plays a key role in inactivating thyroid hormones when their levels exceed the optimal concentration. DIO3 is particularly important during fetal development and early life, as it helps protect developing tissues from excessive thyroid hormone activity that could interfere with normal growth and differentiation. The regulation of DIOs expression are crucial as their enzymatic deiodination actions fine-tune the thyroid hormone status in various tissues, ensuring proper metabolic function, growth, and development.

nodes.name: Methionine sulfoxide reductases
nodes.description: MSRs catalyse the reduction of free and protein-bound methionine sulfoxides to methionine. Two distinct enzyme families have evolved for the reduction of methionine sulfoxide residues in proteins. MSRA is specific for the S-form of methionine sulfoxide, whereas MSRB can only reduce the R-form. Mammals have one MSRA and three MSRB genes. MSRA that contains the N-terminal MTS (mitochondrial targeting signal) is targeted to the cytosol, nucleus and mitochondria. Among three MSRBs, MSRB1 contains selenocysteine (U) in the catalytic site and is present in the cytosol and nucleus. MSRB2 has a typical MTS and localizes to the mitochondria. Human MSRB3 occurs in two forms, owing to alternative first exon splicing, and the two proteins have an N-terminal ERTS (ER targeting signal) or a MTS.

nodes.name: Mitochondrial amidoxime reducing component family
nodes.description: All mammalian genomes studied to date contain two MTARC genes: MTARC1 and MTARC2. The proteins encoded by these genes represent the simplest form of eukaryotic molybdenum enzymes, only binding the molybdenum cofactor. In the presence of NADH, MTARC proteins exert N-reductive activity together with the two electron transport proteins cytochrome b5 type B and NADH cytochrome b5 reductase. This enzyme system is capable of reducing a great variety of N-hydroxylated substrates. It plays a decisive role in the activation of prodrugs containing an amidoxime structure, and in detoxification pathways, e.g., of N-hydroxylated purine and pyrimidine bases. It belongs to a group of drug metabolism enzymes, in particular as a counterpart of P450 formed N-oxygenated metabolites.

nodes.name: Glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenases
nodes.description: The glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle (GPS) is composed of two different enzymes: cytosolic NAD+-linked glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase 1 (GPD1) and mitochondrial FAD-linked glycerol 3-phosphate dehydrogenase 2 (GPD2). These two enzymes work together to act as an NADH shuttle for mitochondrial bioenergetics and function as an important bridge between glucose and lipid metabolism. GPD1L has 84% amino acid homology to GPD1.

nodes.name: Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: Glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) is a ubiquitously expressed enzyme that lies at the center of the glycolytic pathway. Although traditionally thought of as a housekeeping gene, it functions in other aspects of metabolism as well as nonmetabolic moonlighting functions. GAPDHS paralog of GAPDH, with an expression pattern limited only to developing spermatocytes, where it plays a critical role in glycolysis, ATP generation, and sperm motility. GAPDHS shares 70% amino acid sequence homology with its somatic counterpart GAPDH, and biochemical assays suggest these differences endow GAPDHS with enhanced protein stability and increased catalytic efficiency.

nodes.name: Ferroxidases
nodes.description: This group contains families of genes associated with ferroxidase activity (EC 1.16.3.1).

nodes.name: Ferritin ferroxidases
nodes.description: The catalytic activity of ferritin is associated with the presence of a dinuclear A and B metal-binding site in each heavy subunit but not in the light subunits. This di-iron center called the 'ferroxidase center' plays a critical role particularly during the early stages of iron oxidation and mineralization in ferritin.

nodes.name: Thioredoxin reductase family
nodes.description: Mammalian thioredoxin reductases are selenium-containing flavoprotein oxidoreductases, dependent upon a selenocysteine residue for reduction of the active site disulfide in thioredoxins. Their activity is required for normal thioredoxin function. The mammalian thioredoxin reductases also display surprisingly multifaceted properties and functions beyond thioredoxin reduction. Expressed from three separate genes (in human named TXNRD1, TXNRD2 and TXNRD3), the thioredoxin reductases can each reduce a number of different types of substrates in different cellular compartments. Their expression patterns involve intriguingly complex transcriptional mechanisms resulting in several splice variants, encoding a number of protein variants likely to have specialized functions in a cell- and tissue-type restricted manner. The thioredoxin reductases are also targeted by a number of drugs and compounds having an impact on cell function and promoting oxidative stress, some of which are used in treatment of rheumatoid arthritis, cancer or other diseases.

nodes.name: Polyamine oxidases
nodes.description: The polyamine oxidases, SMOX (EC 1.5.3.16) and PAOX (EC 1.5.3.13), are enzymes involved in the normal metabolism of polyamines. Both enzymes are implicated in numerous human diseases including cancer, reperfusion injury, and neurodegenerative diseases.

nodes.name: Prenylcysteine oxidase family
nodes.description: Prenylcysteine oxidases (PCYOXs) metabolize prenylated cysteines produced by protein degradation. They utilize oxygen as a co-substrate to produce free cysteine, an aldehyde, and hydrogen peroxide through the unusual oxidation of a thioether bond. A gene duplication event in jawed vertebrates gave rise to the PCYOX paralogs (PCYOX1 and PCYOX1L). Both enzymes are active on farnesyl- and geranylgeranylcysteine, but inactive on molecules with shorter prenyl groups. Kinetics experiments outline a mechanism where flavin reduction and re-oxidation occur rapidly without any detectable intermediates, with the overall reaction rate limited by product release.

nodes.name: Quinone dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: Quinone reductases 1 and 2 (NQO1 and NQO2) are paralogous FAD-linked enzymes found in all amniotes. NQO1 and NQO2 have similar structures, and both catalyze the reduction of quinones and other electrophiles; however, the two enzymes differ in their cosubstrate preference. While NQO1 can use both redox couples NADH and NADPH, NQO2 is almost inactive with these cosubstrates and instead must use dihydronicotinamide riboside (NRH) and small synthetic cosubstrates such as N-benzyl-dihydronicotinamide (BNAH) for efficient catalysis.

nodes.name: Malic enzyme family
nodes.description: The malic enzyme (ME) family catalyzes the oxidative decarboxylation of malate to pyruvate with the concomitant reduction of NAD+ or NADP+, thereby linking TCA cycle flux, mitochondrial pyruvate supply, and redox balance. In mammals, three ME isoforms (ME1, ME2, and ME3) differ in subcellular localization, cofactor preference, and regulatory properties, enabling malate metabolism to be tuned to distinct cellular compartments and metabolic states. Dysregulation of ME activity has been implicated in a range of metabolic conditions, including altered redox homeostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, and proliferative diseases like cancer.

nodes.name: Pyruvate dehydrogenase E1 subunits
nodes.description: The E1 component of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (PDC) is the component with pyruvate dehydrogenase activity. In mammals it is a heterotetramer of two alpha and two beta subunits. The alpha subunits are encoded by two closely related genes PDHA1 and PDHA2; PDHA1 encodes the alpah subunit found in somatic complexes whereas PDHA2 encodes a testis specific isoform. The beta subunit is encoded by a single gene, PDHB.

nodes.name: Proline dehydrogenase family
nodes.description: The first step of proline catabolism is catalyzed by proline dehydrogenase (PRODH also known as proline oxidase, POX). PRODH oxidizes proline to P5C using flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) as the electron accepting coenzyme (reductive half-reaction). The reduced FAD produced through this reaction is re-oxidized via reduction of CoQ in the oxidative half-reaction catalyzed by PRODH. These reactions are carried out in the mitochondria where PRODH is localized to the inner mitochondrial membrane with access to CoQ of the respiratory chain. There are two isoforms of human PRODH: PRODH1 (encoded by PRODH) and PRODH2. PRODH1 is selective for L-proline, whereas PRODH2 is selective for trans-4-hydroxy-L-proline, with PRODH1 forming P5C and PRODH2 forming L-Δ1-pyrroline-3-hydroxy-5-carboxylate.

nodes.name: MTHFD family
nodes.description: The MTHFD gene family comprises four closely related genes (MTHFD1, MTHFD1L, MTHFD2 and MTHFD2L) that catalyse key steps of folate-mediated one-carbon (1C) metabolism. They interconvert different folate-bound one-carbon molecules, thereby supplying carbon units for nucleotide synthesis, amino-acid metabolism and methylation. MTHFD1 is a trifunctional cytosolic enzyme with methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase, cyclohydrolase and formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase activities. In mitochondria these activities are split between MTHFD1L, which has only formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase activity, and the dual function enzymes MTHFD2/MTHFD2L which have both methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase and cyclohydrolase activities.

nodes.name: Copper-dependent amine oxidases
nodes.description: Copper amine oxidases are a class of enzymes that contain Cu2+ and a tyrosine-derived quinone cofactor, catalyze the conversion of a primary amine functional group to an aldehyde, and generate hydrogen peroxide and ammonia as byproducts. These enzymes can be classified into two non-homologous families: 2,4,5-trihydroxyphenylalanine quinone (TPQ)-dependent CAOs and the lysine tyrosylquinone (LTQ)-dependent lysyl oxidase (LOX) family of proteins.

nodes.name: Methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases
nodes.description: Methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenases are encoded by MTHFD1, MTHFD2 and MTHFD2L. MTHFD1 activity is NADP dependent (EC 1.5.1.5) whereas MTHFD2 activity is NAD dependent (EC 1.5.1.15). MTHFD2L is predicted to have both NAD and NADP dependent activities based on similarity to rodents.

nodes.name: Ankyrin family
nodes.description: Ankyrins are membrane-associated scaffolding proteins widely expressed in various tissues and cell types throughout the body including neurons, glial cells, erythrocytes, cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle cells, and epithelial cells. The ankyrin family consists of ANK1 (Ankyrin-R, AnkR), ANK2 (Ankyrin-B, AnkB), and ANK3 (Ankyrin-G, AnkG). Ankyrins connect the submembranous spectrin-based cytoskeleton to the cytoplasmic domain of diverse transmembrane proteins including ion channels, transporters, and cell adhesion molecules. Ankyrins are also critical for membrane organization as they facilitate the recruitment, stabilization, and maintenance of ion channels, transporters, signaling proteins and other membrane proteins to precise subcellular domains. The importance of ankyrins is highlighted by the fact that disruptions to ANK1-3 cause or are strongly associated with several diseases and disorders, including hereditary spherocytosis, cardiac arrhythmia, Alzheimer's disease, schizophrenia, autism spectrum disorders, and bipolar disorder

nodes.name: TATA-box binding protein family
nodes.description: The assembly of transcription complexes on eukaryotic promoters involves a series of steps, including chromatin remodeling, recruitment of TATA-binding protein (TBP)-containing complexes, the RNA polymerase II holoenzyme, and additional basal transcription factors. This review describes the transcriptional regulation by TBP and its corresponding homologs that constitute the TBP family and their interactions with promoter DNA. The C-terminal core domain of TBP is highly conserved and contains two structural repeats that fold into a saddle-like structure, essential for the interaction with the TATA-box on DNA. Based on the TBP C-terminal core domain similarity, two TBP-like factors (TBPLs) have been discovered in mammals, TBPL1, and TBPL2. TBP is autoregulated, and once bound to DNA, repressors such as BTAF1 (Mot1) induce TBP to dissociate, while other factors such as NC2 and the NOT complex convert the active TBP/DNA complex into inactive, negatively regulating TBP. TFIIA antagonizes the TBP repressors but may be effective only in conjunction with the RNA polymerase II holoenzyme recruitment to the promoter by promoter-bound activators. TBPL1 cannot bind to the TATA-box; instead, TBPL1 prefers binding to TATA-less promoters. However, TBPL1 shows a stronger association with TFIIA than TBP. The TCT core promoter element is present in most ribosomal protein genes in Drosophila and humans, and TBPL1 is required for the transcription of these genes. TBPL2 is closely related to its TBP paralog, showing 95% sequence similarity with the TBP core domain. Like TBP, TBPL2 also binds to the TATA-box and shows interactions with TFIIA, TFIIB, and other basal transcription factors.

nodes.name: IQ motif containing F family
nodes.description: The IQ motif containing F family are a set of paralogs that show enriched expression in testis. IQCF1 is an acrosomal protein involved in tyrosine phosphorylation of sperm proteins through interaction with calmodulin.

nodes.name: Tectonin beta-propeller repeat containing
nodes.description: This group contains genes that encode proteins containing beta-propeller repeats similar to those found in Physarum polycephalum (Slime mold) tectonin I and II, the two dominant proteins in the nuclei and nuclear matrix.

nodes.name: Motile sperm domain containing
nodes.description: The Motile sperm domain (also known as Major sperm protein (MSP) domain, InterPro: IPR000535) is found in 6 human proteins. Five of these act as ER-localized tether proteins. VAPA, VAPB, and MOSPD2 have an MSP domain exposed to the cytosol; this domain hooks proteins that possess a small linear motif named FFAT (two phenylalanines in an acidic tract). MOSPD1 and MOSPD3 are paralogs and encode an MSP domain that recognizes FFNT (two phenylalanines in a neutral tract) motifs. The final gene encoding an MSP, CFAP65 is involved in ciliogenesis.

nodes.name: HORMA domain containing
nodes.description: The HORMA domain (named for the yeast genes HOP1, REV7 and MAD2) is an about 180-240 amino acids region containing several conserved motifs. It has been suggested that the HORMA domain recognises chromatin states that result from DNA adducts, double-stranded breaks or non-attachment to the spindle and acts as an adaptor that recruits other proteins involved in repair. The four human genes that encode HORMA domains are HORMAD1, HORMAD2 (orthologs of HOP1), MAD2L1 (ortholog of MAD2) and MAD2L2 (ortholog of REV7).

nodes.name: EVA1 family
nodes.description: The paralogs EVA1A, EVA1B and EVA1C were named based on homology to the C. elegans gene eva-1, a SLIT receptor subunit that is required for axon guidance. The EVA1C protein (441aa) is most similar to eva-1 (461aa); based of expression studies in mouse, EVA1C is likely have a conserved role in axon guidance. The N-terminal regions of EVA1A and EVA1B are truncated relative to EVA1C resulting in significantly shorter proteins of 152aa and 165aa respectively. EVA1A is reported to be regulator of programmed cell death, mediating both autophagy and apoptosis.

nodes.name: Sigma receptors
nodes.description: Sigma-1 and sigma-2 receptors σ1R (approved symbol: SIGMAR1) and σ2R (approved symbol: TMEM97) are molecularly and functionally distinct proteins that regulate neuronal excitability, proteostasis, and neuroimmune communication, all mechanisms that characterize neuronal excitability and cellular stress adaptation. σ1R acts as a ligand-operated molecular chaperone at the mitochondria-associated endoplasmic reticulum membrane. σ2R, identified as transmembrane protein 97 (σ2R/TMEM97), functions as a regulator of cholesterol trafficking, lysosomal integrity, and integrated stress response (ISR).

nodes.name: Ligases
nodes.description: Genes encoding Ligases (EC 6.-.-.-). Note that this grouping does not include ubiquitin-protein ligases as they are classed as transferases (EC class 2,), rather than ligases (EC class 6), in the current Enzyme Commission (EC) classification.

nodes.name: Adenylosuccinate synthase family
nodes.description: Adenylosuccinate synthetase (AdSS, IMP: L-aspartate ligase (GDP-forming), EC 6.3.4.4) catalyzes the first committed step in de novo biosyntheses of AMP. In vertebrates the synthetase is also a component of the purine nucleotide cycle, which interconverts IMP and AMP. Vertebrates have muscle (ADSS1) and non-muscle isozymes of adenylosuccinate synthetase (ADSS2).

nodes.name: Carbamoyl-phosphate synthetases
nodes.description: There are two human genes that encode carbamoyl-phosphate synthetase activity (EC 6.3.4.16). It is one of three activities encoded by the multifunctional cytosolic enzyme CAD (CPS2) that functions in de novo pyrimidine synthesis. CPS1 is a mitochondrial enzyme that functions in the urea cycle.

nodes.name: Glutamate-cysteine ligase subunits
nodes.description: The first and rate-limiting step in glutathione (GSH) synthesis is catalyzed by glutamate cysteine ligase (GCL, previously known as gamma-glutamylcysteine synthetase). GCL is a heterodimeric protein composed of catalytic (GCLC) and modifier (GCLM) subunits that are expressed from different genes. GCLC catalyzes a unique gamma-carboxyl linkage from glutamate to cysteine and requires ATP and Mg(++) as cofactors in this reaction. GCLM increases the V(max) and K(cat) of GCLC, decreases the K(m) for glutamate and ATP, and increases the K(i) for GSH-mediated feedback inhibition of GCL.

nodes.name: Formyltetrahydrofolate synthetases
nodes.description: There are two human genes that encode formyltetrahydrofolate synthetase activity (EC 6.3.4.3). It is one of three activities encoded by the cytosolic enzyme MTHFD1. MTHFD1L is a mitochondrial enzyme with only this activity.

nodes.name: RNA ligases
nodes.description: There are only two identified proteins that catalyse RNA ligation in human cells, namely RTCB, which catalyses 3′–5′ RNA ligation (EC 6.5.1.8) and RLIG1, which catalyses 5′–3′ RNA ligation (EC 6.5.1.3).

nodes.name: CTP synthase family
nodes.description: CTP synthetase (EC 6.3.4.2, UTP:ammonia ligase (ADP-forming)) is an essential enzyme in all organisms; it generates the CTP required for the synthesis of nucleic acids and membrane phospholipids. The two human genes encoding CTP synthetase, CTPS1 and CTPS2, share 75% amino acid identity.

nodes.name: Asparagine synthase family
nodes.description: ASNS is the canonical, well-characterized human glutamine-dependent asparagine synthase (EC 6.3.5.4). ASNSD1 is a related human protein sharing both the N-terminal Glutamine amidotransferase type 2 domain (IPR017932) and C-terminal Asparagine synthase domain (IPR001962) with ASNS but whose enzymatic and physiological role remains unclear.

nodes.name: Mastermind like transcriptional coactivator family
nodes.description: There are three human homologs of the Drosophila mastermind gene (MAML1-3). All of the proteins contain an N-terminal basic domain and two acidic domains (N- and C-terminal). The three human proteins show remarkable similarities in their functions while having unusual structural diversity. Each can act as coactivators in NOTCH transcription activation complexes.

nodes.name: Odd-skipped related transcription factor family
nodes.description: Odd-skipped genes encode zinc-finger transcription factors with widespread roles in embryonic development. In Drosophila, odd-skipped acts as a pair-rule gene, while its orthologous gene in Caenorhabditis elegans is involved in gut development. In human two paralogs exist, OSR1 and OSR2. The mouse genes Osr1 and Osr2 have reported functions in heart and urogenital, and in secondary palate development, respectively.

nodes.name: Sterol regulatory element binding transcription factor family
nodes.description: Sterol regulatory element binding transcrition factor 1 (SREBP1) and SREBP2 are structurally related proteins that control cholesterol homeostasis by stimulating transcription of sterol-regulated genes, including those encoding the low-density lipoprotein (LDL) receptor and 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl CoA synthase. SREBP1 and SREBP2 are 47% identical, and they share a novel structure comprising a transcriptionally active NH2-terminal basic helix-loop-helix-leucine zipper (bHLH-Zip) domain followed by a membrane attachment domain. Cleavage by a sterol-regulated protease frees the bHLH-Zip domain from the membrane and allows it to enter the nucleus.

nodes.name: Heat shock transcription factor family
nodes.description: Heat shock factors (HSFs) are a highly conserved family of transcription factors (TFs) within the winged–alpha–helix family that drive gene expression programs that maintain protein homeostasis (proteostasis) in response to intrinsic and extrinsic stressors.

nodes.name: EVI5 family
nodes.description: Ecotopic viral integration site 5 (EVI5) and ecotopic viral integration site 5 like (EVI5L) belong to a small subfamily of the Tre-2/Bub2/Cdc16 (TBC) domain-containing proteins with enigmatically divergent roles as modulators of cell cycle progression, cytokinesis, and cellular membrane traffic. First recognized as a potential oncogene and a cell cycle regulator, Evi5 acts as a GTPase Activating Protein (GAP) for RAB11 in cytokinesis. On the other hand, its homologue EVI5L has Rab-GAP activity towards RAB10 as well as RAB23, and has been implicated in primary cilia formation.

nodes.name: Thioester hydrolases
nodes.description: Genes associated with EC 3.1.2.x numbers. These genes encode enzymes that hydrolyse thioester bonds.

nodes.name: Acyltransferases
nodes.description: These genes encode enzymes with carbon-carbon lyase activities (EC 2.3.-.-).

nodes.name: GABA type A receptor-associated protein family
Microtubule associated protein 1 light chain 3 family
Carbon-carbon lyases
nodes.description: These genes encode enzymes with carbon-carbon lyase activities (EC 4.1.-.-).

nodes.name: Aldehyde lyases
nodes.description: These genes encode enzymes with aldehyde lyase activities (EC 4.1.2.-).

nodes.name: tRNA-yW synthesizing protein 1 homologs
nodes.description: Based on homology to the S. cerevisiae gene TYW1, the human paralogs TYW1 and TYW1B are predicted to be radical S-adenosyl-l-methionine (SAM) enzymes that catalyze the condensation of pyruvate and N-methylguanosine-containing tRNA-Phe, forming 4-demethylwyosine-containing tRNA-Phe.

nodes.name: Oxo-acid lyases
nodes.description: These genes encode enzymes with oxo-acid lyase activities (EC 4.1.3.-).

nodes.name: Phosphoribosyltransferases
nodes.description: Phosphoribosyltransferase (PRTase) enzymes carry out phosphoryl transfer reactions on 5-phosphoribosyl-α1-pyrophosphate (PRPP), an activated form of ribose-5-phosphate. Type I PRTases (HPRT, APRT, PPAT, UMPS) include a 13-residue sequence PRT motif that consists of four hydrophobic amino acids, two acidic amino acids and seven amino acids of variable character, usually including glycine and threonine. The motif is a PRPP-binding site and is only found in PRTases from the nucleotide synthesis and salvage pathways. Other PRTases lack the PRT sequence motif and appear to be unrelated to each other and unrelated to the type I PRTases.

nodes.name: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase family
nodes.description: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase (PRPS) is an enzyme conserved across all forms of life, tracing back to the last universal common ancestor. PRPS catalyzes the rate-limiting step in converting ribose-5-phosphate (R5P) to phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP), a crucial precursor in the biosynthesis of nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids. Mammals exclusively possess three Class I PRPS isozymes–PRPS1, PRPS2, and PRPS3, which form a heteromeric complex with two additional homologs–PRPS associated protein 1 (PRPSAP1) and PRPS associated protein 2 (PRPSAP2).

nodes.name: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase complex
nodes.description: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase (PRPS) is an enzyme conserved across all forms of life, tracing back to the last universal common ancestor. PRPS catalyzes the rate-limiting step in converting ribose-5-phosphate (R5P) to phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate (PRPP), a crucial precursor in the biosynthesis of nucleotides, amino acids, and lipids. Mammals exclusively possess three Class I PRPS isozymes–PRPS1, PRPS2, and PRPS3, which form a heteromeric complex with two additional homologs–PRPS associated protein 1 (PRPSAP1) and PRPS associated protein 2 (PRPSAP2).

nodes.name: Phosphoribosyl pyrophosphate synthetase associated protein family
Hypoxia inducible factor subunits
nodes.description: The chronic response to hypoxia (limited oxygen availability) in humans and other animals is substantially mediated by hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) transcription factors. HIF-alpha protein levels are increased in hypoxia; it travels to the nucleus, dimerises with HIF-beta and binds to hypoxia response elements (HREs) in the promoter regions of HIF target genes. Active Hypoxia inducible transcription factors (HIFs) are comprised of an oxygen-regulated alpha-subunit and a constitutive beta-subunit. In humans there are three HIF-alpha isoforms, of which HIF1A and HIF2A are the best characterised; together with the HIF beta subunit (encoded by ARNT) they form active transcription factors termed HIF-1 and HIF-2, respectively. HIF-1 and HIF-2 are closely related, but upregulate distinct (and sometimes overlapping) sets of genes in hypoxia. HIF alpha- and beta-subunits belong to the bHLH/PAS (basic helix-loop-helix/Per-ARNT-Sim homology) family of transcription factors. The bHLH and PAS domains mediate alpha,beta-dimerisation and DNA binding, while N- and C-terminal transcriptional activation domains (NAD and CAD, respectively) recruit coactivator proteins to form active transcriptional complexes on DNA. HIF alpha-subunits also contain an oxygen-dependent degradation (ODD) domain, the hydroxylation of which renders them labile in oxygenated conditions.

nodes.name: Inorganic pyrophosphatase family
nodes.description: Inorganic pyrophosphate (PPi, also termed diphosphate) is formed by several important nucleotide triphosphate-dependent reactions necessary for DNA, RNA, protein, and lipid synthesis. Pyrophosphate has to be hydrolyzed to orthophosphate (Pi). An enzyme that catalyzes this reaction is termed inorganic pyrophosphatase (PPA [EC 3.6.1.1]) and provides Pi for biomolecules via synthesis of ATP, the terminal product of cellular energy metabolism. PPAs are found in all kingdoms of life. Type I enzymes present in Escherichia coli and eukaryotes depend on divalent ions, preferably Mg2+ ions. Humans, similar to the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae, have two PPAs that share sequence homology. These comprise a cytoplasmic soluble PPA1 and a mitochondrial-located PPA2.

nodes.name: PRUNE family
nodes.description: PRUNE1 and PRUNE2 are both homologs of the Drosophila gene prune. PRUNE1 is a relatively small DHH-family phosphoesterase/exopolyphosphatase, whereas PRUNE2 is a very large multidomain protein that contains an N-terminal PRUNE1-like/DHH region plus a large C-terminal region containing a BCH (BNIP2/Cdc42GAP homology) domain.

nodes.name: Cysteine endopeptidases
nodes.description: These genes encode cysteine endopeptidases (EC 3.4.22.-)

nodes.name: 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA synthase family
nodes.description: Hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA synthase (HMGCS) is a key enzyme converting acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA into HMG-CoA, an intermediate in both sterol synthesis and ketogenesis. There are at least two isoenzymes of HMGCS (EC 2.3.3.10) encoded by two different genes. HMGCS1 is located in cytoplasm and participates in sterol biosynthesis. HMGCS2 functions as a key enzyme for ketogenesis and is located in the mitochondrial matrix.

nodes.name: Saposin B type domain containing
nodes.description: The saposin B-type domain is a ~80 amino acid domain present in saposins and related proteins that interact with lipids. The domain is named after the small lysosomal proteins, saposins, which serve as sphingolipid hydrolase activator proteins in vertebrates. The mammalian saposins are synthesized as a single precursor molecule (prosaposin) which contains two saposin A-type domains in the extremities that are removed in the activation reaction, and four saposin B-type domains yielding the active saposins A, B, C and D after proteolytic cleavage. Saposin-like proteins (SAPLIPs) can have different functions, such as enzymatic activities, as cofactors of enzymes involved in lipid metabolism, as components of lung surfactant reducing the surface tension, as part of a complex involved in stage regulation of Dictyostelium, as antimicrobial effector molecules, or as a stimulator of dendritic outgrowth.

nodes.name: ATP-sensitive potassium channel subunits
nodes.description: The ATP-sensitive potassium (KATP) channel is a large hetero-octameric protein complex comprising four regulatory and four pore-forming subunits. Sulfonylurea receptor (SUR) 1 and 2 constitute the regulatory subunits of the channel and are encoded by the ABCC8 and ABCC9 genes, respectively. The inwardly rectifying potassium channel (Kir) subunits 6.1 and 6.2 form the pore and are encoded by the KCNJ8 and KCNJ11 genes, respectively.  The KATP channel directly regulates microglial activity and is a major component of the inflammatory response following CNS injury. First detected in cardiomyocytes, the KATP channel is also expressed by other cell types such as pancreatic beta-cells and neurons from various brain regions, where it controls important cellular processes by coupling the electrical activity of the cell to its energy availability.

nodes.name: SH3 domain containing ring finger family
Basic leucine zipper and W2 domains family
nodes.description: The efficiency of start codon selection during ribosomal scanning in eukaryotic translation initiation is influenced by the context or flanking nucleotides surrounding the AUG codon. The levels of eukaryotic translation initiation factors 1 (eIF1) and 5 (eIF5) play critical roles in controlling the stringency of translation start site selection. The basic leucine zipper and W2 domain-containing proteins 1 and 2 (BZW1 and BZW2), also known as eIF5-mimic proteins, are paralogous human proteins containing C-terminal HEAT domains that resemble the HEAT domain of eIF5.

nodes.name: RING finger E3 ubiquitin protein ligases
Degenerate RING E3 ubiquitin ligases
nodes.description: The term degenerate RING (dRING) is used for non-conventional RING domain-containing proteins with altered zinc coordination and/or structural deviation from the canonical RING cross-brace fold, which may nevertheless retain E3 activity.

nodes.name: SEA domain containing
nodes.description: SEA domains are commonly found in highly glycosylated, membrane-attached extracellular matrix proteins. SEA domains are generally 120–150 amino acids long and are rich in serine, threonine, and proline residues. Structurally, they are defined by their distinctive globular shape, composed of four alpha helices and four beta sheets. This structure provides a stable yet flexible framework, enabling interactions with a variety of biomolecules, a feature that is critical for the domain autoproteolytic activity.
